SigLIP — Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) is a technique for training a pair of neural network models, one for image understanding and one for text understanding, using a contrastive objective.
SigLIP — This method has enabled broad applications across multiple domains, including cross-modal retrieval, text-to-image generation, and aesthetic ranking.
SigLIP — One model takes in a piece of text as input and outputs a single vector representing its semantic content.
SigLIP — The other model takes in an image and similarly outputs a single vector representing its visual content.
SigLIP — The models are trained so that the vectors corresponding to semantically similar text-image pairs are close together in the shared vector space, while those corresponding to dissimilar pairs are far apart.
SigLIP — To train a pair of CLIP models, one would start by preparing a large dataset of image-caption pairs.
SigLIP — During training, the models are presented with batches of N {\displaystyle N} image-caption pairs.
SigLIP — Let the outputs from the text and image models be respectively v 1 , . . . , v N , w 1 , . . . , w N {\displaystyle v_{1},...,v_{N},w_{1},...,w_{N}} .
SigLIP — The loss incurred on this batch is the multi-class N-pair loss, which is a symmetric cross-entropy loss over similarity scores: − 1 N ∑ i ln ⁡ e v i ⋅ w i / T ∑ j e v i ⋅ w j / T − 1 N ∑ j ln ⁡ e v j ⋅ w j / T ∑ i e v i ⋅ w j / T {\displaystyle -{\frac {1}{N}}\sum _{i}\ln {\frac {e^{v_{i}\cdot w_{i}/T}}{\sum _{j}e^{v_{i}\cdot w_{j}/T}}}-{\frac {1}{N}}\sum _{j}\ln {\frac {e^{v_{j}\cdot w_{j}/T}}{\sum _{i}e^{v_{i}\cdot w_{j}/T}}}} In essence, this loss function encourages the dot product between matching image and text vectors ( v i ⋅ w i {\displaystyle v_{i}\cdot w_{i}} ) to be high, while discouraging high dot products between non-matching pairs.
SigLIP — The parameter T > 0 {\displaystyle T>0} is the temperature, which is parameterized in the original CLIP model as T = e − τ {\displaystyle T=e^{-\tau }} where τ ∈ R {\displaystyle \tau \in \mathbb {R} } is a learned parameter.
SigLIP — For example, Sigmoid CLIP (SigLIP) proposes the following loss function: L = 1 N ∑ i , j ∈ 1 : N f ( ( 2 δ i , j − 1 ) ( e τ w i ⋅ v j + b ) ) {\displaystyle L={\frac {1}{N}}\sum _{i,j\in 1:N}f((2\delta _{i,j}-1)(e^{\tau }w_{i}\cdot v_{j}+b))} where f ( x ) = ln ⁡ ( 1 + e − x ) {\displaystyle f(x)=\ln(1+e^{-x})} is the negative log sigmoid loss, and the Dirac delta symbol δ i , j {\displaystyle \delta _{i,j}} is 1 if i = j {\displaystyle i=j} else 0.
SigLIP — == CLIP models == While the original model was developed by OpenAI, subsequent models have been trained by other organizations as well.
SigLIP — The naming convention for these models often reflects the specific ViT architecture used.
SigLIP — For instance, "ViT-L/14" means a "vision transformer large" (compared to other models in the same series) with a patch size of 14, meaning that the image is divided into 14-by-14 pixel patches before being processed by the transformer.
SigLIP — The size indicator ranges from B, L, H, G (base, large, huge, giant), in that order.
SigLIP — Other than ViT, the image model is typically a convolutional neural network, such as ResNet (in the original series by OpenAI), or ConvNeXt (in the OpenCLIP model series by LAION).
SigLIP — Since the output vectors of the image model and the text model must have exactly the same length, both the image model and the text model have fixed-length vector outputs, which in the original report is called "embedding dimension".
SigLIP — For example, in the original OpenAI model, the ResNet models have embedding dimensions ranging from 512 to 1024, and for the ViTs, from 512 to 768.
SigLIP — Its implementation of ViT was the same as the original one, with one modification: after position embeddings are added to the initial patch embeddings, there is a LayerNorm.
SigLIP — Its implementation of ResNet was the same as the original one, with 3 modifications:
SigLIP — In the start of the CNN (the "stem"), they used three stacked 3x3 convolutions instead of a single 7x7 convolution, as suggested by.
SigLIP — There is an average pooling of stride 2 at the start of each downsampling convolutional layer (they called it rect-2 blur pooling according to the terminology of ).
SigLIP — ALIGN a model with similar capabilities, trained by researchers from Google used EfficientNet, a kind of convolutional neural network.
SigLIP — In the original OpenAI report, they reported using a Transformer (63M-parameter, 12-layer, 512-wide, 8 attention heads) with lower-cased byte pair encoding (BPE) with 49152 vocabulary size.
SigLIP — Like BERT, the text sequence is bracketed by two special tokens [SOS] and [EOS] ("start of sequence" and "end of sequence").
SigLIP — Take the activations of the highest layer of the transformer on the [EOS], apply LayerNorm, then a final linear map.
SigLIP — The final linear map has output dimension equal to the embedding dimension of whatever image encoder it is paired with.
SigLIP — === WebImageText === The CLIP models released by OpenAI were trained on a dataset called "WebImageText" (WIT) containing 400 million pairs of images and their corresponding captions scraped from the internet.
SigLIP — The total number of words in this dataset is similar in scale to the WebText dataset used for training GPT-2, which contains about 40 gigabytes of text data.
SigLIP — The dataset contains 500,000 text-queries, with up to 20,000 (image, text) pairs per query.
SigLIP — The text-queries were generated by starting with all words occurring at least 100 times in English Wikipedia, then extended by bigrams with high mutual information, names of all Wikipedia articles above a certain search volume, and WordNet synsets.
SigLIP — The dataset is private and has not been released to the public, and there is no further information on it.
SigLIP — ==== Data preprocessing ==== For the CLIP image models, the input images are preprocessed by first dividing each of the R, G, B values of an image by the maximum possible value, so that these values fall between 0 and 1, then subtracting by [0.48145466, 0.4578275, 0.40821073], and dividing by [0.26862954, 0.26130258, 0.27577711].
SigLIP — The rationale was that these are the mean and standard deviations of the images in the WebImageText dataset, so this preprocessing step roughly whitens the image tensor.
SigLIP — These numbers slightly differ from the standard preprocessing for ImageNet, which uses [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and [0.229, 0.224, 0.225].
SigLIP — If the input image does not have the same resolution as the native resolution (224×224 for all except ViT-L/14@336px, which has 336×336 resolution), then the input image is scaled down by bicubic interpolation, so that its shorter side is the same as the native resolution, then the central square of the image is cropped out.
SigLIP — === Others === ALIGN used over one billion image-text pairs, obtained by extracting images and their alt-tags from online crawling.
SigLIP — The method was described as similar to how the Conceptual Captions dataset was constructed, but instead of complex filtering, they only applied a frequency-based filtering.
SigLIP — For example, LAION trained OpenCLIP with published datasets LAION-400M, LAION-2B, and DataComp-1B.
SigLIP — == Training == In the original OpenAI CLIP report, they reported training 5 ResNet and 3 ViT (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14).
SigLIP — The ViT-L/14 was then boosted to 336×336 resolution by FixRes, resulting in a model.
SigLIP — In the OpenCLIP series, the ViT-L/14 model was trained on 384 A100 GPUs on the LAION-2B dataset, for 160 epochs for a total of 32B samples seen.
SigLIP — === Cross-modal retrieval === CLIP's cross-modal retrieval enables the alignment of visual and textual data in a shared latent space, allowing users to retrieve images based on text descriptions and vice versa, without the need for explicit image annotations.
SigLIP — In text-to-image retrieval, users input descriptive text, and CLIP retrieves images with matching embeddings.
SigLIP — CLIP’s ability to connect visual and textual data has found applications in multimedia search, content discovery, and recommendation systems.
SigLIP — === Image classification === CLIP can perform zero-shot image classification tasks.
SigLIP — This is achieved by prompting the text encoder with class names and selecting the class whose embedding is closest to the image embedding.
SigLIP — For example, to classify an image, they compared the embedding of the image with the embedding of the text "A photo of a {class}.", and the {class} that results in the highest dot product is outputted.
SigLIP — === CLIP for multimodal learning === CLIP has been used as a component in multimodal learning.
SigLIP — For example, during the training of Google DeepMind's Flamingo (2022), the authors trained a CLIP pair, with BERT as the text encoder and NormalizerFree ResNet F6 as the image encoder.
SigLIP — The image encoder of the CLIP pair was taken with parameters frozen and the text encoder was discarded.
SigLIP — The frozen image encoder was then combined with a frozen Chinchilla language model, by finetuning with some further parameters that connect the two frozen models.
SigLIP — === Applications in other domains === CLIP's image encoder is a pre-trained image featurizer.
SigLIP — Models like Stable Diffusion use CLIP's text encoder to transform text prompts into embeddings for image generation.
SigLIP — CLIP can also be used as a gradient signal for directly guiding diffusion ("CLIP guidance") or other generative art.
SigLIP — Fine-tuned CLIP models can be used to rank images by aesthetic quality, which may be useful as a step in filtering a large dataset into a smaller one with higher quality.
SigLIP — CLIP can be used to generate image captions by matching text inputs to image embeddings.

Generative model — In statistical classification, two main approaches are called the generative approach and the discriminative approach.
Generative model — These compute classifiers by different approaches, differing in the degree of statistical modelling.
Generative model — A generative model is a statistical model of the joint probability distribution P ( X , Y ) {\displaystyle P(X,Y)} on a given observable variable X and target variable Y; A generative model can be used to "generate" random instances (outcomes) of an observation x.
Generative model — A discriminative model is a model of the conditional probability P ( Y ∣ X = x ) {\displaystyle P(Y\mid X=x)} of the target Y, given an observation x.
Generative model — It can be used to "discriminate" the value of the target variable Y, given an observation x.
Generative model — Classifiers computed without using a probability model are also referred to loosely as "discriminative".
Generative model — The distinction between these last two classes is not consistently made; Jebara (2004) refers to these three classes as generative learning, conditional learning, and discriminative learning, but Ng & Jordan (2002) only distinguish two classes, calling them generative classifiers (joint distribution) and discriminative classifiers (conditional distribution or no distribution), not distinguishing between the latter two classes.
Generative model — Analogously, a classifier based on a generative model is a generative classifier, while a classifier based on a discriminative model is a discriminative classifier, though this term also refers to classifiers that are not based on a model.
Generative model — generative classifiers: naive Bayes classifier and linear discriminant analysis discriminative model: logistic regression In application to classification, one wishes to go from an observation x to a label y (or probability distribution on labels).
Generative model — One can compute this directly, without using a probability distribution (distribution-free classifier); one can estimate the probability of a label given an observation, P ( Y | X = x ) {\displaystyle P(Y|X=x)} (discriminative model), and base classification on that; or one can estimate the joint distribution P ( X , Y ) {\displaystyle P(X,Y)} (generative model), from that compute the conditional probability P ( Y | X = x ) {\displaystyle P(Y|X=x)} , and then base classification on that.
Generative model — These are increasingly indirect, but increasingly probabilistic, allowing more domain knowledge and probability theory to be applied.
Generative model — In practice different approaches are used, depending on the particular problem, and hybrids can combine strengths of multiple approaches.
Generative model — a generative model is a model of the conditional probability of the observable X, given a target y, symbolically, P ( X ∣ Y = y ) {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y=y)}
Generative model — a discriminative model is a model of the conditional probability of the target Y, given an observation x, symbolically, P ( Y ∣ X = x ) {\displaystyle P(Y\mid X=x)}
Generative model — Regardless of precise definition, the terminology is constitutional because a generative model can be used to "generate" random instances (outcomes), either of an observation and target ( x , y ) {\displaystyle (x,y)} , or of an observation x given a target value y, while a discriminative model or discriminative classifier (without a model) can be used to "discriminate" the value of the target variable Y, given an observation x.
Generative model — The difference between "discriminate" (distinguish) and "classify" is subtle, and these are not consistently distinguished. (The term "discriminative classifier" becomes a pleonasm when "discrimination" is equivalent to "classification".) The term "generative model" is also used to describe models that generate instances of output variables in a way that has no clear relationship to probability distributions over potential samples of input variables.
Generative model — Generative adversarial networks are examples of this class of generative models, and are judged primarily by the similarity of particular outputs to potential inputs.
Generative model — === Relationships between models === In application to classification, the observable X is frequently a continuous variable, the target Y is generally a discrete variable consisting of a finite set of labels, and the conditional probability P ( Y ∣ X ) {\displaystyle P(Y\mid X)} can also be interpreted as a (non-deterministic) target function f : X → Y {\displaystyle f\colon X\to Y} , considering X as inputs and Y as outputs.
Generative model — Given a finite set of labels, the two definitions of "generative model" are closely related.
Generative model — A model of the conditional distribution P ( X ∣ Y = y ) {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y=y)} is a model of the distribution of each label, and a model of the joint distribution is equivalent to a model of the distribution of label values P ( Y ) {\displaystyle P(Y)} , together with the distribution of observations given a label, P ( X ∣ Y ) {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y)} ; symbolically, P ( X , Y ) = P ( X ∣ Y ) P ( Y ) . {\displaystyle P(X,Y)=P(X\mid Y)P(Y).} Thus, while a model of the joint probability distribution is more informative than a model of the distribution of label (but without their relative frequencies), it is a relatively small step, hence these are not always distinguished.
Generative model — Given a model of the joint distribution, P ( X , Y ) {\displaystyle P(X,Y)} , the distribution of the individual variables can be computed as the marginal distributions P ( X ) = ∑ y P ( X , Y = y ) {\displaystyle P(X)=\sum _{y}P(X,Y=y)} and P ( Y ) = ∫ x P ( Y , X = x ) {\displaystyle P(Y)=\int _{x}P(Y,X=x)} (considering X as continuous, hence integrating over it, and Y as discrete, hence summing over it), and either conditional distribution can be computed from the definition of conditional probability: P ( X ∣ Y ) = P ( X , Y ) / P ( Y ) {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y)=P(X,Y)/P(Y)} and P ( Y ∣ X ) = P ( X , Y ) / P ( X ) {\displaystyle P(Y\mid X)=P(X,Y)/P(X)} .
Generative model — Given a model of one conditional probability, and estimated probability distributions for the variables X and Y, denoted P ( X ) {\displaystyle P(X)} and P ( Y ) {\displaystyle P(Y)} , one can estimate the opposite conditional probability using Bayes' rule:
Generative model — P ( X ∣ Y ) P ( Y ) = P ( Y ∣ X ) P ( X ) . {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y)P(Y)=P(Y\mid X)P(X).}
Generative model — For example, given a generative model for P ( X ∣ Y ) {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y)} , one can estimate:
Generative model — P ( Y ∣ X ) = P ( X ∣ Y ) P ( Y ) / P ( X ) , {\displaystyle P(Y\mid X)=P(X\mid Y)P(Y)/P(X),}
Generative model — and given a discriminative model for P ( Y ∣ X ) {\displaystyle P(Y\mid X)} , one can estimate:
Generative model — P ( X ∣ Y ) = P ( Y ∣ X ) P ( X ) / P ( Y ) . {\displaystyle P(X\mid Y)=P(Y\mid X)P(X)/P(Y).}
Generative model — Note that Bayes' rule (computing one conditional probability in terms of the other) and the definition of conditional probability (computing conditional probability in terms of the joint distribution) are frequently conflated as well.
Generative model — == Contrast with discriminative classifiers == A generative algorithm models how the data was generated in order to categorize a signal.
Generative model — It asks the question: based on my generation assumptions, which category is most likely to generate this signal?
Generative model — A discriminative algorithm does not care about how the data was generated, it simply categorizes a given signal.
Generative model — So, discriminative algorithms try to learn p ( y | x ) {\displaystyle p(y|x)} directly from the data and then try to classify data.
Generative model — On the other hand, generative algorithms try to learn p ( x , y ) {\displaystyle p(x,y)} which can be transformed into p ( y | x ) {\displaystyle p(y|x)} later to classify the data.
Generative model — One of the advantages of generative algorithms is that you can use p ( x , y ) {\displaystyle p(x,y)} to generate new data similar to existing data.
Generative model — On the other hand, it has been proved that some discriminative algorithms give better performance than some generative algorithms in classification tasks.
Generative model — Despite the fact that discriminative models do not need to model the distribution of the observed variables, they cannot generally express complex relationships between the observed and target variables.
Generative model — But in general, they don't necessarily perform better than generative models at classification and regression tasks.
Generative model — The two classes are seen as complementary or as different views of the same procedure.
Generative model — == Deep generative models == With the rise of deep learning, a new family of methods, called deep generative models (DGMs), is formed through the combination of generative models and deep neural networks.
Generative model — An increase in the scale of the neural networks is typically accompanied by an increase in the scale of the training data, both of which are required for good performance.
Generative model — Popular DGMs include variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and auto-regressive models.
Generative model — For example, GPT-3, and its precursor GPT-2, are auto-regressive neural language models that contain billions of parameters, BigGAN and VQ-VAE which are used for image generation that can have hundreds of millions of parameters, and Jukebox is a very large generative model for musical audio that contains billions of parameters.

Generative model — Restricted Boltzmann machine, Deep belief network) Variational autoencoder Generative adversarial network Flow-based generative model Energy based model Diffusion model If the observed data are truly sampled from the generative model, then fitting the parameters of the generative model to maximize the data likelihood is a common method.
Generative model — However, since most statistical models are only approximations to the true distribution, if the model's application is to infer about a subset of variables conditional on known values of others, then it can be argued that the approximation makes more assumptions than are necessary to solve the problem at hand.
Generative model — In such cases, it can be more accurate to model the conditional density functions directly using a discriminative model (see below), although application-specific details will ultimately dictate which approach is most suitable in any particular case.

Generative model — === Text generation === Shannon (1948) gives an example in which a table of frequencies of English word pairs is used to generate a sentence beginning with "representing and speedily is an good"; which is not proper English but which will increasingly approximate it as the table is moved from word pairs to word triplets etc.
Autoregressive model — In statistics, econometrics, and signal processing, an autoregressive (AR) model is a representation of a type of random process; as such, it can be used to describe certain time-varying processes in nature, economics, behavior, etc.
Autoregressive model — The autoregressive model specifies that the output variable depends linearly on its own previous values and on a stochastic term (an imperfectly predictable term); thus the model is in the form of a stochastic difference equation (or recurrence relation) which should not be confused with a differential equation.
Autoregressive model — Together with the moving-average (MA) model, it is a special case and key component of the more general autoregressive–moving-average (ARMA) and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models of time series, which have a more complicated stochastic structure; it is also a special case of the vector autoregressive model (VAR), which consists of a system of more than one interlocking stochastic difference equation in more than one evolving random variable.
Autoregressive model — Another important extension is the time-varying autoregressive (TVAR) model, where the autoregressive coefficients are allowed to change over time to model evolving or non-stationary processes.
Autoregressive model — TVAR models are widely applied in cases where the underlying dynamics of the system are not constant, such as in sensors time series modelling, finance, climate science, economics, signal processing and telecommunications, radar systems, and biological signals.
Autoregressive model — Unlike the moving-average (MA) model, the autoregressive model is not always stationary; non-stationarity can arise either due to the presence of a unit root or due to time-varying model parameters, as in time-varying autoregressive (TVAR) models.
Autoregressive model — Large language models are called autoregressive, but they are not a classical autoregressive model in this sense because they are not linear.
Autoregressive model — == Definition == The notation A R ( p ) {\displaystyle AR(p)} indicates an autoregressive model of order p.
Autoregressive model — X t = ∑ i = 1 p φ i X t − i + ε t {\displaystyle X_{t}=\sum _{i=1}^{p}\varphi _{i}X_{t-i}+\varepsilon _{t}}
Autoregressive model — where φ 1 , … , φ p {\displaystyle \varphi _{1},\ldots ,\varphi _{p}} are the parameters of the model, and ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}} is white noise.
Autoregressive model — X t = ∑ i = 1 p φ i B i X t + ε t {\displaystyle X_{t}=\sum _{i=1}^{p}\varphi _{i}B^{i}X_{t}+\varepsilon _{t}}
Autoregressive model — so that, moving the summation term to the left side and using polynomial notation, we have
Autoregressive model — An autoregressive model can thus be viewed as the output of an all-pole infinite impulse response filter whose input is white noise.
Autoregressive model — Some parameter constraints are necessary for the model to remain weak-sense stationary.
Autoregressive model — For example, processes in the AR(1) model with | φ 1 | ≥ 1 {\displaystyle |\varphi _{1}|\geq 1} are not stationary.
Autoregressive model — More generally, for an AR(p) model to be weak-sense stationary, the roots of the polynomial Φ ( z ) := 1 − ∑ i = 1 p φ i z i {\displaystyle \Phi (z):=\textstyle 1-\sum _{i=1}^{p}\varphi _{i}z^{i}} must lie outside the unit circle, i.e., each (complex) root z i {\displaystyle z_{i}} must satisfy | z i | > 1 {\displaystyle |z_{i}|>1} (see pages 89,92 ).
Autoregressive model — == Intertemporal effect of shocks == In an AR process, a one-time shock affects values of the evolving variable infinitely far into the future.
Autoregressive model — For example, consider the AR(1) model X t = φ 1 X t − 1 + ε t {\displaystyle X_{t}=\varphi _{1}X_{t-1}+\varepsilon _{t}} .
Autoregressive model — A non-zero value for ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}} at say time t=1 affects X 1 {\displaystyle X_{1}} by the amount ε 1 {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{1}} .
Autoregressive model — Then by the AR equation for X 2 {\displaystyle X_{2}} in terms of X 1 {\displaystyle X_{1}} , this affects X 2 {\displaystyle X_{2}} by the amount φ 1 ε 1 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}\varepsilon _{1}} .
Autoregressive model — Then by the AR equation for X 3 {\displaystyle X_{3}} in terms of X 2 {\displaystyle X_{2}} , this affects X 3 {\displaystyle X_{3}} by the amount φ 1 2 ε 1 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}^{2}\varepsilon _{1}} .
Autoregressive model — Continuing this process shows that the effect of ε 1 {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{1}} never ends, although if the process is stationary then the effect diminishes toward zero in the limit.
Autoregressive model — Because each shock affects X values infinitely far into the future from when they occur, any given value Xt is affected by shocks occurring infinitely far into the past.
Autoregressive model — (where the constant term has been suppressed by assuming that the variable has been measured as deviations from its mean) as
Autoregressive model — X t = 1 ϕ ( B ) ε t . {\displaystyle X_{t}={\frac {1}{\phi (B)}}\varepsilon _{t}\,.}
Autoregressive model — When the polynomial division on the right side is carried out, the polynomial in the backshift operator applied to ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}} has an infinite order—that is, an infinite number of lagged values of ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}} appear on the right side of the equation.
Autoregressive model — == Characteristic polynomial == The autocorrelation function of an AR(p) process can be expressed as
Autoregressive model — ρ ( τ ) = ∑ k = 1 p a k y k − | τ | , {\displaystyle \rho (\tau )=\sum _{k=1}^{p}a_{k}y_{k}^{-|\tau |},}
Autoregressive model — ϕ ( B ) = 1 − ∑ k = 1 p φ k B k {\displaystyle \phi (B)=1-\sum _{k=1}^{p}\varphi _{k}B^{k}}
Autoregressive model — where B is the backshift operator, where ϕ ( ⋅ ) {\displaystyle \phi (\cdot )} is the function defining the autoregression, and where φ k {\displaystyle \varphi _{k}} are the coefficients in the autoregression.
Autoregressive model — The autocorrelation function of an AR(p) process is a sum of decaying exponentials.
Autoregressive model — Each real root contributes a component to the autocorrelation function that decays exponentially.
Autoregressive model — Similarly, each pair of complex conjugate roots contributes an exponentially damped oscillation.
Autoregressive model — Only the error/innovation/noise term contributes to the output of the process, so in the figure, AR(0) corresponds to white noise.
Autoregressive model — For an AR(1) process with a positive φ {\displaystyle \varphi } , only the previous term in the process and the noise term contribute to the output.
Autoregressive model — If φ {\displaystyle \varphi } is close to 0, then the process still looks like white noise, but as φ {\displaystyle \varphi } approaches 1, the output gets a larger contribution from the previous term relative to the noise.
Autoregressive model — This results in a "smoothing" or integration of the output, similar to a low pass filter.
Autoregressive model — For an AR(2) process, the previous two terms and the noise term contribute to the output.
Autoregressive model — If both φ 1 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}} and φ 2 {\displaystyle \varphi _{2}} are positive, the output will resemble a low pass filter, with the high frequency part of the noise decreased.
Autoregressive model — If φ 1 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}} is positive while φ 2 {\displaystyle \varphi _{2}} is negative, then the process favors changes in sign between terms of the process.
Autoregressive model — == Example: An AR(1) process == An AR(1) process is given by: X t = φ X t − 1 + ε t {\displaystyle X_{t}=\varphi X_{t-1}+\varepsilon _{t}\,} where ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}} is a white noise process with zero mean and constant variance σ ε 2 {\displaystyle \sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2}} . (Note: The subscript on φ 1 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}} has been dropped.) The process is weak-sense stationary if | φ | < 1 {\displaystyle |\varphi |<1} since it is obtained as the output of a stable filter whose input is white noise. (If φ = 1 {\displaystyle \varphi =1} then the variance of X t {\displaystyle X_{t}} depends on time lag t, so that the variance of the series diverges to infinity as t goes to infinity, and is therefore not weak-sense stationary.) Assuming | φ | < 1 {\displaystyle |\varphi |<1} , the mean E ⁡ ( X t ) {\displaystyle \operatorname {E} (X_{t})} is identical for all values of t by definition of weak sense stationarity.
Autoregressive model — If the mean is denoted by μ {\displaystyle \mu } , it follows from E ⁡ ( X t ) = φ E ⁡ ( X t − 1 ) + E ⁡ ( ε t ) , {\displaystyle \operatorname {E} (X_{t})=\varphi \operatorname {E} (X_{t-1})+\operatorname {E} (\varepsilon _{t}),} that μ = φ μ + 0 , {\displaystyle \mu =\varphi \mu +0,} and hence

Autoregressive model — var ( X t ) = φ 2 var ( X t − 1 ) + σ ε 2 , {\displaystyle {\textrm {var}}(X_{t})=\varphi ^{2}{\textrm {var}}(X_{t-1})+\sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2},}
Autoregressive model — and then by noticing that the quantity above is a stable fixed point of this relation.
Autoregressive model — B n = E ⁡ ( X t + n X t ) − μ 2 = σ ε 2 1 − φ 2 φ | n | . {\displaystyle B_{n}=\operatorname {E} (X_{t+n}X_{t})-\mu ^{2}={\frac {\sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2}}{1-\varphi ^{2}}}\,\,\varphi ^{|n|}.}

Autoregressive model — B ( t ) ≈ σ ε 2 1 − φ 2 φ | t | {\displaystyle B(t)\approx {\frac {\sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2}}{1-\varphi ^{2}}}\,\,\varphi ^{|t|}}

Autoregressive model — === Explicit mean/difference form of AR(1) process === The AR(1) model is the discrete-time analogy of the continuous Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.

Autoregressive model — In this form, the AR(1) model, with process parameter θ ∈ R {\displaystyle \theta \in \mathbb {R} } , is given by
Autoregressive model — X t + 1 = X t + ( 1 − θ ) ( μ − X t ) + ε t + 1 {\displaystyle X_{t+1}=X_{t}+(1-\theta )(\mu -X_{t})+\varepsilon _{t+1}} , where | θ | < 1 {\displaystyle |\theta |<1\,} , μ := E ( X ) {\displaystyle \mu :=E(X)} is the model mean, and { ϵ t } {\displaystyle \{\epsilon _{t}\}} is a white-noise process with zero mean and constant variance σ {\displaystyle \sigma } .
Autoregressive model — By rewriting this as X t + 1 = θ X t + ( 1 − θ ) μ + ε t + 1 {\displaystyle X_{t+1}=\theta X_{t}+(1-\theta )\mu +\varepsilon _{t+1}} and then deriving (by induction) X t + n = θ n X t + ( 1 − θ n ) μ + Σ i = 1 n ( θ n − i ϵ t + i ) {\displaystyle X_{t+n}=\theta ^{n}X_{t}+(1-\theta ^{n})\mu +\Sigma _{i=1}^{n}\left(\theta ^{n-i}\epsilon _{t+i}\right)} , one can show that
Autoregressive model — E ⁡ ( X t + n | X t ) = μ [ 1 − θ n ] + X t θ n {\displaystyle \operatorname {E} (X_{t+n}|X_{t})=\mu \left[1-\theta ^{n}\right]+X_{t}\theta ^{n}} and
Autoregressive model — Var ⁡ ( X t + n | X t ) = σ 2 1 − θ 2 n 1 − θ 2 {\displaystyle \operatorname {Var} (X_{t+n}|X_{t})=\sigma ^{2}{\frac {1-\theta ^{2n}}{1-\theta ^{2}}}} .
Autoregressive model — The partial autocorrelation of an AR(p) process equals zero at lags larger than p, so the appropriate maximum lag p is the one after which the partial autocorrelations are all zero.
Autoregressive model — == Calculation of the AR parameters == There are many ways to estimate the coefficients, such as the ordinary least squares procedure or method of moments (through Yule–Walker equations).
Autoregressive model — X t = ∑ i = 1 p φ i X t − i + ε t . {\displaystyle X_{t}=\sum _{i=1}^{p}\varphi _{i}X_{t-i}+\varepsilon _{t}.\,}
Autoregressive model — There is a direct correspondence between these parameters and the covariance function of the process, and this correspondence can be inverted to determine the parameters from the autocorrelation function (which is itself obtained from the covariances).
Autoregressive model — === Yule–Walker equations === The Yule–Walker equations, named for Udny Yule and Gilbert Walker, are the following set of equations.
Autoregressive model — γ m = ∑ k = 1 p φ k γ m − k + σ ε 2 δ m , 0 , {\displaystyle \gamma _{m}=\sum _{k=1}^{p}\varphi _{k}\gamma _{m-k}+\sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2}\delta _{m,0},}
Autoregressive model — Here γ m {\displaystyle \gamma _{m}} is the autocovariance function of Xt, σ ε {\displaystyle \sigma _{\varepsilon }} is the standard deviation of the input noise process, and δ m , 0 {\displaystyle \delta _{m,0}} is the Kronecker delta function.
Autoregressive model — Because the last part of an individual equation is non-zero only if m = 0, the set of equations can be solved by representing the equations for m > 0 in matrix form, thus getting the equation
Autoregressive model — [ γ 1 γ 2 γ 3 ⋮ γ p ] = [ γ 0 γ − 1 γ − 2 ⋯ γ 1 γ 0 γ − 1 ⋯ γ 2 γ 1 γ 0 ⋯ ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ ⋱ γ p − 1 γ p − 2 γ p − 3 ⋯ ] [ φ 1 φ 2 φ 3 ⋮ φ p ] {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}\gamma _{1}\\\gamma _{2}\\\gamma _{3}\\\vdots \\\gamma _{p}\\\end{bmatrix}}={\begin{bmatrix}\gamma _{0}&\gamma _{-1}&\gamma _{-2}&\cdots \\\gamma _{1}&\gamma _{0}&\gamma _{-1}&\cdots \\\gamma _{2}&\gamma _{1}&\gamma _{0}&\cdots \\\vdots &\vdots &\vdots &\ddots \\\gamma _{p-1}&\gamma _{p-2}&\gamma _{p-3}&\cdots \\\end{bmatrix}}{\begin{bmatrix}\varphi _{1}\\\varphi _{2}\\\varphi _{3}\\\vdots \\\varphi _{p}\\\end{bmatrix}}}
Autoregressive model — which can be solved for all { φ m ; m = 1 , 2 , … , p } . {\displaystyle \{\varphi _{m};m=1,2,\dots ,p\}.} The remaining equation for m = 0 is
Autoregressive model — γ 0 = ∑ k = 1 p φ k γ − k + σ ε 2 , {\displaystyle \gamma _{0}=\sum _{k=1}^{p}\varphi _{k}\gamma _{-k}+\sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2},}
Autoregressive model — which, once { φ m ; m = 1 , 2 , … , p } {\displaystyle \{\varphi _{m};m=1,2,\dots ,p\}} are known, can be solved for σ ε 2 . {\displaystyle \sigma _{\varepsilon }^{2}.}
Autoregressive model — The AR parameters are determined by the first p+1 elements ρ ( τ ) {\displaystyle \rho (\tau )} of the autocorrelation function.
Autoregressive model — The full autocorrelation function can then be derived by recursively calculating
Autoregressive model — ρ ( τ ) = ∑ k = 1 p φ k ρ ( k − τ ) {\displaystyle \rho (\tau )=\sum _{k=1}^{p}\varphi _{k}\rho (k-\tau )}
Autoregressive model — Hence ρ 1 = γ 1 / γ 0 = φ 1 {\displaystyle \rho _{1}=\gamma _{1}/\gamma _{0}=\varphi _{1}}
Autoregressive model — γ 1 = φ 1 γ 0 + φ 2 γ − 1 {\displaystyle \gamma _{1}=\varphi _{1}\gamma _{0}+\varphi _{2}\gamma _{-1}}
Autoregressive model — γ 2 = φ 1 γ 1 + φ 2 γ 0 {\displaystyle \gamma _{2}=\varphi _{1}\gamma _{1}+\varphi _{2}\gamma _{0}}
Autoregressive model — Using the first equation yields ρ 1 = γ 1 / γ 0 = φ 1 1 − φ 2 {\displaystyle \rho _{1}=\gamma _{1}/\gamma _{0}={\frac {\varphi _{1}}{1-\varphi _{2}}}}
Autoregressive model — Using the recursion formula yields ρ 2 = γ 2 / γ 0 = φ 1 2 − φ 2 2 + φ 2 1 − φ 2 {\displaystyle \rho _{2}=\gamma _{2}/\gamma _{0}={\frac {\varphi _{1}^{2}-\varphi _{2}^{2}+\varphi _{2}}{1-\varphi _{2}}}}
Autoregressive model — === Estimation of AR parameters === The above equations (the Yule–Walker equations) provide several routes to estimating the parameters of an AR(p) model, by replacing the theoretical covariances with estimated values.
Autoregressive model — There are different ways of doing this and the choice between these affects the properties of the estimation scheme.
Autoregressive model — For example, negative estimates of the variance can be produced by some choices.
Autoregressive model — Formulation as a least squares regression problem in which an ordinary least squares prediction problem is constructed, basing prediction of values of Xt on the p previous values of the same series.
Autoregressive model — The normal equations for this problem can be seen to correspond to an approximation of the matrix form of the Yule–Walker equations in which each appearance of an autocovariance of the same lag is replaced by a slightly different estimate.
Autoregressive model — Here two sets of prediction equations are combined into a single estimation scheme and a single set of normal equations.
Autoregressive model — One set is the set of forward-prediction equations and the other is a corresponding set of backward prediction equations, relating to the backward representation of the AR model:
Autoregressive model — X t = ∑ i = 1 p φ i X t + i + ε t ∗ . {\displaystyle X_{t}=\sum _{i=1}^{p}\varphi _{i}X_{t+i}+\varepsilon _{t}^{*}\,.}
Autoregressive model — Here predicted values of Xt would be based on the p future values of the same series.
Autoregressive model — This way of estimating the AR parameters is due to John Parker Burg, and is called the Burg method: Burg and later authors called these particular estimates "maximum entropy estimates", but the reasoning behind this applies to the use of any set of estimated AR parameters.
Autoregressive model — Compared to the estimation scheme using only the forward prediction equations, different estimates of the autocovariances are produced, and the estimates have different stability properties.
Autoregressive model — Burg estimates are particularly associated with maximum entropy spectral estimation.
Autoregressive model — Two distinct variants of maximum likelihood are available: in one (broadly equivalent to the forward prediction least squares scheme) the likelihood function considered is that corresponding to the conditional distribution of later values in the series given the initial p values in the series; in the second, the likelihood function considered is that corresponding to the unconditional joint distribution of all the values in the observed series.
Autoregressive model — Substantial differences in the results of these approaches can occur if the observed series is short, or if the process is close to non-stationarity.
Autoregressive model — The power spectral density (PSD) of an AR(p) process with noise variance V a r ( Z t ) = σ Z 2 {\displaystyle \mathrm {Var} (Z_{t})=\sigma _{Z}^{2}} is
Autoregressive model — S ( f ) = σ Z 2 | 1 − ∑ k = 1 p φ k e − i 2 π f k | 2 . {\displaystyle S(f)={\frac {\sigma _{Z}^{2}}{|1-\sum _{k=1}^{p}\varphi _{k}e^{-i2\pi fk}|^{2}}}.}
Autoregressive model — S ( f ) = σ Z 2 | 1 − φ 1 e − 2 π i f | 2 = σ Z 2 1 + φ 1 2 − 2 φ 1 cos ⁡ 2 π f {\displaystyle S(f)={\frac {\sigma _{Z}^{2}}{|1-\varphi _{1}e^{-2\pi if}|^{2}}}={\frac {\sigma _{Z}^{2}}{1+\varphi _{1}^{2}-2\varphi _{1}\cos 2\pi f}}}
Autoregressive model — If φ 1 > 0 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}>0} there is a single spectral peak at f = 0 {\displaystyle f=0} , often referred to as red noise.
Autoregressive model — As φ 1 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}} becomes nearer 1, there is stronger power at low frequencies, i.e. larger time lags.
Autoregressive model — This is then a low-pass filter, when applied to full spectrum light, everything except for the red light will be filtered.
Autoregressive model — If φ 1 < 0 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}<0} there is a minimum at f = 0 {\displaystyle f=0} , often referred to as blue noise.
Autoregressive model — This similarly acts as a high-pass filter, everything except for blue light will be filtered.
Autoregressive model — === AR(2) === The behavior of an AR(2) process is determined entirely by the roots of it characteristic equation, which is expressed in terms of the lag operator as:
Autoregressive model — or equivalently by the poles of its transfer function, which is defined in the Z domain by:
Autoregressive model — H z = ( 1 − φ 1 z − 1 − φ 2 z − 2 ) − 1 . {\displaystyle H_{z}=(1-\varphi _{1}z^{-1}-\varphi _{2}z^{-2})^{-1}.}
Autoregressive model — 1 − φ 1 z − 1 − φ 2 z − 2 = 0 {\displaystyle 1-\varphi _{1}z^{-1}-\varphi _{2}z^{-2}=0} , which yields:
Autoregressive model — z 1 , z 2 = 1 2 φ 2 ( φ 1 ± φ 1 2 + 4 φ 2 ) {\displaystyle z_{1},z_{2}={\frac {1}{2\varphi _{2}}}\left(\varphi _{1}\pm {\sqrt {\varphi _{1}^{2}+4\varphi _{2}}}\right)} .
Autoregressive model — z 1 {\displaystyle z_{1}} and z 2 {\displaystyle z_{2}} are the reciprocals of the characteristic roots, as well as the eigenvalues of the temporal update matrix:
Autoregressive model — [ φ 1 φ 2 1 0 ] {\displaystyle {\begin{bmatrix}\varphi _{1}&\varphi _{2}\\1&0\end{bmatrix}}}
Autoregressive model — AR(2) processes can be split into three groups depending on the characteristics of their roots/poles:
Autoregressive model — When φ 1 2 + 4 φ 2 < 0 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}^{2}+4\varphi _{2}<0} , the process has a pair of complex-conjugate poles, creating a mid-frequency peak at:
Autoregressive model — f ∗ = 1 2 π cos − 1 ⁡ ( φ 1 2 − φ 2 ) , {\displaystyle f^{*}={\frac {1}{2\pi }}\cos ^{-1}\left({\frac {\varphi _{1}}{2{\sqrt {-\varphi _{2}}}}}\right),}
Autoregressive model — with bandwidth about the peak inversely proportional to the moduli of the poles:
Autoregressive model — | z 1 | = | z 2 | = − φ 2 . {\displaystyle |z_{1}|=|z_{2}|={\sqrt {-\varphi _{2}}}.}
Autoregressive model — The terms involving square roots are all real in the case of complex poles since they exist only when φ 2 < 0 {\displaystyle \varphi _{2}<0} .
Autoregressive model — When φ 1 > 0 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}>0} it acts as a low-pass filter on the white noise with a spectral peak at f = 0 {\displaystyle f=0}
Autoregressive model — When φ 1 < 0 {\displaystyle \varphi _{1}<0} it acts as a high-pass filter on the white noise with a spectral peak at f = 1 / 2 {\displaystyle f=1/2} .
Autoregressive model — The process is non-stationary when the poles are on or outside the unit circle, or equivalently when the characteristic roots are on or inside the unit circle.
Autoregressive model — The process is stable when the poles are strictly within the unit circle (roots strictly outside the unit circle), or equivalently when the coefficients are in the triangle − 1 ≤ φ 2 ≤ 1 − | φ 1 | {\displaystyle -1\leq \varphi _{2}\leq 1-|\varphi _{1}|} .
Autoregressive model — S ( f ) = σ Z 2 1 + φ 1 2 + φ 2 2 − 2 φ 1 ( 1 − φ 2 ) cos ⁡ ( 2 π f ) − 2 φ 2 cos ⁡ ( 4 π f ) {\displaystyle S(f)={\frac {\sigma _{Z}^{2}}{1+\varphi _{1}^{2}+\varphi _{2}^{2}-2\varphi _{1}(1-\varphi _{2})\cos(2\pi f)-2\varphi _{2}\cos(4\pi f)}}}
Autoregressive model — == Implementations in statistics packages == R – the stats package includes ar function; the astsa package includes sarima function to fit various models including AR.
Autoregressive model — MATLAB – the Econometrics Toolbox and System Identification Toolbox include AR models.
Autoregressive model — MATLAB and Octave – the TSA toolbox contains several estimation functions for uni-variate, multivariate, and adaptive AR models.
Autoregressive model — PyMC3 – the Bayesian statistics and probabilistic programming framework supports AR modes with p lags. bayesloop – supports parameter inference and model selection for the AR-1 process with time-varying parameters.
Autoregressive model — == Impulse response == The impulse response of a system is the change in an evolving variable in response to a change in the value of a shock term k periods earlier, as a function of k.
Autoregressive model — Since the AR model is a special case of the vector autoregressive model, the computation of the impulse response in vector autoregression#impulse response applies here.
Autoregressive model — X t = ∑ i = 1 p φ i X t − i + ε t {\displaystyle X_{t}=\sum _{i=1}^{p}\varphi _{i}X_{t-i}+\varepsilon _{t}\,}
Autoregressive model — have been estimated, the autoregression can be used to forecast an arbitrary number of periods into the future.
Autoregressive model — First use t to refer to the first period for which data is not yet available; substitute the known preceding values Xt-i for i=1, ..., p into the autoregressive equation while setting the error term ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}} equal to zero (because we forecast Xt to equal its expected value, and the expected value of the unobserved error term is zero).
Autoregressive model — The output of the autoregressive equation is the forecast for the first unobserved period.
Autoregressive model — Next, use t to refer to the next period for which data is not yet available; again the autoregressive equation is used to make the forecast, with one difference: the value of X one period prior to the one now being forecast is not known, so its expected value—the predicted value arising from the previous forecasting step—is used instead.
Autoregressive model — Then for future periods the same procedure is used, each time using one more forecast value on the right side of the predictive equation until, after p predictions, all p right-side values are predicted values from preceding steps.
Autoregressive model — There are four sources of uncertainty regarding predictions obtained in this manner: (1) uncertainty as to whether the autoregressive model is the correct model; (2) uncertainty about the accuracy of the forecasted values that are used as lagged values in the right side of the autoregressive equation; (3) uncertainty about the true values of the autoregressive coefficients; and (4) uncertainty about the value of the error term ε t {\displaystyle \varepsilon _{t}\,} for the period being predicted.
Autoregressive model — Each of the last three can be quantified and combined to give a confidence interval for the n-step-ahead predictions; the confidence interval will become wider as n increases because of the use of an increasing number of estimated values for the right-side variables.

README — Qdrant** (read: _quadrant_) is a vector similarity search engine and vector database.
README — It provides a production-ready service with a convenient API to store, search, and manage points—vectors with an additional payload
README — Qdrant is tailored to extended filtering support. It makes it useful for all sorts of neural-network or semantic-based matching, faceted search, and other applications.
README — Qdrant is written in Rust 🦀, which makes it fast and reliable even under high load. See [benchmarks](https://qdrant.tech/benchmarks/).
README — With Qdrant, embeddings or neural network encoders can be turned into full-fledged applications for matching, searching, recommending, and much more!
README — Qdrant is also available as a fully managed **[Qdrant Cloud](https://cloud.qdrant.io/)** ⛅ including a **free tier**.

README — Features
README — Filtering and Payload
README — Qdrant can attach any JSON payloads to vectors, allowing for both the storage and filtering of data based on the values in these payloads.
README — Payload supports a wide range of data types and query conditions, including keyword matching, full-text filtering, numerical ranges, geo-locations, and more.
README — Filtering conditions can be combined in various ways, including `should`, `must`, and `must_not` clauses,
README — ensuring that you can implement any desired business logic on top of similarity matching.
README — Hybrid Search with Sparse Vectors
README — To address the limitations of vector embeddings when searching for specific keywords, Qdrant introduces support for sparse vectors in addition to the regular dense ones.
README — Sparse vectors can be viewed as an generalization of BM25 or TF-IDF ranking. They enable you to harness the capabilities of transformer-based neural networks to weigh individual tokens effectively.
README — Vector Quantization and On-Disk Storage
README — Qdrant provides multiple options to make vector search cheaper and more resource-efficient.
README — Built-in vector quantization reduces RAM usage by up to 97% and dynamically manages the trade-off between search speed and precision.
README — Distributed Deployment
README — Qdrant offers comprehensive horizontal scaling support through two key mechanisms:
README — Size expansion via sharding and throughput enhancement via replication
README — Zero-downtime rolling updates and seamless dynamic scaling of the collections
README — Highlighted Features
README — Query Planning and Payload Indexes** - leverages stored payload information to optimize query execution strategy.
README — SIMD Hardware Acceleration** - utilizes modern CPU x86-x64 and Neon architectures to deliver better performance.
README — Async I/O** - uses `io_uring` to maximize disk throughput utilization even on a network-attached storage.
README — Write-Ahead Logging** - ensures data persistence with update confirmation, even during power outages.

PRETRAIN — Pre-training MAE
PRETRAIN — To pre-train ViT-Large (recommended default) with **multi-node distributed training**, run the following on 8 nodes with 8 GPUs each:
PRETRAIN — Here the effective batch size is 64 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 8 (`nodes`) * 8 (gpus per node) = 4096. If memory or # gpus is limited, use `--accum_iter` to maintain the effective batch size, which is `batch_size` (per gpu) * `nodes` * 8 (gpus per node) * `accum_iter`.
PRETRAIN — `blr` is the base learning rate. The actual `lr` is computed by the [linear scaling rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677): `lr` = `blr` * effective batch size / 256.
PRETRAIN — Here we use `--norm_pix_loss` as the target for better representation learning. To train a baseline model (e.g., for visualization), use pixel-based construction and turn off `--norm_pix_loss`.
PRETRAIN — The exact same hyper-parameters and configs (initialization, augmentation, etc.) are used as our TF/TPU implementation. In our sanity checks, this PT/GPU re-implementation can reproduce the TF/TPU results within reasonable random variation. We get 85.5% [fine-tuning](FINETUNE.md) accuracy by pre-training ViT-Large for 800 epochs (85.4% in paper Table 1d with TF/TPU).
PRETRAIN — Training time is ~42h in 64 V100 GPUs (800 epochs).
PRETRAIN — To train ViT-Base or ViT-Huge, set `--model mae_vit_base_patch16` or `--model mae_vit_huge_patch14`.

FINETUNE — Fine-tuning
FINETUNE — Get our pre-trained checkpoints from [here](https://github.com/fairinternal/mae/#pre-trained-checkpoints).
FINETUNE — To fine-tune with **multi-node distributed training**, run the following on 4 nodes with 8 GPUs each:
FINETUNE — Install submitit (`pip install submitit`) first.
FINETUNE — Here the effective batch size is 32 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 4 (`nodes`) * 8 (gpus per node) = 1024.
FINETUNE — `blr` is the base learning rate. The actual `lr` is computed by the [linear scaling rule](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02677): `lr` = `blr` * effective batch size / 256.
FINETUNE — We have run 4 trials with different random seeds. The resutls are 83.63, 83.66, 83.52, 83.46 (mean 83.57 and std 0.08).
FINETUNE — Training time is ~7h11m in 32 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — Script for ViT-Large:
FINETUNE — We have run 4 trials with different random seeds. The resutls are 85.95, 85.87, 85.76, 85.88 (mean 85.87 and std 0.07).
FINETUNE — Training time is ~8h52m in 32 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — Script for ViT-Huge:
FINETUNE — Training time is ~13h9m in 64 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — To fine-tune our pre-trained ViT-Base with **single-node training**, run the following on 1 node with 8 GPUs:
FINETUNE — Here the effective batch size is 32 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 4 (`accum_iter`) * 8 (gpus) = 1024. `--accum_iter 4` simulates 4 nodes.
FINETUNE — The [pre-trained models we provide](https://github.com/fairinternal/mae/#pre-trained-checkpoints) are trained with *normalized* pixels `--norm_pix_loss` (1600 epochs, Table 3 in paper). The fine-tuning hyper-parameters are slightly different from the default baseline using *unnormalized* pixels.
FINETUNE — The original MAE implementation was in TensorFlow+TPU with no explicit mixed precision. This re-implementation is in PyTorch+GPU with automatic mixed precision (`torch.cuda.amp`). We have observed different numerical behavior between the two platforms. In this repo, we use `--global_pool` for fine-tuning; using `--cls_token` performs similarly, but there is a chance of producing NaN when fine-tuning ViT-Huge in GPUs. We did not observe this issue in TPUs. Turning off amp could solve this issue, but is slower.
FINETUNE — Here we use RandErase following DeiT: `--reprob 0.25`. Its effect is smaller than random variance.
FINETUNE — Linear Probing
FINETUNE — Run the following on 4 nodes with 8 GPUs each:
FINETUNE — Here the effective batch size is 512 (`batch_size` per gpu) * 4 (`nodes`) * 8 (gpus per node) = 16384.
FINETUNE — Training time is ~2h20m for 90 epochs in 32 V100 GPUs.
FINETUNE — To run single-node training, follow the instruction in fine-tuning.
FINETUNE — To train ViT-Large or ViT-Huge, set `--model vit_large_patch16` or `--model vit_huge_patch14`. It is sufficient to train 50 epochs `--epochs 50`.
FINETUNE — This PT/GPU code produces *better* results for ViT-L/H (see the table below). This is likely caused by the system difference between TF and PT.

README — Towards Robust Monocular Depth Estimation: Mixing Datasets for Zero-shot Cross-dataset Transfer
README — This repository contains code to compute depth from a single image. It accompanies our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01341v3):
README — René Ranftl, Katrin Lasinger, David Hafner, Konrad Schindler, Vladlen Koltun
README — and our [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13413):
README — Vision Transformers for Dense Prediction
README — René Ranftl, Alexey Bochkovskiy, Vladlen Koltun
README — For the latest release MiDaS 3.1, a [technical report](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.14460.pdf) and [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UjaeNNFf9sE&t=3s) are available.
README — MiDaS was trained on up to 12 datasets (ReDWeb, DIML, Movies, MegaDepth, WSVD, TartanAir, HRWSI, ApolloScape, BlendedMVS, IRS, KITTI, NYU Depth V2) with
README — multi-objective optimization.
README — The original model that was trained on 5 datasets (`MIX 5` in the paper) can be found [here](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/tag/v2).
README — The figure below shows an overview of the different MiDaS models; the bubble size scales with number of parameters.
README — ![](figures/Improvement_vs_FPS.png)
README — Pick one or more models and download the corresponding weights to the `weights` folder:
README — MiDaS 3.1
README — For highest quality: [dpt_beit_large_512](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_beit_large_512.pt)
README — For moderately less quality, but better speed-performance trade-off: [dpt_swin2_large_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_swin2_large_384.pt)
README — For embedded devices: [dpt_swin2_tiny_256](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_swin2_tiny_256.pt), [dpt_levit_224](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/dpt_levit_224.pt)
README — For inference on Intel CPUs, OpenVINO may be used for the small legacy model: openvino_midas_v21_small [.xml](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/openvino_midas_v21_small_256.xml), [.bin](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3_1/openvino_midas_v21_small_256.bin)
README — MiDaS 3.0: Legacy transformer models [dpt_large_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3/dpt_large_384.pt) and [dpt_hybrid_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v3/dpt_hybrid_384.pt)
README — MiDaS 2.1: Legacy convolutional models [midas_v21_384](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v2_1/midas_v21_384.pt) and [midas_v21_small_256](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/download/v2_1/midas_v21_small_256.pt)

README — where ```<model_type>``` is chosen from [dpt_beit_large_512](#model_type), [dpt_beit_large_384](#model_type),
README — [dpt_beit_base_384](#model_type), [dpt_swin2_large_384](#model_type), [dpt_swin2_base_384](#model_type),

README — The resulting depth maps are written to the `output` folder.
README — By default, the inference resizes the height of input images to the size of a model to fit into the encoder. This
README — size is given by the numbers in the model names of the [accuracy table](#accuracy). Some models do not only support a single
README — inference height but a range of different heights. Feel free to explore different heights by appending the extra
README — command line argument `--height`. Unsupported height values will throw an error. Note that using this argument may
README — decrease the model accuracy.
README — By default, the inference keeps the aspect ratio of input images when feeding them into the encoder if this is
README — supported by a model (all models except for Swin, Swin2, LeViT). In order to resize to a square resolution,
README — disregarding the aspect ratio while preserving the height, use the command line argument `--square`.

README — Accuracy
README — We provide a **zero-shot error** $\epsilon_d$ which is evaluated for 6 different datasets
README — (see [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.01341v3)). **Lower error values are better**.
README — $\color{green}{\textsf{Overall model quality is represented by the improvement}}$ ([Imp.](#improvement)) with respect to
README — MiDaS 3.0 DPT<sub>L-384</sub>. The models are grouped by the height used for inference, whereas the square training resolution is given by
README — the numbers in the model names. The table also shows the **number of parameters** (in millions) and the

README — &ast; No zero-shot error, because models are also trained on KITTI and NYU Depth V2\
README — $\square$ Validation performed at **square resolution**, either because the transformer encoder backbone of a model
README — does not support non-square resolutions (Swin, Swin2, LeViT) or for comparison with these models. All other
README — validations keep the aspect ratio. A difference in resolution limits the comparability of the zero-shot error and the
README — improvement, because these quantities are averages over the pixels of an image and do not take into account the
README — advantage of more details due to a higher resolution.\
README — Best values per column and same validation height in bold
README — Improvement
README — The improvement in the above table is defined as the relative zero-shot error with respect to MiDaS v3.0
README — DPT<sub>L-384</sub> and averaging over the datasets. So, if $\epsilon_d$ is the zero-shot error for dataset $d$, then
README — the $\color{green}{\textsf{improvement}}$ is given by $100(1-(1/6)\sum_d\epsilon_d/\epsilon_{d,\rm{DPT_{L-384}}})$%.
README — Note that the improvements of 10% for MiDaS v2.0 &rarr; v2.1 and 21% for MiDaS v2.1 &rarr; v3.0 are not visible from the
README — improvement column (Imp.) in the table but would require an evaluation with respect to MiDaS v2.1 Large<sub>384</sub>
README — and v2.0 Large<sub>384</sub> respectively instead of v3.0 DPT<sub>L-384</sub>.

README — Applications
README — MiDaS is used in the following other projects from Intel Labs:
README — [ZoeDepth](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.12288.pdf) (code available [here](https://github.com/isl-org/ZoeDepth)): MiDaS computes the relative depth map given an image. For metric depth estimation, ZoeDepth can be used, which combines MiDaS with a metric depth binning module appended to the decoder.
README — [LDM3D](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.10853.pdf) (Hugging Face model available [here](https://huggingface.co/Intel/ldm3d-4c)): LDM3D is an extension of vanilla stable diffusion designed to generate joint image and depth data from a text prompt. The depth maps used for supervision when training LDM3D have been computed using MiDaS.
README — Changelog
README — [Dec 2022] Released [MiDaS v3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.14460.pdf):
README — New models based on 5 different types of transformers ([BEiT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.08254.pdf), [Swin2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.09883.pdf), [Swin](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14030.pdf), [Next-ViT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.05501.pdf), [LeViT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.01136.pdf))
README — Training datasets extended from 10 to 12, including also KITTI and NYU Depth V2 using [BTS](https://github.com/cleinc/bts) split
README — Best model, BEiT<sub>Large 512</sub>, with resolution 512x512, is on average about [28% more accurate](#Accuracy) than MiDaS v3.0
README — Integrated live depth estimation from camera feed
README — [Sep 2021] Integrated to [Huggingface Spaces](https://huggingface.co/spaces) with [Gradio](https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio). See [Gradio Web Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/akhaliq/DPT-Large).
README — [Apr 2021] Released MiDaS v3.0:
README — New models based on [Dense Prediction Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13413) are on average [21% more accurate](#Accuracy) than MiDaS v2.1
README — Additional models can be found [here](https://github.com/isl-org/DPT)
README — [Nov 2020] Released MiDaS v2.1:
README — New model that was trained on 10 datasets and is on average about [10% more accurate](#Accuracy) than [MiDaS v2.0](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/releases/tag/v2)
README — New light-weight model that achieves [real-time performance](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/tree/master/mobile) on mobile platforms.
README — Sample applications for [iOS](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/tree/master/mobile/ios) and [Android](https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS/tree/master/mobile/android)

README — Installation
README — Make sure you have `Python>=3.10` installed on your machine.
README — Install JAX and python dependencies by running:
README — For newer versions of [JAX](https://github.com/google/jax), follow the instructions
README — provided in the corresponding repository linked here. Note that installation
README — instructions for CPU, GPU and TPU differs slightly.
README — Install [Flaxformer](https://github.com/google/flaxformer), follow the instructions
README — provided in the corresponding repository linked here.
README — For more details refer to the section [Running on cloud](#running-on-cloud)
README — Fine-tuning a model
README — You can run fine-tuning of the downloaded model on your dataset of interest. All
README — models share the same command line interface.
README — For example for fine-tuning a ViT-B/16 (pre-trained on imagenet21k) on CIFAR10
README — (note how we specify `b16,cifar10` as arguments to the config, and how we
README — instruct the code to access the models directly from a GCS bucket instead of
README — first downloading them into the local directory):
README — In order to fine-tune a Mixer-B/16 (pre-trained on imagenet21k) on CIFAR10:
README — The "How to train your ViT? ..." paper added >50k checkpoints that you can
README — fine-tune with the [`configs/augreg.py`] config. When you only specify the model
README — name (the `config.name` value from [`configs/model.py`]), then the best i21k
README — checkpoint by upstream validation accuracy ("recommended" checkpoint, see
README — section 4.5 of the paper) is chosen. To make up your mind which model you want
README — to use, have a look at Figure 3 in the paper. It's also possible to choose a
README — different checkpoint (see Colab [`vit_jax_augreg.ipynb`]) and then specify the
README — value from the `filename` or `adapt_filename` column, which correspond to the
README — filenames without `.npz` from the [`gs://vit_models/augreg`] directory.
README — Currently, the code will automatically download CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.
README — Other public or custom datasets can be easily integrated, using [tensorflow
README — datasets library](https://github.com/tensorflow/datasets/). Note that you will
README — also need to update `vit_jax/input_pipeline.py` to specify some parameters about
README — any added dataset.
README — Note that our code uses all available GPUs/TPUs for fine-tuning.
README — To see a detailed list of all available flags, run `python3 -m vit_jax.train
README — Notes on memory:
README — Different models require different amount of memory. Available memory also
README — depends on the accelerator configuration (both type and count). If you
README — encounter an out-of-memory error you can increase the value of
README — `--config.accum_steps=8` -- alternatively, you could also decrease the
README — `--config.batch=512` (and decrease `--config.base_lr` accordingly).
README — The host keeps a shuffle buffer in memory. If you encounter a host OOM (as
README — opposed to an accelerator OOM), you can decrease the default
README — `--config.shuffle_buffer=50000`.
README — Vision Transformer
README — by Alexey Dosovitskiy\*†, Lucas Beyer\*, Alexander Kolesnikov\*, Dirk
README — Weissenborn\*, Xiaohua Zhai\*, Thomas Unterthiner, Mostafa Dehghani, Matthias
README — Minderer, Georg Heigold, Sylvain Gelly, Jakob Uszkoreit and Neil Houlsby\*†.
README — (\*) equal technical contribution, (†) equal advising.
README — ![Figure 1 from paper](vit_figure.png)
README — Overview of the model: we split an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embed
README — each of them, add position embeddings, and feed the resulting sequence of
README — vectors to a standard Transformer encoder. In order to perform classification,
README — we use the standard approach of adding an extra learnable "classification token"
README — to the sequence.
README — Available ViT models
README — We provide a variety of ViT models in different GCS buckets. The models can be
README — downloaded with e.g.:
README — The model filenames (without the `.npz` extension) correspond to the
README — `config.model_name` in [`vit_jax/configs/models.py`]
README — [`gs://vit_models/imagenet21k`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet-21k.
README — [`gs://vit_models/imagenet21k+imagenet2012`] - Models pre-trained on
README — ImageNet-21k and fine-tuned on ImageNet.
README — [`gs://vit_models/augreg`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet-21k,
README — applying varying amounts of [AugReg]. Improved performance.
README — [`gs://vit_models/sam`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet with [SAM].
README — [`gs://vit_models/gsam`] - Models pre-trained on ImageNet with [GSAM].
README — We recommend using the following checkpoints, trained with [AugReg] that have
README — the best pre-training metrics:

README — MLP-Mixer
README — by Ilya Tolstikhin\*, Neil Houlsby\*, Alexander Kolesnikov\*, Lucas Beyer\*,
README — Xiaohua Zhai, Thomas Unterthiner, Jessica Yung, Andreas Steiner, Daniel Keysers,
README — Jakob Uszkoreit, Mario Lucic, Alexey Dosovitskiy.
README — (\*) equal contribution.
README — ![Figure 1 from paper](mixer_figure.png)
README — MLP-Mixer (*Mixer* for short) consists of per-patch linear embeddings, Mixer
README — layers, and a classifier head. Mixer layers contain one token-mixing MLP and one
README — channel-mixing MLP, each consisting of two fully-connected layers and a GELU
README — nonlinearity. Other components include: skip-connections, dropout, and linear
README — classifier head.
README — For installation follow [the same steps](#installation) as above.
README — Available Mixer models
README — We provide the Mixer-B/16 and Mixer-L/16 models pre-trained on the ImageNet and
README — ImageNet-21k datasets. Details can be found in Table 3 of the Mixer paper. All
README — the models can be found at:
README — https://console.cloud.google.com/storage/mixer_models/
README — Note that these models are also available directly from TF-Hub:
README — [sayakpaul/collections/mlp-mixer] (external contribution by [Sayak
README — [sayakpaul/collections/mlp-mixer]: https://tfhub.dev/sayakpaul/collections/mlp-mixer
README — Expected Mixer results
README — We ran the fine-tuning code on Google Cloud machine with four V100 GPUs with the
README — default adaption parameters from this repository. Here are the results:
README — upstream | model | dataset | accuracy | wall_clock_time | link
README — :----------- | :--------- | :------ | -------: | :-------------- | :---
README — ImageNet | Mixer-B/16 | cifar10 | 96.72% | 3.0h | [tensorboard.dev](https://tensorboard.dev/experiment/j9zCYt9yQVm93nqnsDZayA/)
README — ImageNet | Mixer-L/16 | cifar10 | 96.59% | 3.0h | [tensorboard.dev](https://tensorboard.dev/experiment/Q4feeErzRGGop5XzAvYj2g/)
README — ImageNet-21k | Mixer-B/16 | cifar10 | 96.82% | 9.6h | [tensorboard.dev](https://tensorboard.dev/experiment/mvP4McV2SEGFeIww20ie5Q/)
README — ImageNet-21k | Mixer-L/16 | cifar10 | 98.34% | 10.0h | [tensorboard.dev](https://tensorboard.dev/experiment/dolAJyQYTYmudytjalF6Jg/)
README — LiT models
README — For details, refer to the Google AI blog post
README — [LiT: adding language understanding to image models](http://ai.googleblog.com/2022/04/locked-image-tuning-adding-language.html),
README — or read the CVPR paper "LiT: Zero-Shot Transfer with Locked-image text Tuning"
README — (https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.07991).
README — We published a Transformer B/16-base model with an ImageNet zeroshot accuracy of
README — %, and a L/16-large model with an ImageNet zeroshot accuracy of 75.7%. For
README — more details about these models, please refer to the
README — [LiT model card](model_cards/lit.md).
README — We provide a in-browser demo with small text encoders for interactive use (the
README — smallest models should even run on a modern cell phone):
README — https://google-research.github.io/vision_transformer/lit/
README — And finally a Colab to use the JAX models with both image and text encoders:
README — https://colab.research.google.com/github/google-research/vision_transformer/blob/main/lit.ipynb
README — Note that none of above models support multi-lingual inputs yet, but we're
README — working on publishing such models and will update this repository once they
README — become available.
README — This repository only contains evaluation code for LiT models. You can find the
README — training code in the `big_vision` repository:
README — https://github.com/google-research/big_vision/tree/main/big_vision/configs/proj/image_text

README — In reverse chronological order:
README — : Added LiT-B16B_2 model that was trained for 60k steps
README — (LiT_B16B: 30k) without linear head on the image side (LiT_B16B: 768) and has
README — better performance.
README — : Added the ViT and Mixer models trained from scratch using
README — [GSAM] on ImageNet without strong data augmentations. The resultant ViTs
README — outperform those of similar sizes trained using AdamW optimizer or the
README — original [SAM] algorithm, or with strong data augmentations.
README — : Added models and Colab for [LiT models](#lit-models).
README — : Added ViT-B/8 AugReg models (3 upstream checkpoints and adaptations
README — with resolution=224).
README — : Added the "When Vision Transformers Outperform
README — ResNets..." paper
README — : Added [SAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01412)
README — (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) optimized ViT and MLP-Mixer checkpoints.
README — : Added the "How to train your ViT? ..." paper, and a new
README — Colab to explore the >50k pre-trained and fine-tuned checkpoints mentioned in
README — the paper.
README — : This repository was rewritten to use Flax Linen API and
README — `ml_collections.ConfigDict` for configuration.
README — : With publication of the "How to train your ViT? ..."
README — paper, we added more than 50k ViT and hybrid models pre-trained on ImageNet and
README — ImageNet-21k with various degrees of data augmentation and model regularization,
README — and fine-tuned on ImageNet, Pets37, Kitti-distance, CIFAR-100, and Resisc45.
README — Check out [`vit_jax_augreg.ipynb`] to navigate this treasure trove of models!
README — For example, you can use that Colab to fetch the filenames of recommended
README — pre-trained and fine-tuned checkpoints from the `i21k_300` column of Table 3 in
README — : Added the R50+ViT-B/16 hybrid model (ViT-B/16 on
README — top of a Resnet-50 backbone). When pretrained on imagenet21k, this model
README — achieves almost the performance of the L/16 model with less than half the
README — computational finetuning cost. Note that "R50" is somewhat modified for the
README — B/16 variant: The original ResNet-50 has [3,4,6,3] blocks, each reducing the
README — resolution of the image by a factor of two. In combination with the ResNet
README — stem this would result in a reduction of 32x so even with a patch size of
README — (1,1) the ViT-B/16 variant cannot be realized anymore. For this reason we
README — instead use [3,4,9] blocks for the R50+B/16 variant.
README — : Added the ViT-L/16 model.
README — : Added ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 models pretrained
README — on ImageNet-21k and then fine-tuned on ImageNet at 224x224 resolution (instead
README — of default 384x384). These models have the suffix "-224" in their name.
README — They are expected to achieve 81.2% and 82.7% top-1 accuracies respectively.

CONTRIBUTING — Agreement (CLA). You (or your employer) retain the copyright to your
CONTRIBUTING — contribution; this simply gives us permission to use and redistribute your
CONTRIBUTING — contributions as part of the project. Head over to
CONTRIBUTING — <https://cla.developers.google.com/> to see your current agreements on file or
CONTRIBUTING — to sign a new one.
CONTRIBUTING — You generally only need to submit a CLA once, so if you've already submitted one
CONTRIBUTING — (even if it was for a different project), you probably don't need to do it

CONTRIBUTING — use GitHub pull requests for this purpose. Consult
CONTRIBUTING — [GitHub Help](https://help.github.com/articles/about-pull-requests/) for more
CONTRIBUTING — information on using pull requests.

awesome-transformers — Awesome projects built with Transformers
awesome-transformers — This page lists awesome projects built on top of Transformers. Transformers is more than a toolkit to use pretrained
awesome-transformers — models: it's a community of projects built around it and the Hugging Face Hub. We want Transformers to enable
awesome-transformers — developers, researchers, students, professors, engineers, and anyone else to build their dream projects.
awesome-transformers — In this list, we showcase incredibly impactful and novel projects that have pushed the field forward. We celebrate
awesome-transformers — of these projects as we reach the milestone of 100k stars as a community; but we're very open to pull requests
awesome-transformers — adding other projects to the list. If you believe a project should be here and it's not, then please, open a PR
awesome-transformers — to add it.
awesome-transformers — [gpt4all](https://github.com/nomic-ai/gpt4all)
awesome-transformers — [gpt4all](https://github.com/nomic-ai/gpt4all) is an ecosystem of open-source chatbots trained on massive collections of clean assistant data including code, stories and dialogue. It offers open-source, large language models such as LLaMA and GPT-J trained in an assistant-style.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Open-source, LLaMa, GPT-J, instruction, assistant
awesome-transformers — [recommenders](https://github.com/recommenders-team/recommenders)
awesome-transformers — This repository contains examples and best practices for building recommendation systems, provided as Jupyter notebooks. It goes over several aspects required to build efficient recommendation systems: data preparation, modeling, evaluation, model selection & optimization, as well as operationalization
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Recommender systems, AzureML
awesome-transformers — [IOPaint](https://github.com/Sanster/IOPaint)
awesome-transformers — Image inpainting tool powered by Stable Diffusion. Remove any unwanted object, defect, people from your pictures or erase and replace anything on your pictures.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: inpainting, SD, Stable Diffusion
awesome-transformers — [flair](https://github.com/flairNLP/flair)
awesome-transformers — FLAIR is a powerful PyTorch NLP framework, covering several important tasks: NER, sentiment-analysis, part-of-speech tagging, text and document embeddings, among other things.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: NLP, text embedding, document embedding, biomedical, NER, PoS, sentiment-analysis
awesome-transformers — [mindsdb](https://github.com/mindsdb/mindsdb)
awesome-transformers — MindsDB is a low-code ML platform, which automates and integrates several ML frameworks into the data stack as "AI Tables" to streamline the integration of AI into applications, making it accessible to developers of all skill levels.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Database, low-code, AI table
awesome-transformers — [langchain](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain)
awesome-transformers — [langchain](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain) is aimed at assisting in the development of apps merging both LLMs and other sources of knowledge. The library allows chaining calls to applications, creating a sequence across many tools.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: LLMs, Large Language Models, Agents, Chains
awesome-transformers — [LlamaIndex](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index)
awesome-transformers — [LlamaIndex](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index) is a project that provides a central interface to connect your LLM's with external data. It provides various kinds of indices and retrieval mechanisms to perform different LLM tasks and obtain knowledge-augmented results.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: LLMs, Large Language Models, Data Retrieval, Indices, Knowledge Augmentation
awesome-transformers — [ParlAI](https://github.com/facebookresearch/ParlAI)
awesome-transformers — [ParlAI](https://github.com/facebookresearch/ParlAI) is a python framework for sharing, training and testing dialogue models, from open-domain chitchat, to task-oriented dialogue, to visual question answering. It provides more than 100 datasets under the same API, a large zoo of pretrained models, a set of agents, and has several integrations.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Dialogue, Chatbots, VQA, Datasets, Agents
awesome-transformers — [sentence-transformers](https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers)
awesome-transformers — This framework provides an easy method to compute dense vector representations for sentences, paragraphs, and images. The models are based on transformer networks like BERT / RoBERTa / XLM-RoBERTa etc. and achieve state-of-the-art performance in various task. Text is embedding in vector space such that similar text is close and can efficiently be found using cosine similarity.
awesome-transformers — Keywords: Dense vector representations, Text embeddings, Sentence embeddings
awesome-transformers — [ludwig](https://github.com/ludwig-ai/ludwig)
awesome-transformers — Ludwig is a declarative machine learning framework that makes it easy to define machine learning pipelines using a simple and flexible data-driven configuration system.
