20211215-milvus timesync — Timesync -- All The things you should know
20211215-milvus timesync — `Time Synchronization` is the kernel part of Milvus 2.0; it affects all components of the system. This document describes the detailed design of `Time Synchronization`.
20211215-milvus timesync — There are 2 kinds of events in Milvus 2.0:
20211215-milvus timesync — DDL events
20211215-milvus timesync — create collection
20211215-milvus timesync — drop collection
20211215-milvus timesync — create partition
20211215-milvus timesync — drop partition
20211215-milvus timesync — DML events
20211215-milvus timesync — All events have a `Timestamp` to indicate when this event occurs.
20211215-milvus timesync — Suppose there are two users, `u1` and `u2`. They connect to Milvus and do the following operations at the respective timestamps.
20211215-milvus timesync — | ts | u1 | u2 |
20211215-milvus timesync — | --- | -------------------- | ------------ |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t0 | create Collection C0 | - |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t2 | - | search on C0 |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t5 | insert A1 into C0 | - |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t7 | - | search on C0 |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t10 | insert A2 | - |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t12 | - | search on C0 |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t15 | delete A1 from C0 | - |
20211215-milvus timesync — | t17 | - | search on C0 |
20211215-milvus timesync — Ideally, `u2` expects `C0` to be empty at `t2`, and could only see `A1` at `t7`; while `u2` could see both `A1` and `A2` at `t12`, but only see `A2` at `t17`.
20211215-milvus timesync — It's easy to achieve this in a `single-node` database. But for a `Distributed System`, such as `Milvus`, it's a little difficult; the following problems need to be solved:
20211215-milvus timesync — If `u1` and `u2` are on different nodes, and their time clock is not synchronized. To give an extreme example, suppose that the time of `u2` is 24 hours later than `u1`, then all the operations of `u1` can't be seen by `u2` until the next day.
20211215-milvus timesync — Network latency. If `u2` starts the `Search on C0` at `t17`, then how can it be guaranteed that all the `events` before `t17` have been processed? If the events of `delete A1 from C0` have been delayed due to the network latency, then it would lead to an incorrect state: `u2` would see both `A1` and `A2` at `t17`.
20211215-milvus timesync — `Time synchronization system` is used to solve the above problems.
20211215-milvus timesync — Timestamp Oracle(TSO)
20211215-milvus timesync — Like [TiKV](https://github.com/tikv/tikv), Milvus 2.0 provides `TSO` service. All the events must alloc timestamp from `TSO`, not from the local clock, so the first problem can be solved.
20211215-milvus timesync — `TSO` is provided by the `RootCoord` component. Clients could alloc one or more timestamp in a single request; the `proto` is defined as follows.
20211215-milvus timesync — `Timestamp` is of type `uint64`, and contains physical and logical parts.
20211215-milvus timesync — This is the format of `Timestamp`
20211215-milvus timesync — ![Timestamp struct](./graphs/time_stamp_struct.jpg)
20211215-milvus timesync — In an `AllocTimestamp` request, if `AllocTimestampRequest.count` is greater than `1`, `AllocTimestampResponse.timestamp` indicates the first available timestamp in the response.
20211215-milvus timesync — Time Synchronization
20211215-milvus timesync — To better understand `Time Synchronization`, let's introduce the data operation of Milvus 2.0 briefly.
20211215-milvus timesync — Take `Insert Operation` as an example.
20211215-milvus timesync — User can configure lots of `Proxy` to achieve load balancing, in `Milvus 2.0`
20211215-milvus timesync — User can use `SDK` to connect to any `Proxy`
20211215-milvus timesync — When `Proxy` receives `Insert` Request from `SDK`, it splits `InsertMsg` into different `MsgStream` according to the hash value of `Primary Key`
20211215-milvus timesync — Each `InsertMsg` would be assigned with a `Timestamp` before sending to the `MsgStream`
20211215-milvus timesync — Note: `MsgStream` is the wrapper of message queue, the default message queue in `Milvus 2.0` is `pulsar`*
20211215-milvus timesync — ![proxy insert](./graphs/timesync_proxy_insert_msg.png)
20211215-milvus timesync — Based on the above information, we know that the `MsgStream` has the following characteristics:
20211215-milvus timesync — In `MsgStream`, `InsertMsg` from the same `Proxy` must be incremented in timestamp
20211215-milvus timesync — In `MsgStream`, `InsertMsg` from different `Proxy` have no relationship in timestamp
20211215-milvus timesync — The following figure shows an example of `InsertMsg` in `MsgStream`. The snippet contains 5 `InsertMsg`, 3 of them from `Proxy1` and others from `Proxy2`.
20211215-milvus timesync — The 3 `InsertMsg` from `Proxy1` are incremented in timestamp, and the 2 `InsertMsg` from `Proxy2` are also incremented in timestamps, but there is no relationship between `Proxy1` and `Proxy2`.
20211215-milvus timesync — ![msgstream](./graphs/timesync_msgstream.png)
20211215-milvus timesync — So the second problem has turned into this: After reading a message from `MsgStream`, how to make sure that all the messages with smaller timestamp have been consumed?
20211215-milvus timesync — For example, when reading a message with timestamp `110` produced by `Proxy2`, but the message with timestamp `80` produced by `Proxy1`, is still in the `MsgStream`. How can this situation be handled?
20211215-milvus timesync — The following graph shows the core logic of `Time Synchronization System` in `Milvus 2.0`; it should solve the second problem.
20211215-milvus timesync — Each `Proxy` will periodically report its latest timestamp of every `MsgStream` to `RootCoord`; the default interval is `200ms`
20211215-milvus timesync — For each `Msgstream`, `Rootcoord` finds the minimum timestamp of all `Proxy` on this `Msgstream`, and inserts this minimum timestamp into the `Msgstream`
20211215-milvus timesync — When the consumer reads the timestamp inserted by the `RootCoord` on the `MsgStream`, it indicates that all messages with smaller timestamp have been consumed, so all actions that depend on this timestamp can be executed safely
20211215-milvus timesync — The message inserted by `RootCoord` into `MsgStream` is of type `TimeTick`
20211215-milvus timesync — ![upload time tick](./graphs/timesync_proxy_upload_time_tick.png)
20211215-milvus timesync — This is the `Proto` that is used by `Proxy` to report timestamp to `RootCoord`:
20211215-milvus timesync — After inserting `Timetick`, the `Msgstream` should look like this:
20211215-milvus timesync — ![msgstream time tick](./graphs/timesync_msgtream_timetick.png)
20211215-milvus timesync — `MsgStream` will process the messages in batches according to `TimeTick`, and ensure that the output messages meet the requirements of timestamp. For more details, please refer to the `MsgStream` design details.
20210731-index design — IndexCoord Design
20210731-index design — update: 7.31.2021, by [Cai.Zhang](https://github.com/xiaocai2333)
20210731-index design — Component Description
20210731-index design — IndexCoord is a component responsible for scheduling index construction tasks and maintaining index status. IndexCoord accepts requests from rootCoord to build indexes, delete indexes, and query index information. IndexCoord is responsible for assigning IndexBuildID to the request to build the index, and forwarding the request to build the index to IndexNode. IndexCoord records the status of the index, and the index file.
20210731-index design — The following figure shows the design of the indexCoord component:
20210731-index design — ![indexcoord](graphs/indexcoord_design.png)
20210731-index design — Use etcd as a reliable service
20210731-index design — IndexCoord, like the other Milvus components, relies on etcd to implement
20210731-index design — service discovery. IndexCoord relies on the lease mechanism of etcd to sense the online and offline news of IndexNode.
20210731-index design — In addition to service discovery, Milvus also uses etcd as a reliable meta storage and writes all
20210731-index design — persistent status information to etcd. The purpose is to restore a certain Milvus component to its original
20210731-index design — state after power off and restart.
20210731-index design — Receive requests about index from RootCoord
20210731-index design — IndexCoord receives requests from RootCoord to build an index, delete an index, and query the status of an index.
20210731-index design — In Milvus, index building is performed asynchronously. When IndexCoord receives a request to build an index from
20210731-index design — RootCoord, it will first check whether the same index has been created according to the index parameters. If yes, it would
20210731-index design — return the IndexBuildID of the existing task. Otherwise, it would assign a globally unique IndexBuildID to the task,
20210731-index design — record the task in the MetaTable, write the MetaTable to etcd, and then return the IndexBuildID to RootCoord.
20210731-index design — RootCoord confirms that the index building is generated successfully by the IndexBuildID. At this time, the index construction
20210731-index design — is not completed yet. IndexCoord starts a background process to find all the index tasks that need to be
20210731-index design — allocated periodically and then allocates them to IndexNode for actual execution.
20210731-index design — When IndexCoord receives a request to delete an index from RootCoord, IndexCoord traverses the MetaTable,
20210731-index design — marks the corresponding index task as deleted, and returns. It is not deleted from the MetaTable at this time.
20210731-index design — IndexCoord has another background process that periodically queries the index tasks that need to be deleted.
20210731-index design — When the index task is marked as deleted, and the index status is complete, the corresponding index task is actually
20210731-index design — deleted from the MetaTable.
20210731-index design — When IndexCoord receives a query index status request from other components, it will first check whether the corresponding
20210731-index design — index task is marked for deletion in the MetaTable. If marked for deletion, it returns that index does not exist, otherwise,
20210731-index design — it returns the index information.
20210731-index design — Feature Design
20210731-index design — IndexCoord has two main structures, NodeManager and MetaTable. NodeManager is used to manage IndexNode node information,
20210731-index design — and MetaTable is used to maintain index-related information.
20210731-index design — IndexCoord mainly has these functions:
20210731-index design — `watchNodeLoop` is mainly responsible for monitoring the changes of IndexNode nodes;
20210731-index design — `watchMetaLoop` is mainly responsible for monitoring the changes of Meta;
20210731-index design — `assignTaskLoop` is mainly responsible for assigning index building tasks;
20210731-index design — `recycleUnusedIndexFiles` is mainly responsible for cleaning up useless index files and deleted index records;
20210731-index design — The relationship between IndexCoord and IndexNode
20210731-index design — IndexCoord is responsible for assigning index construction tasks and maintaining index status.
20210731-index design — IndexNode is a node that executes index building tasks.
20210731-index design — NodeManager
20210731-index design — NodeManager is responsible for managing the node information of IndexNode, and contains a priority queue to save the load information of each IndexNode.
20210731-index design — The load information of IndexNode is based on the number of tasks executed. When the IndexCoord service starts, it first obtains the node information of all current IndexNodes from etcd,
20210731-index design — and then adds the node information to the NodeManager. After that, the online and offline information of IndexNode node is obtained from watchNodeLoop.
20210731-index design — Then it will traverse the entire MetaTable, get the load information corresponding to each IndexNode node, and update the priority queue in the NodeManager.
20210731-index design — When an index building task needs to be allocated, the IndexNode with the lowest load will be selected according to the priority queue to execute the task.
20210731-index design — MetaTable
20210731-index design — To maintain the status information of the index, we introduced MetaTable to record the status information
20210731-index design — of the index. In order to ensure that the MetaTable information is not lost after IndexCoord is powered off and
20210731-index design — restarted, we write the MetaTable information into etcd. When the IndexCoord service starts, it will first load the
20210731-index design — existing Meta information from etcd, and then monitor the changes of Meta through watchNodeLoop. In order to distinguish
20210731-index design — whether the modification of Meta was initiated by IndexCoord or IndexNode, the revision was introduced in Meta.
20210731-index design — When watchMetaLoop detects that the Meta in etcd is updated, compare the revision in Meta with the Event.Kv.Version
20210731-index design — of the etcd event. If the revision equals to Event.Kv.Version, it means that the update was initiated by IndexCoord.
20210731-index design — If the revision is less than Event.Kv.Version, it means that this Meta update was initiated by IndexNode, and IndexCoord
20210731-index design — needs to update Meta. There will be no situation where revision is greater than Event.Kv.Version.
20210731-index design — In order to prevent IndexNode from appearing in a suspended animation state, Version is introduced. When IndexCoord
20210731-index design — finds that IndexNode is offline, it assigns the unfinished tasks that IndexNode is responsible for to other IndexNodes,
20210731-index design — and adds 1 to Version. After the task is completed, it is found that the version corresponding to the task is already
20210731-index design — larger than the version corresponding to the task it is executing, and the Meta is not updated.
20210731-index design — watchNodeLoop
20210731-index design — `watchNodeLoop` is used to monitor IndexNode going online and offline. When IndexNode goes online and offline,
20210731-index design — IndexCoord adds or deletes the corresponding IndexNode information in NodeManager.
20210731-index design — watchMetaLoop
20210731-index design — `watchMetaLoop` is used to monitor whether the Meta in etcd has been changed. When the Meta in etcd is monitored,
20210731-index design — the result of the Meta update is obtained from etcd, and the `Event.Kv.Version` of the update event is compared
20210731-index design — with the `revision` in the MetaTable. If the `Event.Kv.Version` is greater than the `revision` in the MetaTable,
20210731-index design — it means that this update is initiated by IndexNode, and then updates the MetaTable in IndexCoord. Since this update
20210731-index design — is initiated by IndexNode, it indicates that this IndexNode has completed this task, so update the load of this
20210731-index design — IndexNode in NodeManager, and the task amount is reduced by one.
20210731-index design — assignTaskLoop
20210731-index design — `assignTaskLoop` is used to assign index construction tasks. There is a timer here to traverse the MetaTable regularly
20210731-index design — to filter out the tasks that need to be allocated, including unallocated tasks and tasks that have been failed due to
20210731-index design — indexNode crash. Then sort according to the version size of each task, and assign tasks with a smaller
20210731-index design — version first. The purpose is to prevent certain special tasks from occupying resources all the time and always failing
20210731-index design — to execute successfully. When a task is assigned, its corresponding Version is increased by one. Then send the task to
20210731-index design — IndexNode for execution, and update the index status in the MetaTable.
20210731-index design — recycleUnusedIndexFiles
20210731-index design — Delete useless index files, including lower version index files and index files corresponding to the deleted index.
20210731-index design — In order to distinguish whether the low version index file corresponding to the index has been cleaned up, recycled is
20210731-index design — introduced as a mark. Only after the index task is completed, the lower version index files will be cleaned up, and the
20210731-index design — index file corresponding to the lower version index file will be marked as True.
20210731-index design — This is also a timer, which periodically traverses the MetaTable to obtain the index corresponding to the index file
20210731-index design — that need to be cleaned up. If the index is marked as deleted, the information corresponding to the index is deleted
20210731-index design — in the MetaTable. Otherwise, only the lower version index file is cleaned up.
20210731-index design — IndexNode Create Index
20210731-index design — IndexNode is the execution node of index building tasks, and all index building tasks are forwarded to IndexNode by
20210731-index design — IndexCoord for execution. When IndexNode executes an index build request, it first reads IndexMeta information
20210731-index design — from etcd, and checks whether the index task is marked for deletion when IndexCoord is forwarded to IndexNode.
20210731-index design — If it is marked as deleted, then there is no need to actually build the index, just mark the index task status as
20210731-index design — completed, and then write it to etcd. When IndexCoord perceives that the status corresponding to the index is
20210731-index design — complete, it deletes the index task from the MetaTable. If it is checked that the index is not marked for deletion,
20210731-index design — then the index needs to be built. The original data must be loaded first when building the index. The original data
20210731-index design — is stored in MinIO/S3, and the storage path is notified by RootCoord in the index build request. After loading the
20210731-index design — original data, the data is deserialized into data blocks, and then cgo is called to build the index. When the index is
20210731-index design — built, the index data is serialized into data blocks, and then written into the file. The directory organization of the
20210731-index design — index file is "indexBuildID/IndexTaskVersion/partitionID/segmentID/key", where key corresponds to the serialized key
20210731-index design — of index data. After the index is built, record the index file directory in IndexMeta, and then write it to etcd.
20210731-index design — BuildIndex
20210731-index design — Index building is asynchronous, so when an index building request comes, an IndexBuildID is assigned to the task, and
20210731-index design — the task is recorded in Meta. The background process assignTaskLoop will find this task and assign it to IndexNode for
20210731-index design — execution.
20210731-index design — The following figure shows the state machine of IndexTask during execution:
20210731-index design — ![IndexState](graphs/IndexState.png)
20210731-index design — DropIndex
20210731-index design — DropIndex deletes an index based on IndexID. One IndexID corresponds to the index of an entire column. A column is
20210731-index design — divided into many segments, and each segment corresponds to an IndexBuildID. IndexCoord uses IndexBuildID to record
20210731-index design — index tasks. Therefore, when DropIndex, delete all tasks corresponding to IndexBuildID corresponding to IndexID.
20210731-index design — Key Term
20210731-index design — Meta is used to record the state of the index.
20210731-index design — Revision: The number of times IndexMeta has been changed in etcd. It's the same as Event.Kv.Version in etcd.
20210731-index design — When IndexCoord watches the IndexMeta in etcd is changed, can compare `revision` and Event.Kv.Version to determine
20210731-index design — this modification of IndexMeta is caused by IndexCoord or IndexNode. If it is caused by IndexNode, the Meta in
20210731-index design — IndexCoord must be updated.
20210731-index design — IndexMeta
20210731-index design — indexBuildID: ID of the index task.
20210731-index design — state: The state of the index.
20210731-index design — fail_reason: The reason why the index build failed.
20210731-index design — req: The request for the building index.
20210731-index design — index_file_paths: The paths of index files.
20210731-index design — mark_deleted: Mark whether the index has been deleted.
20210731-index design — nodeID: ID of the IndexNode that built the index.
20210731-index design — version: Number of retries for the index.
20210731-index design — recycled: Mark whether the unused files of the index have been cleaned up.
20211115-milvus drop collection — Drop Collection
20211115-milvus drop collection — `Milvus 2.0` uses `Collection` to represent a set of data, like `Table` in traditional database. Users can create or drop `Collection`.
20211115-milvus drop collection — This article introduces the execution path of `Drop Collection`. At the end of this article, you should know which components are involved in `Drop Collection`.
20211115-milvus drop collection — The execution flow of `Drop Collection` is shown in the following figure:
20211115-milvus drop collection — ![drop_collection](./graphs/dml_drop_collection.png)
20211115-milvus drop collection — Firstly, `SDK` sends a `DropCollection` request to `Proxy` via `Grpc`, the `proto` is defined as follows:
20211115-milvus drop collection — Once the `DropCollection` request is received, the `Proxy` would wrap this request into `DropCollectionTask`, and push this task into `DdTaskQueue` queue. After that, `Proxy` would call `WaitToFinish` method to wait until the task is finished.
20211115-milvus drop collection — There is a background service in `Proxy`, this service would get the `DropCollectionTask` from `DdTaskQueue`, and execute it in three phases:
20211115-milvus drop collection — `PreExecute`, do some static checking at this phase, such as check if `Collection Name` is legal etc.
20211115-milvus drop collection — `Execute`, at this phase, `Proxy` would send `DropCollection` request to `RootCoord` via `Grpc`, and wait the response, the `proto` is defined as below:
20211115-milvus drop collection — `PostExecute`, `Proxy` would delete `Collection`'s meta from global meta table at this phase.
20211115-milvus drop collection — `RootCoord` would wrap the `DropCollection` request into `DropCollectionReqTask`, and then call function `executeTask`. `executeTask` would return until the `context` is done or `DropCollectionReqTask.Execute` is returned.
20211115-milvus drop collection — Firstly, `RootCoord` would delete `Collection`'s meta from `metaTable`, including `schema`,`partition`, `segment`,`index`. All of these delete operations are committed in one transaction.
20211115-milvus drop collection — After `Collection`'s meta has been deleted from `metaTable`, `Milvus` would consider this collection has been deleted successfully.
20211115-milvus drop collection — `RootCoord` would alloc a timestamp from `TSO` before deleting `Collection`'s meta from `metaTable`. This timestamp is considered as the point when the collection was deleted.
20211115-milvus drop collection — `RootCoord` would send a message of `DropCollectionRequest` into `MsgStream`. Thus other components, who have subscribed to the `MsgStream`, would be notified. The `Proto` of `DropCollectionRequest` is defined as below:
20211115-milvus drop collection — After these operations, `RootCoord` would update internal timestamp.
20211115-milvus drop collection — Then `RootCoord` would start a `ReleaseCollection` request to `QueryCoord` via `Grpc` , notify `QueryCoord` to release all resources that related to this `Collection`. This `Grpc` request is done in another `goroutine`, so it would not block the main thread. The `proto` is defined as follows:
20211115-milvus drop collection — At last, `RootCoord` would send `InvalidateCollectionMetaCache` request to each `Proxy`, notify `Proxy` to remove `Collection`'s meta. The `proto` is defined as follows:
20211115-milvus drop collection — The execution flow of `QueryCoord.ReleaseCollection` is shown in the following figure:
20211115-milvus drop collection — ![release_collection](./graphs/dml_release_collection.png)
20211115-milvus drop collection — `QueryCoord` would wrap `ReleaseCollection` into `ReleaseCollectionTask`, and push the task into `TaskScheduler`
20211115-milvus drop collection — There is a background service in `QueryCoord`. This service would get the `ReleaseCollectionTask` from `TaskScheduler`, and execute it in three phases:
20211115-milvus drop collection — `PreExecute`, `ReleaseCollectionTask` would only print debug log at this phase.
20211115-milvus drop collection — `Execute`, there are two jobs at this phase:
20211115-milvus drop collection — send a `ReleaseDQLMessageStream` request to `RootCoord` via `Grpc`, `RootCoord` would redirect the `ReleaseDQLMessageStream` request to each `Proxy`, and notify the `Proxy` that stop processing any message of this `Collection` anymore. The `proto` is defined as follows:
20211115-milvus drop collection — send a `ReleaseCollection` request to each `QueryNode` via `Grpc`, and notify the `QueryNode` to release all the resources related to this `Collection`, including `Index`, `Segment`, `FlowGraph`, etc. `QueryNode` would no longer read any message from this `Collection`'s `MsgStream` anymore
20211115-milvus drop collection — `PostExecute`, `ReleaseCollectionTask` would only print debug log at this phase.
20211115-milvus drop collection — After these operations, `QueryCoord` would send `ReleaseCollection`'s response to `RootCoord`.
20211115-milvus drop collection — At `Step 8`, `RootCoord` has sent a message of `DropCollectionRequest` into `MsgStream`. `DataNode` would subscribe this `MsgStream`, so that it would be notified to release related resources. The execution flow is shown in the following figure.
20211115-milvus drop collection — ![release_collection](./graphs/dml_release_flow_graph_on_data_node.png)
20211115-milvus drop collection — In `DataNode`, each `MsgStream` will have a `FlowGraph`, which processes all messages. When the `DataNode` receives the message of `DropCollectionRequest`, `DataNode` would notify `BackGroundGC`, which is a background service on `DataNode`, to release resources.
20211115-milvus drop collection — _Notes_:
20211115-milvus drop collection — Currently, the `DataCoord` doesn't have response to the `DropCollection`. So the `Collection`'s `segment meta` still exists in the `DataCoord`'s `metaTable`, and the `Binlog` files belonging to this `Collection` still exist in the persistent storage.
20211115-milvus drop collection — Currently, the `IndexCoord` doesn't have response to the `DropCollection`. So the `Collection`'s `index file` still exists in the persistent storage.
20220725-dynamic-config — MEP: Dynamic Configuration
20220725-dynamic-config — Current state: "Accepted"
20220725-dynamic-config — ISSUE: https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/issues/18300
20220725-dynamic-config — Keywords: config etcd
20220725-dynamic-config — Released: 2.3.0
20220725-dynamic-config — Summary(required)
20220725-dynamic-config — At present, there are numerous configurations in Milvus that require a restart of Milvus to take effect. This can interrupt service in production environments and is not friendly to operations and maintenance. In this MEP, a solution for dynamically updating configurations will be provided so that users can make configuration changes without restarting the cluster.
20220725-dynamic-config — Motivation(required)
20220725-dynamic-config — Ability to dynamically modify configurations and expose current configuration information through API, simplifying operational complexity.
20220725-dynamic-config — Public Interfaces(optional)
20220725-dynamic-config — No new public interfaces changed.
20220725-dynamic-config — Design Details(required)
20220725-dynamic-config — Support multiple config sources, including Etcd, environment variables, and configuration files. On this basis, add watch events for changes in the Etcd config path and file changes. When a change event occurs, broadcast it to subscribers through an event handler. Subscribers can decide on subsequent logic based on this to achieve the requirement of dynamically modifying configurations.
20220725-dynamic-config — Configuration priority: Etcd > Environment > milvus.yaml; higher-priority configurations override lower-priority ones. Even if a higher-priority configuration is deleted, lower-priority configurations can still be used.
20220725-dynamic-config — To ensure compatibility, ignore case sensitivity and characters such as / . \_ when dealing with configuration item keys.
20220725-dynamic-config — ![flowchart](graphs/dynamic_config_flowchart.jpg)
20220725-dynamic-config — ref: https://github.com/go-chassis/go-archaius/
20220725-dynamic-config — No-Goal (Not in this release plan)
20220725-dynamic-config — Configuration grading
20220725-dynamic-config — Node override config
20220725-dynamic-config — Collection override config
20220725-dynamic-config — Support for more cloud configs such as Consul, Zookeeper, etc.
20220725-dynamic-config — Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan(optional)
20220725-dynamic-config — Compatible with old versions.
20220725-dynamic-config — Test Plan(required)
20220725-dynamic-config — Verify the ability to dynamically modify configurations in etcd.
20220725-dynamic-config — Verify the ability of helm and operator to deploy milvus.yaml and modify configurations.
20220725-dynamic-config — Verify the effectiveness of business operations after partially modifying dynamic configurations.
20220725-dynamic-config — Verify version compatibility under dynamic configuration.
20220725-dynamic-config — Rejected Alternatives(optional)
20220725-dynamic-config — References(optional)
20220105-proxy — As the user access layer of Milvus, Proxy mainly plays a role that does some checks and preprocessing for requests from
20220105-proxy — clients and then forwards these requests to other components, such as Root Coordinator, Data Coordinator, Query
20220105-proxy — Coordinator, Index Coordinator. The below figure shows how Proxy interacts with other components.
20220105-proxy — <img src="./graphs/proxy.png" width=700>
20220105-proxy — Proxy divides requests from clients into three classes: `DdRequest`, `DmRequest`, `DqRequest`.
20220105-proxy — DdRequest is the shorthand of `Data Definition Request`. It means an operation on the meta information of
20220105-proxy — collections, including two parts. One part is of the writing operations on collections, such as defining a schema,
20220105-proxy — creating or dropping a partition, creating or dropping the index, etc. Another part is of the reading operations on
20220105-proxy — collections, such as listing all collections or partitions, checking if a collection or a partition exists.
20220105-proxy — DmRequest means `Data Manipulation Request`. These requests perform a writing operation on collections, including
20220105-proxy — inserting records into a collection, deleting some specific records of a collection.
20220105-proxy — DqRequest means `Data Query Request`. These requests perform a reading operation on collections, such as searching on a
20220105-proxy — collection, querying for specific records of a collection, etc.
20220105-proxy — For every request, Proxy will first check if it's valid to be executed by Milvus and if the request is invalid then
20220105-proxy — Proxy will return the error to clients and won't continue to forward this request to other components. The check
20220105-proxy — operation of Proxy includes two parts, one part is static check and another is dynamic check. The static check includes
20220105-proxy — parameters check, constraints check, etc. The dynamic check will check some related dependencies of the request, take
20220105-proxy — search requests as an example, Proxy should check if the related collection exists in Milvus.
20220105-proxy — Also, Proxy will do some preprocessing for every request. Proxy will do little things for some requests in the
20220105-proxy — preprocessing stage and a lot more for other requests. Every object in Milvus will be assigned with an `ID`, such as
20220105-proxy — `CollectionID`, `PartitionID`, `IndexID`, `SegmentID`, etc. Components in Milvus communicate with each other by the
20220105-proxy — object IDs, however, users only know the object name. So as a user access layer of Milvus, Proxy should translate
20220105-proxy — the object name into object ID. Also taking search request as an example, Proxy should translate the `CollectionName` into
20220105-proxy — `CollectionID` and then the Query Node will recognize the request. Proxy holds a cache that translates object name into
20220105-proxy — object id and dynamically updates the cache.
20220105-proxy — Service Discovery based on etcd
20220105-proxy — As you know, Proxy depends on some other components. So how Proxy knows the other nodes' information such as host and port,
20220105-proxy — it is also called how Milvus implements the service discovery mechanism? As a cloud-native vector database, Milvus uses
20220105-proxy — etcd to provide service registration and service discovery. Every node in Milvus registers its node information(including host,
20220105-proxy — port, ID etc) into etcd after startup. Nodes should specify the prefix and key of etcd when registration. Nodes with the
20220105-proxy — same type have the same prefix in etcd, while nodes with different types have different prefixes. Every key in etcd can be assigned with a lease, and you can specify the `time-to-live(ttl)` of the
20220105-proxy — lease. Milvus uses this mechanism to check if a node is online. When a node is healthy, it will continuously renew the
20220105-proxy — lease in etcd. Otherwise, if some exceptions occurred in a node, or a node stopped to renew the lease, etcd would delete
20220105-proxy — the related node information. By using this mechanism, nodes in Milvus know if there are any other nodes going to be
20220105-proxy — online or offline and synchronize the latest node information.
20220105-proxy — Interaction with Root Coordinator
20220105-proxy — Proxy will forward the DdRequest to Root Coordinator. These requests include:
20220105-proxy — CreateCollection
20220105-proxy — DropCollection
20220105-proxy — HasCollection
20220105-proxy — DescribeCollection
20220105-proxy — ShowCollections
20220105-proxy — CreatePartition
20220105-proxy — DropPartition
20220105-proxy — HasPartition
20220105-proxy — ShowPartitions
20220105-proxy — CreateIndex
20220105-proxy — DropIndex
20220105-proxy — DescribeIndex
20220105-proxy — GetIndexBuildProgress
20220105-proxy — GetIndexState
20220105-proxy — Proxy handles the DdRequest sequentially. When and only when the earlier entered requests are done, the next request
20220105-proxy — would be handled. Proxy forwards these requests to Root Coordinator, waits until getting results from Root Coordinator, and then
20220105-proxy — returns to clients with results or errors.
20220105-proxy — Milvus does not support transactions, but it should guarantee the deterministic execution of every operation. A timestamp
20220105-proxy — is tagged on each request. When a request enters Milvus, Proxy tags a timestamp that was assigned by Root Coordinator.
20220105-proxy — The component that assigns timestamp in Root Coordinator is called `Timestamp Oracle (TSO)`. TSO ensures that each
20220105-proxy — timestamp is globally increasing.
20220105-proxy — Milvus 2.0 implements the unified Lambda architecture, which integrates the processing of the incremental and historical
20220105-proxy — data. Compared with the Kappa architecture, Milvus 2.0 introduces log backfill, which stores log snapshots and indexes
20220105-proxy — in the object storage to improve failure recovery efficiency and query performance. To break unbounded (stream) data
20220105-proxy — down into bounded windows, Milvus embraces a new watermark mechanism, which slices the stream data into multiple message
20220105-proxy — packs according to write time or event time, and maintains a timeline for users to query by time.
20220105-proxy — To support this watermark mechanism, Proxy should report the timestamp statistics of the physical channel to Root
20220105-proxy — Coordinator periodically. When Proxy knows all operations of a specific were done before a `ts`, then Proxy will report
20220105-proxy — the `ts` and inform Root Coordinator that updates the timestamp statistics.
20220105-proxy — Proxy holds a cache about meta information of collections. The meta information includes `CollectionID`, `Schema`,
20220105-proxy — `PartitionID`, etc. Components in Milvus communicate with each other using `CollectionID` and `PartitionID`, so the
20220105-proxy — object name in a request will be translated to object ID in Proxy. When the meta is not hit in the cache, Proxy will update
20220105-proxy — the cache from Root Coordinator. At the same time, in order to keep the consistency of cache, when there are any changes
20220105-proxy — of meta information in Root Coordinator, it will inform all Proxies to clear the related meta cache, and any newer
20220105-proxy — requests will get the latest meta information.
20220105-proxy — For inserts to a collection that is auto_id configured in the collection schema, Proxy assigns a primary key for
20220105-proxy — every row of insert requests. For now, the only supported data type of auto-generated primary field is `int64`. Proxy
20220105-proxy — applies for a batch of primary keys from Root Coordinator and caches them for local assignments. When the primary keys in the cache
20220105-proxy — are not enough, Proxy will continue to apply for another batch of primary keys.
20220105-proxy — Proxy forwards ReleaseCollection and ReleasePartition to Query Coordinator, Query Coordinator then informs Root
20220105-proxy — Coordinator the events. After that, Root Coordinator will inform all Proxies to close the search-related and
20220105-proxy — search-result-related message streams.
20220105-proxy — Interaction with MsgStream
20220105-proxy — In Milvus 2.0, the log broker serves as the system 'backbone': All data insert and update operations must go through the
20220105-proxy — log broker, and worker nodes execute CRUD operations by subscribing to and consuming logs. This design reduces system
20220105-proxy — complexity by moving core functions such as data persistence and flashback down to the storage layer, and log pub-sub
20220105-proxy — make the system even more flexible and better positioned for future scaling.
20220105-proxy — So, we should configure a group of Virtual Channels for every collection. Now every virtual channel has a unique related
20220105-proxy — physical channel. Take pulsar as an example, the physical channel mentioned here means the topic of pulsar.
20220105-proxy — For DmRequest, data will be written to DmChannels, while for DqRequest, requests will be written to DqRequestChannel,
20220105-proxy — and the corresponding results of query requests will be written to DqResultChannel.
20220105-proxy — As the number of tables increases, the number of DmChannels increases on demand, and the number of physical channels
20220105-proxy — also increases on demand. In the future, the number of physical channels in the system can also be limited to a fixed
20220105-proxy — number, such as 1024. In this case, the same physical channel will be mapped to virtual channels of different
20220105-proxy — collections. Shown in the figure below.
20220105-proxy — ![collection_dm_channels](./graphs/collection_dm_channels.png)
20220105-proxy — When a collection is created, Root Coordinator need to decide the number of its DmChannels and the physical
20220105-proxy — channels mapped by each virtual channel, and persist these kinds of information as the meta information of the collection;
20220105-proxy — In addition, when the system finds that the collection receives DmRequest frequently, we can allocate more virtual channels
20220105-proxy — to the collection to increase the parallelism and thus increase the system throughput. This function is a key point of
20220105-proxy — future work.
20220105-proxy — For DqRequest, request and result data are written to the stream. The request data will be written to DqRequestChannel,
20220105-proxy — and the result data will be written to DqResultChannel. Proxy will write the request of the collection into the
20220105-proxy — DqRequestChannel, and the DqRequestChannel will be jointly subscribed by a group of query nodes. When all query nodes
20220105-proxy — receive the DqRequest, they will write the query results into the DqResultChannel corresponding to the collection. As
20220105-proxy — the consumer of the DqResultChannel, Proxy is responsible for collecting the query results and aggregating them,
20220105-proxy — The result is then returned to the client.
20220105-proxy — The allocation logic of DqRequestChannel and DqResultChannel of a collection is allocated by the Query Coordinator. Proxy needs to ask the Query Coordinator for the names of DqRequestChannel and DqResultChannel of a collection.
20220105-proxy — DqRequestChannel and DqResultChannel do not need to be persisted and can be freely allocated by Query Coordinator. In
20220105-proxy — the actual implementation, the DqRequestChannel of each collection can be exclusive, and the DqResultChannel can be
20220105-proxy — exclusive or shared by all collections on Proxy. When Proxy applies for the DqRequestChannel and DqResultChannel
20220105-proxy — information of the collection from the Query Coordinator, it can attach Proxy's own ID: ProxyID.
20220105-proxy — With DqRequestChannel of the collection, Proxy will create a msgstream object to generate data into
20220105-proxy — DqRequestChannel. With the DqResultChannel of the collection, Proxy will create a msgstream object, and Proxy will
20220105-proxy — consume the data in the DqResultChannel. When these msgstream objects are closed, messages cannot be written to or
20220105-proxy — consumed from them.
20220105-proxy — ![proxy_channels](./graphs/proxy_channels.png)
20220105-proxy — Interaction with Data Coordinator
20220105-proxy — In Milvus, segment is the basic read-write and search unit of data. After consuming the data in DmChannel, the data
20220105-proxy — nodes will store the data in the object storage in the unit of segment (in the actual implementation, the segment will
20220105-proxy — be divided into multiple small files for writing). In Milvus, segment is uniquely identified by segment ID, and the
20220105-proxy — allocation logic of segment ID is the responsibility of the Data Coordinator. The SegmentID to which each row of data is
20220105-proxy — written needs to be determined before writing to DmChannel. For a write operation, Proxy will hash each row of data
20220105-proxy — again according to the hash value of its primary key, and then determine into which DmChannel each row of data enters. After
20220105-proxy — collecting the number of pieces to be written by each DmChannel, it applies to the data coordinator for which SegmentIDs the
20220105-proxy — newly written data of these dmchannels belong to. In the specific implementation, Proxy needs to preallocate some
20220105-proxy — quotas to the Data Coordinator to avoid frequent direct GRPC communication with the Data Coordinator.
20220105-proxy — One consideration for uniformly assigning SegmentIDs by Data Coordinator is that Data Coordinator is responsible for
20220105-proxy — coordinating the total number of each segment not to be too large, and the location is near a water level, so that the
20220105-proxy — size of the segment is limited to a certain range.
20220105-proxy — Other interactions between Proxy and Data Coordinator are mainly reflected in Proxy querying Data Coordinator for
20220105-proxy — the status and statistical information of the segment of the collection. LoadCollection is an example. The
20220105-proxy — synchronization semantics of the current LoadCollection needs to know the number of rows currently persisted, so the
20220105-proxy — Proxy needs to ask the Data Coordinator for the total number of rows currently persisted.
20220105-proxy — Interaction with Query Coordinator
20220105-proxy — For LoadCollection, LoadPartition, ReleaseCollection, ReleasePartition requests, Proxy directly forwards these
20220105-proxy — requests to Query Coordinator for execution after checking and preprocessing these requests. When Proxy receives
20220105-proxy — feedback from Query Coordinator, it returns the feedback results to the clients.
20220105-proxy — The semantics of the Load operation is to load Collection or Partition from persistent storage into the memory of Query
20220105-proxy — Nodes, or import streaming data into QueryNode so that it can be queried. If the load operation is not performed, the
20220105-proxy — query operation on the Collection or Partition cannot be performed. For the Load operation, Query Coordinator is
20220105-proxy — responsible for allocating DmChannels to different queryNodes and subscribing to them, and is responsible for receiving
20220105-proxy — those stream data. QueryCoordinator also allocates and loads the segments that have been persisted in storage in
20220105-proxy — Query Nodes.
20220105-proxy — The semantics of the Release operation is the reverse operation of the Load operation, and the function is to unload the
20220105-proxy — data of the Collection or Partition from the memory. For Release operations, Query Coordinator is responsible for
20220105-proxy — notifying query nodes to unload the corresponding Collection or Partition in memory, and then sending the
20220105-proxy — ReleaseDqlMessageStream command to Root Coordinator, and Root Coordinator is responsible for broadcasting the
20220105-proxy — ReleaseDqlMessageStream command to all Proxies, so that all related streams used to send search requests and receive
20220105-proxy — search result in Proxy will be closed.
20220105-proxy — The other interaction between Proxy and Query Coordinator is that Proxy needs to query from Query Coordinator for statistics
20220105-proxy — about Collection, Partition, and Segment. Taking ShowCollections as an example, if the ShowCollections parameter
20220105-proxy — specifies that the query is for Collections that have been loaded into memory, the ShowCollection request will be
20220105-proxy — forwarded to QueryCoordinator, and QueryCoordinator will return a list of all the recorded Collections loaded into
20220105-proxy — memory. Taking LoadCollection as another example, its synchronization semantics is that the number of rows loaded in
20220105-proxy — the memory must be no less than the number of rows that have been persisted. This requires Proxy to ask the Query
20220105-proxy — Coordinator for the sum of the number of rows currently loaded into the query nodes in the Collection.
20220105-proxy — Decouple Functionality and Communication
20220105-proxy — ![decouple](./graphs/decouple.jpeg)
20220105-proxy — As shown in the figure above, there are interactions between various types of components in the Milvus2.0 system. The
20220105-proxy — implementation of these interactions will vary according to the deployment of Milvus. Milvus Standalone allows the
20220105-proxy — various components of Milvus as a whole independent process to be deployed on a single node. Milvus Cluster distributes
20220105-proxy — all components on multiple nodes. In Milvus Standalone, the interaction between components can be parameter transfer
20220105-proxy — between functions or communication between Grpc. The log system can be either Pulsar or RocksDb. In Milvus Cluster, the
20220105-proxy — communication between components is mostly undertaken by grpc, and the message flow is mostly by Pulsar.
20220105-proxy — Therefore, in the original design, Milvus 2.0 decoupled the core function of the component and the communication between
20220105-proxy — components. Taking Proxy as an example, the core function of Proxy component is determined and has nothing to do
20220105-proxy — with the deployment form. In the project's internal/proxy directory, it contains the functions of the core components of
20220105-proxy — Proxy; and internal/distributed/proxy contain the core functions of Proxy in the deployment of cluster distributed
20220105-proxy — which contains the re-encapsulation and communication implementation of Proxy. The following article will mainly
20220105-proxy — introduce the functions of Proxy core layer.
20220105-proxy — Core Components of Proxy
20220105-proxy — Proxy is mainly composed of four modules: taskScheduler, channelsMgr, channelsTimeTicker, globalMetaCache. taskScheduler
20220105-proxy — is responsible for task scheduling; channelsMgr is responsible for the management of DmChannels, DqRequestChannel,
20220105-proxy — DqResultChannel and corresponding MsgStream objects of each Collection; channelsTimeTicker is responsible for collecting
20220105-proxy — the timestamp information of all physical Channels regularly; globalMetaCache is responsible for caching the metadata of
20220105-proxy — Collection and Partition.
20220105-proxy — taskScheduler
20220105-proxy — There are three main functions in taskScheduler:
20220105-proxy — Schedule task
20220105-proxy — Maintain the snapshot of timestamp statistics
20220105-proxy — Receive the search results from all streams and then distribute them to related task
20220105-proxy — taskScheduler maintains three queues: ddQueue, dmQueue and dqQueue correspond to DdRequest, DmRequest, and DqRequest
20220105-proxy — respectively. The interface of taskQueue is defined as follows:
20220105-proxy — Proxy encapsulates each request with a corresponding task object. Each task object implements the task interface. The
20220105-proxy — definition of the task interface is as follows:
20220105-proxy — Each specific task object must implement the interface defined by the task.
20220105-proxy — The key members of taskQueue are unissuedTasks of type List and activateTasks of type maps. Among them, unissuedTasks
20220105-proxy — contain all tasks that have not been scheduled, and activateTasks contain all tasks that are being scheduled.
20220105-proxy — When the external caller of taskScheduler stuffs the task into the corresponding taskQueue, it will call the OnEnqueue
20220105-proxy — interface of the task. When OnEnqueue is called, the SetID of the task will be called to assign the taskID to the task.
20220105-proxy — The taskID is globally unique and is used to identify the task. OnEnqueue will also call task.SetTs to set the timestamp
20220105-proxy — for the task. It can be seen that the timestamp of entering the queue must be greater than the timestamp that already
20220105-proxy — exists in the queue, and it will also be greater than the timestamp of the task that exists in activateTask. At the end
20220105-proxy — of the task's OnEnqueue, call the taskQueue's addUnissuedTask to add the task to the unissuedTasks. When OnEnqueue is
20220105-proxy — executed, the external caller of taskScheduler calls WaitToFinish of the task to synchronously block and wait for the
20220105-proxy — execution of the task to be done.
20220105-proxy — When taskScheduler's background scheduling coroutine decides to schedule a task, it will call the taskQueue's
20220105-proxy — PopUnissuedTask to remove a task from unissuedTasks, and then call the taskQueue's AddActivateTask to put the task in
20220105-proxy — the activateTasks Map. Then perform operations on the task. In the execution process of the task, its PreExecute,
20220105-proxy — Execute, and PostExecute interfaces will be called in sequence. If an exception occurs in a certain step, the error will
20220105-proxy — be returned in advance and the subsequent steps will be skipped. Whether it is a successful execution or an error, the
20220105-proxy — Notify method will be called, this method will wake up the coroutine that is blocking and waiting for the Task. When the
20220105-proxy — task is executed, the PopActivateTask of the taskQueue is called to take the task out of activateTasks.
20220105-proxy — The following figure is a schematic diagram of taskScheduler's scheduling of DdQueue.
20220105-proxy — For the task of taskScheduler in DdQueue, it must be scheduled serially, the task that enters the queue first is
20220105-proxy — executed, and at most only one task is executing. After the task at the head of the queue is executed, other tasks in
20220105-proxy — the queue can be scheduled.
20220105-proxy — ![task_scheduler_1](./graphs/task_scheduler_1.png)
20220105-proxy — The following figure is a schematic diagram of taskScheduler's scheduling of DmQueue.
20220105-proxy — The tasks in DmQueue can be scheduled in parallel. In a scheduling process, taskScheduler will execute several tasks
20220105-proxy — from each task concurrently.
20220105-proxy — ![task_scheduler_2](./graphs/task_scheduler_2.png)
20220105-proxy — The following figure is a schematic diagram of taskScheduler's scheduling of DqQueue.
20220105-proxy — ![task_scheduler_1](./graphs/task_scheduler_2.png)
20220105-proxy — The tasks in DqQueue can be scheduled in parallel. In a scheduling process, taskScheduler will execute several tasks
20220105-proxy — concurrently.
20220105-proxy — In order to facilitate the channelsTimeTicker component to obtain the synchronization point information corresponding to all
20220105-proxy — DmChannels, the taskScheduler needs to maintain a copy of the time statistics of the physical channels of all currently
20220105-proxy — unexecuted and executing tasks in the DmQueue. The member pChanSatisticsInfos is a map containing the mapping from pChan
20220105-proxy — to pChanStatInfo pointers. Among them, pChan is an alias of string, and pChanStatInfo is a custom structure, defined as
20220105-proxy — follows:
20220105-proxy — pChan represents the name of the physical channel corresponding to the DmChannel. The pChanStatInfo structure contains 3
20220105-proxy — members minTs, maxTs and tsSet. minTs and maxTs respectively represent the minimum and maximum timestamps of all tasks
20220105-proxy — related to the pChan in the current DmQueue. tsSet represents the set of timestamps of all tasks in DmQueue. When the
20220105-proxy — task enters the DmQueue, it will call the addPChanStats method of the queue, add the task's own timestamp to the
20220105-proxy — collection of pChanStatInfo's tsSet, and use the task's own maxTs to recalculate the pChanStatInfo's maxTs. The
20220105-proxy — calculation method is if its own maxTs is greater than pChanStatInfo MaxTs in pChanStatInfo, then update maxTs in
20220105-proxy — pChanStatInfo. Since the newly added timestamp is definitely greater than the existing timestamp, there is no need to
20220105-proxy — update minTs. When the PopActivateTask interface of the Queue is called to take the task out of the DmTaskQueue, the
20220105-proxy — popPChanStats interface of the Queue is called to delete the task timestamp from the timestamp set tsSet of
20220105-proxy — pChanStatInfo, and recalculate the minimum timestamp minTs.
20220105-proxy — DmQueue maintains the timestamp statistics of pChans and provides the method getPChanStatsInfo to the caller.
20220105-proxy — pChanStatistics is defined as follows:
20220105-proxy — The return value of this method includes a pChan to pChanStatistics pointer mapping. pChanStatistics includes two
20220105-proxy — members minTs and maxTs, which respectively represent the minimum and maximum timestamps of all tasks that have not been
20220105-proxy — completed on pChan. The channelsTimeTicker collects timestamp information mainly depends on this method. The awakened
20220105-proxy — coroutine reduces the timestamp result and sends the final timestamp result back to the RootCoord.
20220105-proxy — taskScheduler is also responsible for collecting the results of search requests. For each search request, when Proxy
20220105-proxy — writes the request to the DqRequestChannel, it will attach the ReqID, and the query nodes will also bring the ReqID back
20220105-proxy — when writing the search result back to the DqResultChannel. taskScheduler will start a background coroutine to consume
20220105-proxy — search results from DqResultChannel, and then distribute messages according to the ReqID in it. When several results of
20220105-proxy — the same ReqID are collected and the termination condition is reached, these results will be passed to the blocking task
20220105-proxy — coroutine which is waiting. The waken task will reduce the search results and then send the final search result to
20220105-proxy — clients.
20220105-proxy — channelsMgr
20220105-proxy — channelsMgr is responsible for the management of DmChannels, DqRequestChannel, DqResultChannel and corresponding
20220105-proxy — MsgStream objects of each Collection. The interface is defined as follows:
20220105-proxy — getChannels and getVChannels
20220105-proxy — getVChannels returns a list that represents all virtual DmChannels of collection, getChannels returns a list that
20220105-proxy — represents all physical DmChannels of collection. The two lists correspond one-to-one according to a position.
20220105-proxy — createDMLStream and getDMLStream
20220105-proxy — createDMLStream creates the dml message stream of a collection;
20220105-proxy — getDMLStream returns the dml message stream of a collection;
20220105-proxy — Proxy uses these dml message streams to write dml data, such as insert requests.
20220105-proxy — createDQLStream and getDQLStream
20220105-proxy — createDQLStream creates the dql message stream of a collection;
20220105-proxy — getDQLStream returns the dql message stream of a collection;
20220105-proxy — Proxy uses these dql message streams to send search requests.
20220105-proxy — The Remove related operation is to delete the corresponding message stream object, but the stream is not immediately
20220105-proxy — closed because maybe there are some data that needs to be written into stream currently.
20220105-proxy — channelsTimeTicker
20220105-proxy — channelsTimeTicker is responsible for regularly collecting the synchronization timestamp information of all physical channels.
20220105-proxy — addPChan and removePChan
20220105-proxy — addPChan adds a physical channel to channelsTimeTicker, channelsTimeTicker only sends the information of existing
20220105-proxy — pChans to Root Coordinator;
20220105-proxy — getMinTsStatistics
20220105-proxy — getMinTsStatistics returns the timestamp statistics of physical channels, there is a background coroutine in Proxy
20220105-proxy — that call getMinTsStatistics periodically and then send the timestamp statistics to Root Coordinator;
20220105-proxy — getLastTick
20220105-proxy — getLastTick returns the minimum timestamp which has already been synchronized of a physical channel;
20220105-proxy — channelsTimeTicker will maintain the map minTsStatistics that can be synchronized and the map currents that will be
20220105-proxy — synchronized. They are all mappings from pChan to Timestamp. The channelsTimeTicker itself has a background coroutine,
20220105-proxy — which periodically calls getPChanStatsInfo of DmQueue to obtain the minimum and maximum timestamp information pChanStats
20220105-proxy — of all unfinished tasks. channelsTimeTicker will also request a timestamp from Root Coordinator as now.
20220105-proxy — channelsTimeTicker updates minTsStatistics and currents according to the relationship between now, minTsStatistics,
20220105-proxy — currents, and pChanStats. The specific algorithm is as follows:
20220105-proxy — globalMetaCache
20220105-proxy — globalMetaCache is responsible for caching the meta-information of Collection and Partition. These meta-information
20220105-proxy — include CollectionID, PartitionID, CollectionSchema, etc.
20220105-proxy — The interface of Cache is defined as follows:
20220105-proxy — getCollectionID
20220105-proxy — GetCollectionID returns the collection ID of collection;
20220105-proxy — GetPartitions
20220105-proxy — GetPartitions returns a mapping which maps all partition names to partition IDs of collection;
20220105-proxy — GetPartition
20220105-proxy — GetPartition returns the partition ID of a specific partition and collection;
20220105-proxy — GetCollectionSchema
20220105-proxy — GetCollectionSchema returns the schema of collection;
20220105-proxy — RemoveCollection
20220105-proxy — RemoveCollection removes the meta information of collection;
20220105-proxy — RemovePartition
20220105-proxy — RemovePartition removes the meta information of partition;

20211227-milvus create index — Create Index
20211227-milvus create index — `Index system` is the core part of `Milvus`, which is used to speed up the searches, this document introduces which components are involved in `Create Index`,and what these components do.
20211227-milvus create index — The execution flow of `Create Index` is shown in the following figure:
20211227-milvus create index — ![create_index](./graphs/milvus_create_index.png)
20211227-milvus create index — Firstly, `SDK` starts a `CreateIndex` request to `Proxy` via `Grpc`, the `proto` is defined as follows:
20211227-milvus create index — When received the `CreateIndex` request, the `Proxy` would wrap this request into `CreateIndexTask`, and push this task into `DdTaskQueue` queue. After that, `Proxy` would call method of `WatiToFinish` to wait until the task finished.
20211227-milvus create index — There is a background service in `Proxy`, this service would get the `CreateIndexTask` from `DdTaskQueue`, and execute it in three phases.
20211227-milvus create index — `PreExecute`, do some static checking at this phase, such as check if the index param is legal, etc.
20211227-milvus create index — `Execute`, at this phase, `Proxy` would send `CreateIndex` request to `RootCoord` via `Grpc`, and wait the response, the `proto` is defined as the following:
20211227-milvus create index — `PostExecute`, `CreateIndexTask` does nothing at this phase, and returns directly.
20211227-milvus create index — `RootCoord` would wrap the `CreateIndex` request into `CreateIndexReqTask`, and then call function `executeTask`. `executeTask` would return until the `context` is done or `CreateIndexReqTask.Execute` returned.
20211227-milvus create index — According to the index type and index parameters, `RootCoord` lists all the `Segments` that need to be indexed on this `Collection`. `RootCoord` would only check those `Segments` which have been flushed at this stage. We will describe how to deal with those newly added segments and growing segments later.
20211227-milvus create index — For each `Segment`, `RootCoord` would start a `Grpc` request to `DataCoord` to get `Binlog` paths of that `Segment`, the `proto` is defined as following:

20211217-milvus create collection — Create Collection
20211217-milvus create collection — `Milvus 2.0` uses `Collection` to represent a set of data, like `Table` in a traditional database. User can create or drop `Collection`.
20211217-milvus create collection — This article introduces the execution path of `CreateCollection`, at the end of this article, you should know which components are involved in `CreateCollection`.
20211217-milvus create collection — The execution flow of `CreateCollection` is shown in the following figure:
20211217-milvus create collection — ![create_collection](./graphs/dml_create_collection.png)
20211217-milvus create collection — Firstly, `SDK` starts a `CreateCollection` request to `Proxy` via `Grpc`, the `proto` is defined as follows:
20211217-milvus create collection — When receiving the `CreateCollection` request, `Proxy` would wrap this request into `CreateCollectionTask`, and pushes this task into `DdTaskQueue` queue. After that, `Proxy` would call `WaitToFinish` method to wait until the task is finished.
20211217-milvus create collection — There is a background service in `Proxy`, this service would get the `CreateCollectionTask` from `DdTaskQueue`, and execute it in three phases.
20211217-milvus create collection — `PreExecute`, do some static checking at this phase, such as check if `Collection Name` and `Field Name` are legal, if there are duplicate columns, etc.
20211217-milvus create collection — `Execute`, at this phase, `Proxy` would send `CreateCollection` request to `RootCoord` via `Grpc`, and wait for response, the `proto` is defined as follows:
20211217-milvus create collection — `PostExecute`, `CreateCollectionTask` does nothing at this phase, and return directly.
20211217-milvus create collection — `RootCoord` would wrap the `CreateCollection` request into `CreateCollectionReqTask`, and then call function `executeTask`. `executeTask` would return until the `context` is done or `CreateCollectionReqTask.Execute` is returned.
20211217-milvus create collection — `CreateCollectionReqTask.Execute` would alloc `CollectionID` and default `PartitionID`, and set `Virtual Channel` and `Physical Channel`, which are used by `MsgStream`, then write the `Collection`'s meta into `metaTable`
20211217-milvus create collection — After `Collection`'s meta written into `metaTable`, `Milvus` would consider this collection has been created successfully.
20211217-milvus create collection — `RootCoord` would alloc a timestamp from `TSO` before writing `Collection`'s meta into `metaTable`, and this timestamp is considered as the point when the collection was created
20211217-milvus create collection — At last `RootCoord` will send a message of `CreateCollectionRequest` into `MsgStream`, and other components, who have subscribed to the `MsgStream`, would be notified. The `Proto` of `CreateCollectionRequest` is defined as follows:
20211217-milvus create collection — After the above operations, `RootCoord` would update the internal timestamp and return, so `Proxy` would get the response.
20211217-milvus create collection — _Notes:_
20211217-milvus create collection — In `Proxy`, all `DDL` requests will be wrapped into `task`, and push the `task` into `DdTaskQueue`.
20211217-milvus create collection — A background service will read a new `task` from `DdTaskQueue` only when the previous one is finished.
20211217-milvus create collection — So all the `DDL` requests are executed serially on `Proxy`.
20211217-milvus create collection — In `RootCoord`, all `DDL` requests will be wrapped into `reqTask`, but there is no task queue, so the `DDL` requests will be executed in parallel on `RootCoord`.
20230418-querynode v2 — MEP: Refactor QueryNode v2
20230418-querynode v2 — Current state: Merged
20230418-querynode v2 — ISSUE: [[Enhancement]: Refactor QueryNode #21624](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/issues/21624)
20230418-querynode v2 — Keywords: Search, ANN
20230418-querynode v2 — Released: v2.3.0
20230418-querynode v2 — By refactoring querynode, we plan to achieve:
20230418-querynode v2 — Separate "Delegator" and "Worker"
20230418-querynode v2 — Remove delta channel for deletion forwarding
20230418-querynode v2 — Maintain growing segments in distribution
20230418-querynode v2 — Improve the readability of the code
20230418-querynode v2 — Delegator and Worker
20230418-querynode v2 — `Delegator`, aka `ShardLeader` in querynode v1, handles the segment distribution and consumes data from the dml channel. All the distribution changes(load&release) shall be forwarded by delegators so that they shall always have the latest workable segment distribution information for the shard.
20230418-querynode v2 — On the other hand, `Worker` serves as pure computing labor and provides search/query services on the segments on it.
20230418-querynode v2 — One querynode could be `Delegator` and `Worker` at the same time for now. After separating them into two sub packages, we could easily rearrange them into different components in the future if needed.
20230418-querynode v2 — Interface Definition
20230418-querynode v2 — Remove delta channel
20230418-querynode v2 — After supporting `Delete` operation in Milvus 2.0.x, delta channels are needed for forwarding delete operation to the querynodes on which there are no related DML channels.
20230418-querynode v2 — This mechanism makes the system require double the message queue topic compared to earlier Milvus version. Also, it couples the querynode search&query functionality with the forwarder of the delete records. Unfortunately, datanodes took this role, which may lead to search/query unavailability when some datanodes go down for some period of time.
20230418-querynode v2 — Naturally, the Delegator shall become the forwarder since it could consume all the dml data(including delete) from the message queue. There are some critical points that need to be designed carefully:
20230418-querynode v2 — How to determine which segment/querynode shall be the target when forwarding the delete operations
20230418-querynode v2 — How to guarantee that all the segments have the whole picture of the deletion data
20230418-querynode v2 — Primary Key Oracle(PKOracle)
20230418-querynode v2 — We need a component which could determine or estimate which segments might have the data with the provided pk value. Naming after PKOracle, it could be implemented in the following ways:
20230418-querynode v2 — Delegator has all the PK column data
20230418-querynode v2 — Delegator has all the statslog(Bloom filter) files
20230418-querynode v2 — A third party component stores the PK value-segment ID mapping
20230418-querynode v2 — Since we implemented delete using BF before, it's the first choice to have option 2.
20230418-querynode v2 — <img alt="PK Oracle" src="./graphs/pk_oracle.png" width="600" />
20230418-querynode v2 — Delete grpc def:
20230418-querynode v2 — Delete Forwarding Policy
20230418-querynode v2 — Delegators need to forward delete operation via grpc before any search/query operation can be executed. There are still several ways to forward the deletion data.
20230418-querynode v2 — Forward the delete ASAP and blocks the consuming workflow if forwarding fails
20230418-querynode v2 — Forward the delete lazily. Which means deleting data could be forwarded in search or query request when needed with extra periodically "flush" jobs
20230418-querynode v2 — Forward the processed bitset only
20230418-querynode v2 — Policy 3 can not be done without delegators having all the primary key data. So with pre-determined BF PKOracle implementation, we need to choose between policy 1 & 2.
20230418-querynode v2 — After some investigation, it turned out to be that all the deletion records need to be applied strictly in the sequence order by its timestamp. Otherwise, the internal binary search may return wrong bitset for deletion. So Policy 1 became the only choice before we changed the segment inner implementation.
20230418-querynode v2 — Data Integrity Guarantee
20230418-querynode v2 — Since Milvus2.x could be deployed as a distributed system, there are several cases that may damage data integrity
20230418-querynode v2 — Load Asynchronizely
20230418-querynode v2 — In current design, there is no guarantee that all segments will be ready when delegators forward the deletion records while the collection is being loaded.
20230418-querynode v2 — Load a new Segment
20230418-querynode v2 — A new segment might be loaded after the collection loaded due to some compaction might happen. If the consumed position is after the safe point (all delete operations before is synced to delta log), some delete entries might be missing during this procedure.
20230418-querynode v2 — Balance, Node down or Rolling upgrade
20230418-querynode v2 — Similar to the previous case, when balancing segments, some deletion records might be missing as well. The same logic could apply to node down recovery and rolling upgrade.
20230418-querynode v2 — Solution: Delete buffer with failure re-consume
20230418-querynode v2 — To solve the cases in which delete data might be lost, delegators will have a delete buffer to store "recent" delete data. So anytime a segment is loaded, the delegator will try to patch all the "needed" delete data from this buffer.
20230418-querynode v2 — By "recent", it means a limited double buffer with configurable size.
20230418-querynode v2 — And "needed" delete data means the delete records after the segment checkpoint.
20230418-querynode v2 — If the segment checkpoint is beyond the delete buffer,the delegator will re-consume the delete data from the checkpoint as a last resort.
20230418-querynode v2 — Other changes
20230418-querynode v2 — Use pipeline instead of flowgraph
20230418-querynode v2 — Pipeline was a simplified flowgraph that every node could have one in-degree and one out-degree at most.
20230418-querynode v2 — Like an assembly line, pipeline splits a work that needs repeating over a period of time into many different parts. Every node was a single go routine work for one part of these. To improve running speed by improving parallelism.
20230418-querynode v2 — At querynode, pipeline was used to deal with msg from MsgStream, FilterNode filterates the invalid part in msg, Insert Node Insert rows to segment from msg,Delete Node Insert delete rows to segment from Msg and update TSafe.
20230418-querynode v2 — Search/Query tsafe
20230418-querynode v2 — Since the only consumer is the delegator, the waiting tsafer logic is moved to delegator for now.
20230418-querynode v2 — Interfaces
20230418-querynode v2 — Collection
20230418-querynode v2 — PipelineManager

20230418-querynode v2 — All packages in querynode v2 coverage about 80%

clustering compaction — Clustering compaction User Guide
clustering compaction — Introduction
clustering compaction — This guide will help you understand what is clustering compaction and how to use this feature to enhance your search/query performance.
clustering compaction — Feature Overview
clustering compaction — Clustering compaction is designed to accelerate searches/querys and reduce costs in large collections. Key functionalities include:
clustering compaction — Clustering Key**
clustering compaction — Supports specifying a scalar field as the clustering key in the collection schema.
clustering compaction — Clustering Compaction**
clustering compaction — Clustering compaction redistributes the data according to value of the clustering key field, split by range.
clustering compaction — Metadata of the data distribution (referred to as `partitionStats`) is generated and stored.
clustering compaction — Clustering compaction can be triggered manually via the SDK or automatically in the background. The clustering compaction triggering strategy is highly configurable, see Configurations section for more detail.
clustering compaction — Search/Query Optimization Based on Clustering Compaction**
clustering compaction — Perform like a global index, Milvus can prune the data to be scanned in a query/search based on . Optimization takes effect when the query expression contains a scalar filter. A mount of data can be pruned by comparing the filter expr and the partitionStats during execution. The following figure shows a query before and after clustering compaction on a scalar field. The performance benefit is closely related to the data size and query pattern. For more details, see the Performance section.
clustering compaction — <img src="./figs/clustering_compaction.png">
clustering compaction — Get Started
clustering compaction — Enable Milvus clustering compaction**
clustering compaction — Milvus version: 2.4.7 +
clustering compaction — pymilvus > 2.4.5 (Other SDK is developing...)
clustering compaction — Enable config:
clustering compaction — For more detail, see Configuration.
clustering compaction — Create clustering key collection**
clustering compaction — Supported Clustering Key DataType: ```Int8, Int16, Int32, Int64, Float, Double, VarChar```
clustering compaction — Manual Trigger clustering compaction**
clustering compaction — You will automatically get query/search optimization**
clustering compaction — Best Practice
clustering compaction — To use the clustering compaction feature efficiently, here are some tips:
clustering compaction — Use for Large Collections: Clustering compaction provides better benefits for larger collections. It is not very necessary for small datasets. We recommend using it for collections with at least 1 million rows.
clustering compaction — Choose an Appropriate Clustering Key: Set the most frequently used scalar field as the clustering key. For instance, if you provide a multi-tenant service and have a userID field in your data model, and the most common query pattern is userID = ???, then set userID as the clustering key.
clustering compaction — Use PartitionKey As ClusteringKey: If you want all collections in the Milvus cluster to enable this feature by default, or if you have a large collection with a partition key and are still facing performance issues with scalar filtering queries, you can enable this feature. By setting the configuration `common.usePartitionKeyAsClusteringKey=true`, Milvus can treat all partition key as clustering key. Furthermore, you can still specify a clustering key different from the partition key, which will take precedence.
clustering compaction — Performance
clustering compaction — The benefit of clustering compaction is closely related to data size and query patterns.
clustering compaction — A test demonstrates that clustering compaction can yield up to a 25x improvement in QPS (queries per second).
clustering compaction — We conducted this test on a 20-million-record, 768-dimensional LAION dataset, designating the key field (of type Int64) as the clusteringKey. After performing clustering compaction, we ran concurrent searches until CPU usage reached a high water mark. To test the data pruning effect, we adjusted the search expression. By narrowing the search range, the prune_ratio increased, indicating a higher percentage of data being skipped during execution.
clustering compaction — Comparing the first and last rows, searches without clustering compaction scan the entire dataset, whereas searches with clustering compaction using a specific key can achieve up to a 25x speedup.

tls proxy — <details><summary><code>openssl.cnf</code></summary>

tls proxy — The ```openssl.cnf``` file is a default OpenSSL configuration file. See [manual page](https://www.openssl.org/docs/manmaster/man5/config.html) for more information. The ```gen.sh``` file generates relevant certificate files. You can modify the gen.sh file for different purposes such as changing the validity period of the certificate file, the length of the certificate key or the certificate file names.
tls proxy — These variables in the ```gen.sh``` file are crucial to the process of creating a certificate signing request file. The first five variables are the basic signing information, including country, state, location, organization, organization unit. It is necessary to configure the `CommonName` in the ```gen.sh``` file. The `CommonName` refers to the server name that the client should specify while connecting.
