Creativity - Wikipedia — Vandervert argues that when a person is confronted with a challenging new situation, visual-spatial working memory and speech-related working memory are
Creativity - Wikipedia — decomposed and re-composed (fractionated) by the cerebellum and then blended in the cerebral cortex in an aempt to deal with the new situation. With repeated
Creativity - Wikipedia — aempts to deal with challenging situations, the cerebro-cerebellar blending process continues to optimize the eﬃciency of how working memory deals with the
Creativity - Wikipedia — situation or problem.[172] He also argues that this is the same process (only involving visual-spatial working memory and pre-language vocalization) that led to the
Creativity - Wikipedia — evolution of language in humans.[173] Vandervert and Vandervert–Weathers have pointed out that this blending process, because it continuously optimizes eﬃciencies,
Creativity - Wikipedia — constantly improves prototyping aempts toward the invention or innovation of new ideas, music, art, or technology.[174] Prototyping, they argue, not only produces
Creativity - Wikipedia — new products, it trains the cerebro-cerebellar pathways involved to become more eﬃcient at prototyping itself. Furthermore, Vandervert and Vandervert-Weathers
Creativity - Wikipedia — believe that this repetitive "mental prototyping", or mental rehearsal involving the cerebellum and the cerebral cortex, explains the success of the self-driven,
Creativity - Wikipedia — individualized paerning of repetitions initiated by the teaching methods of the Khan Academy.
Creativity - Wikipedia — e model proposed by Vandervert has, however, received incisive critique from several authors.[175]
Creativity - Wikipedia — In 2005, Alice Flaherty presented a three-factor model of the creative drive. Drawing from evidence in brain imaging, drug studies, and lesion analysis, she described the
Creativity - Wikipedia — creative drive as resulting from an interaction of the frontal lobes, the temporal lobes, and dopamine from the limbic system. e frontal lobes may be responsible for
Creativity - Wikipedia — idea generation, and the temporal lobes for idea editing and evaluation. Abnormalities in the frontal lobe (such as depression or anxiety) generally decrease creativity,
Creativity - Wikipedia — while abnormalities in the temporal lobe oen increase creativity. High activity in the temporal lobe typically inhibits activity in the frontal lobe, and vice versa. High
Creativity - Wikipedia — dopamine levels increase general arousal and goal-directed behaviors and reduce latent inhibition, with all three eﬀects increasing the drive to generate ideas.[176]
Creativity - Wikipedia — In 2018, Lin and Vartanian proposed a neuroeconomic framework that precisely describes norepinephrine's role in creativity and modulating large-scale brain networks
Creativity - Wikipedia — associated with creativity.[76] is framework describes how neural activity in diﬀerent brain regions and networks, such as the default mode network, track utility or
Creativity - Wikipedia — subjective values of ideas.
Creativity - Wikipedia — Economic approaches to creativity have focused on three aspects – the impact of creativity on economic growth, methods of modeling markets for creativity, and the
Creativity - Wikipedia — maximization of economic creativity (innovation).[177][178]
Creativity - Wikipedia — In the early 20th century, Joseph Schumpeter introduced the economic theory of creative destruction to describe the way in which old ways of doing things are destroyed
Creativity - Wikipedia — and replaced by the new. Some economists (such as Paul Romer) view creativity as an important element in the recombination of elements to produce new technologies
Creativity - Wikipedia — and products and, consequently, economic growth. Creativity leads to capital, and creative products are protected by intellectual property laws.
Creativity - Wikipedia — Mark A. Runco and Daniel Rubenson have tried to describe a "psychoeconomic" model of creativity.[179] In such a model, creativity is the product of endowments and
Creativity - Wikipedia — active investments in creativity; the costs and beneﬁts of bringing creative activity to market determine the supply of creativity. Such an approach has been criticized

Creativity - Wikipedia — Creativity research for most of the twentieth century was dominated by psychology and business studies, with lile work done in sociology. Since the turn of the
Creativity - Wikipedia — millennium, there has been more aention paid by sociological researchers,[182][183] but sociology has yet to establish creativity as a speciﬁc research ﬁeld, with reviews
Creativity - Wikipedia — of sociological research into creativity a rarity in high-impact literature.[184]
Creativity - Wikipedia — While psychology has tended to focus on the individual as the locus of creativity, sociological research is directed more at the structures and context within which
Creativity - Wikipedia — creative activity takes place, primarily based in sociology of culture, which ﬁnds its roots in the works of Marx, Durkheim, and Weber. is has meant a focus on the
Creativity - Wikipedia — cultural and creative industries as sociological phenomena. Such research has covered a variety of areas, including the economics and production of culture, the role of
Creativity - Wikipedia — creative industries in development, and the rise of the "creative class".[185]
Creativity - Wikipedia — For those who view the conventional system of schooling as stiﬂing creativity, an emphasis is made (particularly in the preschool/kindergarten and early school years)
Creativity - Wikipedia — to provide a creativity-friendly, rich, imagination-fostering environment for young children.[186][187][188] Researchers have seen this as important because technology is
Creativity - Wikipedia — advancing at an unprecedented rate and creative problem-solving will be needed to cope with these challenges as they arise.[188] In addition to helping with problem
Creativity - Wikipedia — solving, creativity also helps students identify problems where others have failed to do so.[186][187][189] e Waldorf School is an example of an education program that
Creativity - Wikipedia — promotes creative thought.
Creativity - Wikipedia — Promoting intrinsic motivation and problem solving are two areas where educators can foster creativity in students. Students are more creative when they see a task as
Creativity - Wikipedia — intrinsically motivating, valued for its own sake.[187][188][190][191] To promote creative thinking, educators need to identify what motivates their students and to
Creativity - Wikipedia — structure teaching around it. Providing students with a choice of activities allows them to become more intrinsically motivated and therefore creative in completing the
Creativity - Wikipedia — tasks.[186][192]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Teaching students to solve problems that do not have well-deﬁned answers is another way to foster their creativity. is is accomplished by allowing students to explore
Creativity - Wikipedia — problems and redeﬁne them, possibly drawing on knowledge that at ﬁrst may seem unrelated to the problem in order to solve it.[186][187][188][190] In adults, mentoring
Creativity - Wikipedia — individuals is another way to foster their creativity.[193] However, the beneﬁts of mentoring creativity apply only to creative contributions considered great in a given
Creativity - Wikipedia — ﬁeld, not to everyday creative expression.[194]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Musical creativity is a gateway to the ﬂow state, which is conducive to spontaneity, improvisation, and creativity. Studies show that it is beneﬁcial to emphasize
Creativity - Wikipedia — students' creative side and integrate more creativity into their curriculums, with a notable strategy being through music.[195] One reason for this is that students are able
Creativity - Wikipedia — to express themselves through musical improvisation in a way that taps into higher order brain regions, while connecting with their peers and allowing them to go
Creativity - Wikipedia — beyond typical paern generation.[196] In this sense, improvisation is a form of self-expression that can generate connectivity between peers and surpass the age-old

Creativity - Wikipedia — to the individual. It involves looking at familiar things with a fresh eye, examining problems with an open mind, making connections, learning from mistakes, and using
Creativity - Wikipedia — imagination to explore new possibilities."[197] e need to develop a shared language and understanding of creativity and its role across every aspect of learning,
Creativity - Wikipedia — teaching, and continuous improvement was identiﬁed as a necessary aim;[198] and a set of four skills is used to allow educators to discuss and develop creativity across
Creativity - Wikipedia — all subjects and sectors of education – curiosity, open-mindedness, imagination, and problem solving.[199] Distinctions are made between creative learning (when
Creativity - Wikipedia — learners are using their creativity skills), creative teaching (when educators are using their own creativity skills), and creative change (when creativity skills are applied
Creativity - Wikipedia — to planning and improvement). Scotland's national Creative Learning Plan[200] supports the development of creativity skills in all learners and of educators' expertise in
Creativity - Wikipedia — developing creativity skills. A range of resources has been created to support and assess this, including a national review of creativity learning by Her Majesty's
Creativity - Wikipedia — Inspectorate for Education.[197]
Creativity - Wikipedia — China recognizes that creativity is crucial for national security, social development, and generally beneﬁing the people. Measures have been proposed to enhance
Creativity - Wikipedia — creative ability in the country.[201]
Creativity - Wikipedia — e European Union sees creativity as important for the development of basic skills, and has declared 2009 the Year of Creativity and Innovation. Countries such as
Creativity - Wikipedia — France, Germany, Italy, and Spain have made the encouragement of creativity a part of their educational and economic policies.[202]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Various research studies set out to establish that organizational eﬀectiveness depends to a large extent on the creativity of the workforce. For any given organization,
Creativity - Wikipedia — measures of eﬀectiveness vary, depending upon the organization's mission, environmental context, nature of work, the product or service it produces, and customer
Creativity - Wikipedia — demands. us, the ﬁrst step in evaluating organizational eﬀectiveness is to understand the organization itself – how it functions, how it is structured, and what it
Creativity - Wikipedia — emphasizes.
Creativity - Wikipedia — Similarly, social psychologists, organizational scientists, and management scientists (who research factors that inﬂuence creativity and innovation in teams and
Creativity - Wikipedia — organizations) have developed integrative theoretical models that emphasize the elements of team composition, team processes, and organizational culture. ese
Creativity - Wikipedia — theoretical models also emphasize the mutually reinforcing relationships between those elements in promoting innovation.[203][204][205][206]

Creativity - Wikipedia — Supportive and motivational environments that create psychological safety, encourage risk-taking, and tolerate mistakes
Creativity - Wikipedia — increase team creativity.[203][204][205][206] Organizations in which help-seeking, help-giving, and collaboration are rewarded
Creativity - Wikipedia — promote innovation by providing opportunities and contexts in which team processes that lead to collective creativity can
Creativity - Wikipedia — occur.[214] Additionally, leadership styles that downplay hierarchies or power diﬀerences within an organization, and
Creativity - Wikipedia — empower people to speak up about their ideas or opinions, also help to create cultures that are conducive to creativity.[203]

Creativity - Wikipedia — e diversity of team members' backgrounds and knowledge can increase team creativity by expanding the collection of
Creativity - Wikipedia — unique information that is available to the team and by introducing diﬀerent perspectives that can be integrated in novel
Creativity - Wikipedia — ways. However, under some conditions, diversity can also decrease team creativity by making it more diﬃcult for team members to communicate about ideas and
Creativity - Wikipedia — causing interpersonal conﬂicts between those with diﬀerent perspectives.[215] us, the potential advantages of diversity must be supported by appropriate team
Creativity - Wikipedia — processes and organizational cultures in order to enhance creativity.[203][204][205][206][216][217]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Team communication norms, such as respecting others' expertise, paying aention to others' ideas, expecting information sharing, tolerating disagreements,
Creativity - Wikipedia — negotiating, remaining open to others' ideas, learning from others, and building on each other's ideas, increase team creativity by facilitating the social processes
Creativity - Wikipedia — involved with brainstorming and problem solving. rough these processes, team members can access their collective pool of knowledge, reach shared understandings,
Creativity - Wikipedia — identify new ways of understanding problems or tasks, and make new connections between ideas. Engaging in these social processes also promotes positive team aﬀect,
Creativity - Wikipedia — which facilitates collective creativity.[203][205][206][216]
Creativity - Wikipedia — ere is a long-standing debate on how material constraints (e.g., lack of money, materials, or equipment) aﬀect creativity. In psychological and managerial research,
Creativity - Wikipedia — there are two competing views. In one view, scholars propose a negative eﬀect of material constraints on innovation and claim that material constraints starve
Creativity - Wikipedia — creativity.[218] Proponents argue that adequate material resources are needed to engage in creative activities such as experimenting with new solutions and idea
Creativity - Wikipedia — exploration.[218] In an opposing view, scholars assert that people tend to stick to established routines or solutions as long as they are not forced to deviate from them by
Creativity - Wikipedia — constraints.[219] For example, material constraints facilitated the development of jet engines in World War II.[220]
Creativity - Wikipedia — To reconcile these competing views, contingency models were proposed.[221][222][223] e rationale behind these models is that certain contingency factors (e.g.,
Creativity - Wikipedia — Organizational culture
Creativity - Wikipedia — Team composition
Creativity - Wikipedia — Team processes
Creativity - Wikipedia — Constraints
Creativity - Wikipedia — creativity climate or creativity-relevant skills) inﬂuence the relationship between constraints and creativity.[221] ese contingency factors reﬂect the need for higher
Creativity - Wikipedia — levels of motivation and skills when working on creative tasks under constraints.[221] Depending on these contingency factors, there is either a positive or negative
Creativity - Wikipedia — relationship between constraints and creativity.[221][222]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Several researchers have proposed methods of increasing a person's creativity. Such ideas range from the psychological-cognitive—such as the Osborn-Parnes Creative
Creativity - Wikipedia — Problem Solving Process, Synectics, science-based creative thinking, Purdue Creative inking Program, and Edward de Bono's lateral thinking—to the highly structured
Creativity - Wikipedia — —such as TRIZ (the eory of Inventive Problem-Solving) and its variant Algorithm of Inventive Problem Solving (developed by the Russian scientist Genrich
Creativity - Wikipedia — Altshuller), and Computer-Aided morphological analysis.
Creativity - Wikipedia — An empirical synthesis, of which methods work best in enhancing creativity, was published by Haase et al.[224] Summarising the results of 84 studies, the authors found
Creativity - Wikipedia — that complex training courses, meditation, and cultural exposure were most eﬀective in enhancing creativity, while the use of cognitive-manipulation drugs was
Creativity - Wikipedia — noneﬀective.[224]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Experiments suggest the need for closure of task participants, whether as a reﬂection of personality or induced (through time pressure), negatively impacts creativity.
Creativity - Wikipedia — [225] Accordingly, it has been suggested that reading ﬁction, which can reduce the cognitive need for closure, may encourage creativity.[226]
Creativity - Wikipedia — "Malevolent creativity" is the "dark side" of creativity.[227][228] is type of creativity is not typically accepted within society and is deﬁned by the intention to cause
Creativity - Wikipedia — harm to others through original and innovative means. While it is oen associated with criminal behavior, it can also be observed in ordinary day-to-day life as lying,
Creativity - Wikipedia — cheating, and betrayal.[229]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Malevolent creativity should be distinguished from negative creativity in that negative creativity may unintentionally cause harm to others, whereas malevolent
Creativity - Wikipedia — creativity is malevolently motivated.
Creativity - Wikipedia — Malevolent creativity is a key contributor to crime and in its most destructive form can even manifest as terrorism. As creativity requires deviating from the
Creativity - Wikipedia — conventional, there is permanent tension between being creative and going too far—in some cases to the point of breaking the law. Aggression is a key predictor of
Creativity - Wikipedia — malevolent creativity, and increased levels of aggression correlate with a higher likelihood of commiing crime.[230]

Creativity - Wikipedia — Although everyone shows some levels of malevolent creativity under certain conditions, those that have a higher propensity towards it have increased tendencies to
Creativity - Wikipedia — deceive and manipulate others for their own gain. While malevolent creativity appears to dramatically increase when an individual is treated unfairly, personality,
Creativity - Wikipedia — particularly aggressiveness, is also a key predictor in anticipating levels of malevolent thinking. Researchers Harris and Reiter-Palmon investigated the role of
Creativity - Wikipedia — aggression in levels of malevolent creativity, in particular levels of implicit aggression and the tendency to employ aggressive actions in response to problem solving.
Creativity - Wikipedia — e personality traits of physical aggression, conscientiousness, emotional intelligence, and implicit aggression all seem to be related with malevolent creativity.[228]
Creativity - Wikipedia — Harris and Reiter-Palmon's research showed that when subjects were presented with a problem that designed to trigger malevolent creativity, participants high in
Creativity - Wikipedia — implicit aggression and low in premeditation expressed the largest number of malevolently themed solutions. When presented with the more benign problem designed
Creativity - Wikipedia — to trigger prosocial motives of helping others and cooperating, those high in implicit aggression, even if they tended to be highly impulsive, were far less destructive in
Creativity - Wikipedia — their imagined solutions. e researchers concluded premeditation, more than implicit aggression, controlled an individual's expression of malevolent creativity.[231]
Creativity - Wikipedia — e current measure for malevolent creativity is the 13-item Malevolent Creativity Behaviour Scale (MCBS).[229]

Fine art - Wikipedia — Fine art
Fine art - Wikipedia — In European academic traditions, ﬁne art (or, ﬁne arts) is made primarily for aesthetics or creative expression,
Fine art - Wikipedia — distinguishing it from popular art, decorative art or applied art, which also either serve some practical function (such as
Fine art - Wikipedia — poery or most metalwork) or is generally of limited artistic quality in order to appeal to the masses. In the aesthetic theories
Fine art - Wikipedia — developed in the Italian Renaissance, the highest art was that which allowed the full expression and display of the artist's
Fine art - Wikipedia — imagination,[1] unrestricted by any of the practical considerations involved in, say, making and decorating a teapot. It was
Fine art - Wikipedia — also considered important that making the artwork did not involve dividing the work between diﬀerent individuals with
Fine art - Wikipedia — specialized skills, as might be necessary with a piece of furniture, for example.[2] Even within the ﬁne arts, there was a
Fine art - Wikipedia — hierarchy of genres based on the amount of creative imagination required, with history painting placed higher than still life.
Fine art - Wikipedia — Historically, the ﬁve main ﬁne arts were painting, sculpture, architecture, music, and poetry. Other "minor or subsidiary arts"
Fine art - Wikipedia — were also included, especially performing arts such as theatre and dance, which were counted as "among the most ancient
Fine art - Wikipedia — and universal."[3] In practice, outside education, the concept is typically only applied to the visual arts. e old master print
Fine art - Wikipedia — and drawing were included as related forms to painting, just as prose forms of literature were to poetry. Today, the range of
Fine art - Wikipedia — what would be considered ﬁne arts (in so far as the term remains in use) is commonly includes additional modern forms,
Fine art - Wikipedia — such as ﬁlm, photography, and video production/editing, as well as traditional forms made in a ﬁne art seing, such as studio
Fine art - Wikipedia — poery and studio glass, with equivalents in other materials.
Fine art - Wikipedia — One deﬁnition of ﬁne art is "a visual art considered to have been created primarily for aesthetic and intellectual purposes and
Fine art - Wikipedia — judged for its beauty and meaningfulness, speciﬁcally, painting, sculpture, drawing, watercolor, graphics, and architecture."[4]
Fine art - Wikipedia — In that sense, there are conceptual diﬀerences between the ﬁne arts and the decorative arts or applied arts (these two terms
Fine art - Wikipedia — covering largely the same media). As far as the consumer of the art was concerned, the perception of aesthetic qualities required a reﬁned judgment usually referred to
Fine art - Wikipedia — as having good taste, which diﬀerentiated ﬁne art from popular art and entertainment.[5]
Fine art - Wikipedia — e word "ﬁne" does not so much denote the quality of the artwork in question, but the purity of the discipline according to traditional European canons.[7] Except in
Fine art - Wikipedia — the case of architecture, where a practical utility was accepted, this deﬁnition originally excluded the "useful" applied or decorative arts, and the products of what were
Fine art - Wikipedia — regarded as cras. In contemporary practice, these distinctions and restrictions have become essentially meaningless, as the concept or intention of the artist is given
Fine art - Wikipedia — primacy, regardless of the means through which it is expressed.[8]
Fine art - Wikipedia — e term is typically only used for Western art from the Renaissance onwards, although similar genre distinctions can apply to the art of other cultures, especially those
Fine art - Wikipedia — of East Asia. e set of "ﬁne arts" are sometimes also called the "major arts", with "minor arts" equating to the decorative arts. is would typically be for medieval and
Fine art - Wikipedia — ancient art.

Fine art - Wikipedia — According to some writers, the concept of a distinct category of ﬁne art is an invention of the early modern period in the
Fine art - Wikipedia — West. Larry Shiner in his e Invention of Art: A Cultural History (2003) locates the invention in the 18th century: "ere was
Fine art - Wikipedia — a traditional "system of the arts" in the West before the eighteenth century. (Other traditional cultures still have a similar
Fine art - Wikipedia — system.) In that system, an artist or artisan was a skilled maker or practitioner, a work of art was the useful product of skilled
Fine art - Wikipedia — work, and the appreciation of the arts was integrally connected with their role in the rest of life. "Art", in other words, meant
Fine art - Wikipedia — approximately the same thing as the Greek word "techne", or in English "skill", a sense that has survived in phrases like "the
Fine art - Wikipedia — art of war", "the art of love", and "the art of medicine".[9] Similar ideas have been expressed by Paul Oskar Kristeller, Pierre
Fine art - Wikipedia — Bourdieu, and Terry Eagleton (e.g. e Ideology of the Aesthetic), though the point of invention is oen placed earlier, in the
Fine art - Wikipedia — Italian Renaissance; Anthony Blunt notes that the term arti di disegno, a similar concept, emerged in Italy in the mid-16th
Fine art - Wikipedia — century.[10]
Fine art - Wikipedia — But it can be argued that the classical world, from which very lile theoretical writing on art survives, in practice had similar
Fine art - Wikipedia — distinctions. e names of artists preserved in literary sources are Greek painters and sculptors, and to a lesser extent the
Fine art - Wikipedia — carvers of engraved gems. Several individuals in these groups were very famous, and copied and remembered for centuries
Fine art - Wikipedia — aer their deaths. e cult of the individual artistic genius, which was an important part of the Renaissance theoretical basis
Fine art - Wikipedia — for the distinction between "ﬁne" and other art, drew on classical precedent, especially as recorded by Pliny the Elder. Some
Fine art - Wikipedia — other types of object, in particular Ancient Greek poery, are oen signed by their makers or the owner of the workshop,
Fine art - Wikipedia — probably partly to advertise their products.
Fine art - Wikipedia — e decline of the concept of "ﬁne art" is dated by George Kubler and others to around 1880. When it "fell out of fashion" as,
Fine art - Wikipedia — by about 1900, folk art was also coming to be regarded as signiﬁcant.[11] Finally, at least in circles interested in art theory,

Fine art - Wikipedia — Printmaking covers the making of images on paper that can be reproduced multiple times by a printing process. It has been an important artistic medium for several
Fine art - Wikipedia — centuries, in the West and East Asia. Major historic techniques include engraving, woodcut and etching in the West, and woodblock printing in East Asia, where the
Fine art - Wikipedia — Japanese ukiyo-e style is the most important. e 19th-century invention of lithography and then photographic techniques have partly replaced the historic techniques.
Fine art - Wikipedia — Older prints can be divided into the ﬁne art Old Master print and popular prints, with book illustrations and other practical images such as maps somewhere in the
Fine art - Wikipedia — middle.
Fine art - Wikipedia — Except in the case of monotyping, the process is capable of producing multiples of the same piece, which is called a print. Each print is considered an original, as
Fine art - Wikipedia — opposed to a copy. e reasoning behind this is that the print is not a reproduction of another work of art in a diﬀerent medium – for instance, a painting – but rather
Fine art - Wikipedia — an image designed from inception as a print. An individual print is also referred to as an impression. Prints are created from a single original surface, known technically
Fine art - Wikipedia — as a matrix. Common types of matrices include: plates of metal, usually copper or zinc for engraving or etching; stone, used for lithography; blocks of wood for
Fine art - Wikipedia — woodcuts, linoleum for linocuts and fabric in the case of screen-printing. But there are many other kinds. Multiple nearly identical prints can be called an edition. In
Fine art - Wikipedia — modern times each print is oen signed and numbered forming a "limited edition". Prints may also be published in book form, as artist's books. A single print could be
Fine art - Wikipedia — the product of one or multiple techniques.

Work of art - Wikipedia — movement or artistic era, such as: a genre, aesthetic convention, culture, or regional-
Work of art - Wikipedia — national distinction.[3] It can also be seen as an item within an artist's "body of work" or
Work of art - Wikipedia — oeuvre. e term is commonly used by museum and cultural heritage curators, the
Work of art - Wikipedia — interested public, the art patron-private art collector community, and art galleries.[4]

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Sculpture
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Sculpture is the branch of the visual arts that operates in three dimensions. Sculpture is the three-dimensional art work
Sculpture - Wikipedia — which is physically presented in the dimensions of height, width and depth. It is one of the plastic arts. Durable sculptural
Sculpture - Wikipedia — processes originally used carving (the removal of material) and modelling (the addition of material, as clay), in stone, metal,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ceramics, wood and other materials but, since Modernism, there has been almost complete freedom of materials and process.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — A wide variety of materials may be worked by removal such as carving, assembled by welding or modelling, or moulded or
Sculpture - Wikipedia — cast.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Sculpture in stone survives far beer than works of art in perishable materials, and oen represents the majority of the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — surviving works (other than poery) from ancient cultures, though conversely traditions of sculpture in wood may have
Sculpture - Wikipedia — vanished almost entirely. In addition, most ancient sculpture was painted, which has been lost.[2]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Sculpture has been central in religious devotion in many cultures, and until recent centuries, large sculptures, too expensive
Sculpture - Wikipedia — for private individuals to create, were usually an expression of religion or politics. ose cultures whose sculptures have
Sculpture - Wikipedia — survived in quantities include the cultures of the ancient Mediterranean, India and China, as well as many in Central and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — South America and Africa.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — e Western tradition of sculpture began in ancient Greece, and Greece is widely seen as producing great masterpieces in the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — classical period. During the Middle Ages, Gothic sculpture represented the agonies and passions of the Christian faith. e
Sculpture - Wikipedia — revival of classical models in the Renaissance produced famous sculptures such as Michelangelo's statue of David. Modernist
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sculpture moved away from traditional processes and the emphasis on the depiction of the human body, with the making of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — constructed sculpture, and the presentation of found objects as ﬁnished artworks.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — A distinction exists between sculpture "in the round", free-standing sculpture such as statues, not aached except possibly at
Sculpture - Wikipedia — the base to any other surface, and the various types of relief, which are at least partly aached to a background surface. Relief
Sculpture - Wikipedia — is oen classiﬁed by the degree of projection from the wall into low or bas-relief, high relief, and sometimes an intermediate
Sculpture - Wikipedia — mid-relief. Sunk-relief is a technique restricted to ancient Egypt. Relief is the usual sculptural medium for large ﬁgure groups
Sculpture - Wikipedia — and narrative subjects, which are diﬃcult to accomplish in the round, and is the typical technique used both for architectural
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sculpture, which is aached to buildings, and for small-scale sculpture decorating other objects, as in much poery, metalwork and jewellery. Relief sculpture may also
Sculpture - Wikipedia — decorate steles, upright slabs, usually of stone, oen also containing inscriptions.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Types
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Michelangelo's Moses, (c. 1513–1515),
Sculpture - Wikipedia — San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome, for the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — tomb of Pope Julius II
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Another basic distinction is between subtractive carving techniques, which remove material from an existing block or lump,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — for example of stone or wood, and modelling techniques which shape or build up the work from the material. Techniques
Sculpture - Wikipedia — such as casting, stamping and moulding use an intermediate matrix containing the design to produce the work; many of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — these allow the production of several copies.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — e term "sculpture" is oen used mainly to describe large works, which are sometimes called monumental sculpture,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — meaning either or both of sculpture that is large, or that is aached to a building. But the term properly covers many types of

Sculpture - Wikipedia — architectural sculpture, which is aached to buildings. Hardstone carving is the carving for artistic purposes of semi-precious stones such as jade, agate, onyx, rock

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Bronze and related copper alloys are the oldest and still the most popular metals for cast metal sculptures; a cast bronze
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sculpture is oen called simply a "bronze". Common bronze alloys have the unusual and desirable property of expanding
Sculpture - Wikipedia — slightly just before they set, thus ﬁlling the ﬁnest details of a mould. eir strength and lack of brileness (ductility) is an
Sculpture - Wikipedia — advantage when ﬁgures in action are to be created, especially when compared to various ceramic or stone materials (see
Sculpture - Wikipedia — marble sculpture for several examples). Gold is the soest and most precious metal, and very important in jewellery; with
Sculpture - Wikipedia — silver it is so enough to be worked with hammers and other tools as well as cast; repoussé and chasing are among the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — techniques used in gold and silversmithing.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Casting is a group of manufacturing processes by which a liquid material (bronze, copper, glass, aluminum, iron) is (usually)
Sculpture - Wikipedia — poured into a mould, which contains a hollow cavity of the desired shape, and then allowed to solidify. e solid casting is
Sculpture - Wikipedia — then ejected or broken out to complete the process,[11] although a ﬁnal stage of "cold work" may follow on the ﬁnished cast.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Casting may be used to form hot liquid metals or various materials that cold set aer mixing of components (such as epoxies,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — concrete, plaster and clay). Casting is most oen used for making complex shapes that would be otherwise diﬃcult or
Sculpture - Wikipedia — uneconomical to make by other methods. e oldest surviving casting is a copper Mesopotamian frog from 3200 BCE.[12]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Speciﬁc techniques include lost-wax casting, plaster mould casting, and sand casting.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Welding is a process where diﬀerent pieces of metal are fused together to create diﬀerent shapes and designs. ere are many
Sculpture - Wikipedia — diﬀerent forms of welding, such as Oxy-fuel welding, Stick welding, MIG welding, and TIG welding. Oxy-fuel is probably the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — most common method of welding when it comes to creating steel sculptures because it is the easiest to use for shaping the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — steel as well as making clean and less noticeable joins of the steel. e key to Oxy-fuel welding is heating each piece of metal
Sculpture - Wikipedia — to be joined evenly until all are red and have a shine to them. Once that shine is on each piece, that shine will soon become a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — 'pool' where the metal is liquiﬁed and the welder must get the pools to join, fusing the metal. Once cooled oﬀ, the location
Sculpture - Wikipedia — where the pools joined are now one continuous piece of metal. Also used heavily in Oxy-fuel sculpture creation is forging.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Forging is the process of heating metal to a certain point to soen it enough to be shaped into diﬀerent forms. One very
Sculpture - Wikipedia — common example is heating the end of a steel rod and hiing the red heated tip with a hammer while on an anvil to form a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — point. In between hammer swings, the forger rotates the rod and gradually forms a sharpened point from the blunt end of a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — steel rod.

Sculpture - Wikipedia — various ways of moulding glass: hot casting can be done by ladling molten glass into moulds that have been created by
Sculpture - Wikipedia — pressing shapes into sand, carved graphite or detailed plaster/silica moulds. Kiln casting glass involves heating chunks of

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Poery is one of the oldest materials for sculpture, as well as clay being the medium in which many sculptures cast in metal
Sculpture - Wikipedia — are originally modelled for casting. Sculptors oen build small preliminary works called maquees of ephemeral materials

Sculpture - Wikipedia — as a vessel with a sculptural form, and small ﬁgurines have oen been as popular as they are in modern Western culture.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Stamps and moulds were used by most ancient civilizations, from ancient Rome and Mesopotamia to China.[16]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Wood carving has been extremely widely practiced, but survives much less well than the other main materials, being
Sculpture - Wikipedia — vulnerable to decay, insect damage, and ﬁre. It therefore forms an important hidden element in the art history of many
Sculpture - Wikipedia — cultures.[5] Outdoor wood sculpture does not last long in most parts of the world, so that we have lile idea how the totem
Sculpture - Wikipedia — pole tradition developed. Many of the most important sculptures of China and Japan in particular are in wood, and the great
Sculpture - Wikipedia — majority of African sculpture and that of Oceania and other regions.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Wood is light, so suitable for masks and other sculpture intended to be carried, and can take very ﬁne detail. It is also much
Sculpture - Wikipedia — easier to work than stone. It has been very oen painted aer carving, but the paint wears less well than the wood, and is
Sculpture - Wikipedia — oen missing in surviving pieces. Painted wood is oen technically described as "wood and polychrome". Typically a layer of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — gesso or plaster is applied to the wood, and then the paint is applied to that.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ree dimensional work incorporating unconventional materials such as cloth, fur, plastics, rubber and nylon, that can thus
Sculpture - Wikipedia — be stuﬀed, sewn, hung, draped or woven, are known as so sculptures. Well known creators of so sculptures include Claes Oldenburg, Yayoi Kusama, Eva Hesse, Sarah
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Lucas and Magdalena Abakanowicz.[17] So sculptures challenge the traditional rigidity of sculpture by introducing pliable, oen ephemeral materials that create a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sense of ﬂuidity and movement. ese works can evoke a wide range of emotions, from playfulness to vulnerability, depending on the materials and forms used. By
Sculpture - Wikipedia — utilizing fabric, foam, and other so elements, artists can manipulate scale and texture in ways that traditional materials like stone or metal do not allow. Additionally,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — so sculptures oen blur the boundaries between ﬁne art, cra, and design, engaging with themes of the body, domesticity, and consumer culture. is versatility has
Sculpture - Wikipedia — made so sculpture a signiﬁcant medium for contemporary artists exploring new dimensions of materiality and meaning in three-dimensional art.

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Worldwide, sculptors have usually been tradespeople whose work is unsigned; in some traditions, for example China, where
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sculpture did not share the prestige of literati painting, this has aﬀected the status of sculpture itself.[18] Even in ancient
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Greece, where sculptors such as Phidias became famous, they appear to have retained much the same social status as other
Sculpture - Wikipedia — artisans, and perhaps not much greater ﬁnancial rewards, although some signed their works.[19] In the Middle Ages artists
Sculpture - Wikipedia — such as the 12th-century Gislebertus sometimes signed their work, and were sought aer by diﬀerent cities, especially from
Sculpture - Wikipedia — the Trecento onwards in Italy, with ﬁgures such as Arnolfo di Cambio, and Nicola Pisano and his son Giovanni. Goldsmiths
Sculpture - Wikipedia — and jewellers, dealing with precious materials and oen doubling as bankers, belonged to powerful guilds and had
Sculpture - Wikipedia — considerable status, oen holding civic oﬃce. Many sculptors also practised in other arts; Andrea del Verrocchio also painted,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — and Giovanni Pisano, Michelangelo, and Jacopo Sansovino were architects. Some sculptors maintained large workshops. Even
Sculpture - Wikipedia — in the Renaissance the physical nature of the work was perceived by Leonardo da Vinci and others as pulling down the status
Sculpture - Wikipedia — of sculpture in the arts, though the reputation of Michelangelo perhaps put this long-held idea to rest.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — From the High Renaissance artists such as Michelangelo, Leone Leoni and Giambologna could become wealthy, and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ennobled, and enter the circle of princes, aer a period of sharp argument over the relative status of sculpture and painting.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — [20] Much decorative sculpture on buildings remained a trade, but sculptors producing individual pieces were recognised on a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — level with painters. From the 18th century or earlier sculpture also aracted middle-class students, although it was slower to
Sculpture - Wikipedia — do so than painting. Women sculptors took longer to appear than women painters, and were less prominent until the 20th
Sculpture - Wikipedia — century.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Aniconism originated with Judaism, which did not accept ﬁgurative sculpture until the 19th century,[21] before expanding to
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Christianity, which initially accepted large sculptures. In Christianity and Buddhism, sculpture became very signiﬁcant. Christian Eastern Orthodoxy has never accepted
Sculpture - Wikipedia — monumental sculpture, and Islam has consistently rejected nearly all ﬁgurative sculpture, except for very small ﬁgures in reliefs and some animal ﬁgures that fulﬁll a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — useful function, like the famous lions supporting a fountain in the Alhambra. Many forms of Protestantism also do not approve of religious sculpture. ere has been
Sculpture - Wikipedia — much iconoclasm of sculpture for religious motives, from the Early Christians and the Beeldenstorm of the Protestant Reformation to the 2001 destruction of the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Buddhas of Bamyan by the Taliban.

Sculpture - Wikipedia — e monumental sculpture of ancient Egypt is world-famous, but reﬁned and delicate small works exist in much greater numbers. e Egyptians used the distinctive
Sculpture - Wikipedia — technique of sunk relief, which is well suited to very bright sunlight. e main ﬁgures in reliefs adhere to the same ﬁgure convention as in painting, with parted legs
Sculpture - Wikipedia — (where not seated) and head shown from the side, but the torso from the front, and a standard set of proportions making up the ﬁgure, using 18 "ﬁsts" to go from the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ground to the hair-line on the forehead.[39] is appears as early as the Narmer Palee from Dynasty I. However, there as elsewhere the convention is not used for
Sculpture - Wikipedia — minor ﬁgures shown engaged in some activity, such as the captives and corpses.[40] Other conventions make statues of males darker than females ones. Very
Sculpture - Wikipedia — conventionalized portrait statues appear from as early as Dynasty II, before 2,780 BCE,[41] and with the exception of the art of the Amarna period of Ahkenaten,[42] and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — some other periods such as Dynasty XII, the idealized features of rulers, like other Egyptian artistic conventions, changed lile until aer the Greek conquest.[43]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Egyptian pharaohs were always regarded as deities, but other deities are much less common in large statues, except when they represent the pharaoh as another deity;
Sculpture - Wikipedia — however the other deities are frequently shown in paintings and reliefs. e famous row of four colossal statues outside the main temple at Abu Simbel each show
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Rameses II, a typical scheme, though here exceptionally large.[44] Small ﬁgures of deities, or their animal personiﬁcations, are very common, and found in popular
Sculpture - Wikipedia — materials such as poery. Most larger sculpture survives from Egyptian temples or tombs; by Dynasty IV (2680–2565 BCE) at the latest the idea of the Ka statue was
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ﬁrmly established. ese were put in tombs as a resting place for the ka portion of the soul, and so we have a good number of less conventionalized statues of well-oﬀ
Sculpture - Wikipedia — administrators and their wives, many in wood as Egypt is one of the few places in the world where the climate allows wood to survive over millennia. e so-called
Sculpture - Wikipedia — reserve heads, plain hairless heads, are especially naturalistic. Early tombs also contained small models of the slaves, animals, buildings and objects such as boats
Sculpture - Wikipedia — necessary for the deceased to continue his lifestyle in the aerworld, and later Ushabti ﬁgures.[45]

Sculpture - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst distinctive style of ancient Greek sculpture developed in the Early Bronze Age Cycladic period (3rd millennium
Sculpture - Wikipedia — BCE), where marble ﬁgures, usually female and small, are represented in an elegantly simpliﬁed geometrical style. Most
Sculpture - Wikipedia — typical is a standing pose with arms crossed in front, but other ﬁgures are shown in diﬀerent poses, including a complicated
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ﬁgure of a harpist seated on a chair.[46]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — e subsequent Minoan and Mycenaean cultures developed sculpture further, under inﬂuence from Syria and elsewhere, but
Sculpture - Wikipedia — it is in the later Archaic period from around 650 BCE that the kouros developed. ese are large standing statues of naked
Sculpture - Wikipedia — youths, found in temples and tombs, with the kore as the clothed female equivalent, with elaborately dressed hair; both have
Sculpture - Wikipedia — the "archaic smile". ey seem to have served a number of functions, perhaps sometimes representing deities and sometimes
Sculpture - Wikipedia — the person buried in a grave, as with the Kroisos Kouros. ey are clearly inﬂuenced by Egyptian and Syrian styles, but the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Greek artists were much more ready to experiment within the style.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — During the 6th century Greek sculpture developed rapidly, becoming more naturalistic, and with much more active and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — varied ﬁgure poses in narrative scenes, though still within idealized conventions. Sculptured pediments were added to
Sculpture - Wikipedia — temples, including the Parthenon in Athens, where the remains of the pediment of around 520 using ﬁgures in the round were fortunately used as inﬁll for new
Sculpture - Wikipedia — buildings aer the Persian sack in 480 BCE, and recovered from the 1880s on in fresh unweathered condition. Other signiﬁcant remains of architectural sculpture come
Sculpture - Wikipedia — from Paestum in Italy, Corfu, Delphi and the Temple of Aphaea in Aegina (much now in Munich).[47] Most Greek sculpture originally included at least some colour; the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek Museum in Copenhagen, Denmark, has done extensive research and recreation of the original colours.[48][49]

Sculpture - Wikipedia — by their Greek trading partners. An Etruscan speciality was near life size tomb eﬃgies in terracoa, usually lying on top of a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sarcophagus lid propped up on one elbow in the pose of a diner in that period. As the expanding Roman Republic began to
Sculpture - Wikipedia — conquer Greek territory, at ﬁrst in Southern Italy and then the entire Hellenistic world except for the Parthian far east,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — oﬃcial and patrician sculpture became largely an extension of the Hellenistic style, from which speciﬁcally Roman elements
Sculpture - Wikipedia — are hard to disentangle, especially as so much Greek sculpture survives only in copies of the Roman period.[58] By the 2nd
Sculpture - Wikipedia — century BCE, "most of the sculptors working at Rome" were Greek,[59] oen enslaved in conquests such as that of Corinth
Sculpture - Wikipedia — (146 BCE), and sculptors continued to be mostly Greeks, oen slaves, whose names are very rarely recorded. Vast numbers of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Greek statues were imported to Rome, whether as booty or the result of extortion or commerce, and temples were oen
Sculpture - Wikipedia — decorated with re-used Greek works.[60]

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Aer moving through a late 2nd-century "baroque" phase,[66] in the 3rd century, Roman art largely abandoned, or simply became unable to produce, sculpture in the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — classical tradition, a change whose causes remain much discussed. Even the most important imperial monuments now showed stumpy, large-eyed ﬁgures in a harsh
Sculpture - Wikipedia — frontal style, in simple compositions emphasizing power at the expense of grace. e contrast is famously illustrated in the Arch of Constantine of 315 in Rome, which
Sculpture - Wikipedia — combines sections in the new style with roundels in the earlier full Greco-Roman style taken from elsewhere, and the Four Tetrarchs (c. 305) from the new capital of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Constantinople, now in Venice. Ernst Kitzinger found in both monuments the same "stubby proportions, angular movements, an ordering of parts through symmetry
Sculpture - Wikipedia — and repetition and a rendering of features and drapery folds through incisions rather than modelling… e hallmark of the style wherever it appears consists of an
Sculpture - Wikipedia — emphatic hardness, heaviness and angularity—in short, an almost complete rejection of the classical tradition".[67]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — is revolution in style shortly preceded the period in which Christianity was adopted by the Roman state and the great majority of the people, leading to the end of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — large religious sculpture, with large statues now only used for emperors. However, rich Christians continued to commission reliefs for sarcophagi, as in the Sarcophagus
Sculpture - Wikipedia — of Junius Bassus, and very small sculpture, especially in ivory, was continued by Christians, building on the style of the consular diptych.[68]

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Beginning in roughly 1000 A.D., there was a rebirth of artistic production in all Europe, led by general economic growth in
Sculpture - Wikipedia — production and commerce, and the new style of Romanesque art was the ﬁrst medieval style to be used in the whole of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Western Europe. e new cathedrals and pilgrim's churches were increasingly decorated with architectural stone reliefs, and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — new focuses for sculpture developed, such as the tympanum over church doors in the 12th century, and the inhabited capital
Sculpture - Wikipedia — with ﬁgures and oen narrative scenes. Outstanding abbey churches with sculpture include in France Vézelay and Moissac
Sculpture - Wikipedia — and in Spain Silos.[71]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Romanesque art was characterised by a very vigorous style in both sculpture and painting. e capitals of columns were
Sculpture - Wikipedia — never more exciting than in this period, when they were oen carved with complete scenes with several ﬁgures.[72] e large
Sculpture - Wikipedia — wooden cruciﬁx was a German innovation right at the start of the period, as were free-standing statues of the enthroned
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Madonna, but the high relief was above all the sculptural mode of the period. Compositions usually had lile depth, and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — needed to be ﬂexible to squeeze themselves into the shapes of capitals, and church typanums; the tension between a tightly
Sculpture - Wikipedia — enclosing frame, from which the composition sometimes escapes, is a recurrent theme in Romanesque art. Figures still oen
Sculpture - Wikipedia — varied in size in relation to their importance portraiture hardly existed.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Objects in precious materials such as ivory and metal had a very high status in the period, much more so than monumental
Sculpture - Wikipedia — sculpture — we know the names of more makers of these than painters, illuminators or architect-masons. Metalwork,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — including decoration in enamel, became very sophisticated, and many spectacular shrines made to hold relics have survived,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — of which the best known is the Shrine of the ree Kings at Cologne Cathedral by Nicholas of Verdun. e bronze Gloucester
Sculpture - Wikipedia — candlestick and the brass font of 1108–17 now in Liège are superb examples, very diﬀerent in style, of metal casting, the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — former highly intricate and energetic, drawing on manuscript painting, while the font shows the Mosan style at its most
Sculpture - Wikipedia — classical and majestic. e bronze doors, a triumphal column and other ﬁings at Hildesheim Cathedral, the Gniezno Doors,

Sculpture - Wikipedia — wash with, appears to have been introduced to Europe in the 11th century, and oen took fantastic zoomorphic forms;
Sculpture - Wikipedia — surviving examples are mostly in brass. Many wax impressions from impressive seals survive on charters and documents,

Sculpture - Wikipedia — be moved outside the church. By the 15th century there was an industry exporting Noingham alabaster altar reliefs in groups of panels over much of Europe for
Sculpture - Wikipedia — economical parishes who could not aﬀord stone retables.[78] Small carvings, for a mainly lay and oen female market, became a considerable industry in Paris and some
Sculpture - Wikipedia — other centres. Types of ivories included small devotional polyptychs, single ﬁgures, especially of the Virgin, mirror-cases, combs, and elaborate caskets with scenes from

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Greco-Buddhist art is the artistic manifestation of Greco-Buddhism, a cultural syncretism between the Classical Greek culture and Buddhism, which developed over a
Sculpture - Wikipedia — period of close to 1000 years in Central Asia, between the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE, and the Islamic conquests of the 7th century CE.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Greco-Buddhist art is characterized by the strong idealistic realism of Hellenistic art and the ﬁrst representations of the Buddha in human form, which have helped
Sculpture - Wikipedia — deﬁne the artistic (and particularly, sculptural) canon for Buddhist art throughout the Asian continent up to the present. ough dating is uncertain, it appears that
Sculpture - Wikipedia — strongly Hellenistic styles lingered in the East for several centuries aer they had declined around the Mediterranean, as late as the 5th century CE. Some aspects of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Greek art were adopted while others did not spread beyond the Greco-Buddhist area; in particular the standing ﬁgure, oen with a relaxed pose and one leg ﬂexed, and
Sculpture - Wikipedia — the ﬂying cupids or victories, who became popular across Asia as apsaras. Greek foliage decoration was also inﬂuential, with Indian versions of the Corinthian capital
Sculpture - Wikipedia — appearing.[95]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — e origins of Greco-Buddhist art are to be found in the Hellenistic Greco-Bactrian kingdom (250–130 BCE), located in today's Afghanistan, from which Hellenistic
Sculpture - Wikipedia — culture radiated into the Indian subcontinent with the establishment of the small Indo-Greek kingdom (180–10 BCE). Under the Indo-Greeks and then the Kushans, the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — interaction of Greek and Buddhist culture ﬂourished in the area of Gandhara, in today's northern Pakistan, before spreading further into India, inﬂuencing the art of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Mathura, and then the Hindu art of the Gupta empire, which was to extend to the rest of South-East Asia. e inﬂuence of Greco-Buddhist art also spread northward
Sculpture - Wikipedia — towards Central Asia, strongly aﬀecting the art of the Tarim Basin and the Dunhuang Caves, and ultimately the sculpted ﬁgure in China, Korea, and Japan.[96]

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Modern classicism contrasted in many ways with the classical sculpture of the 19th century which was characterized by commitments to naturalism (Antoine-Louis
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Barye)—the melodramatic (François Rude) sentimentality (Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux)—or a kind of stately grandiosity (Lord Leighton). Several diﬀerent directions in the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — classical tradition were taken as the century turned, but the study of the live model and the post-Renaissance tradition was still fundamental to them. Auguste Rodin
Sculpture - Wikipedia — was the most renowned European sculptor of the early 20th century.[134][135] He is oen considered a sculptural Impressionist, as are his students including Camille
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Claudel, and Hugo Rheinhold, aempting to model of a ﬂeeting moment of ordinary life. Modern classicism showed a lesser interest in naturalism and a greater interest
Sculpture - Wikipedia — in formal stylization. Greater aention was paid to the rhythms of volumes and spaces—as well as greater aention to the contrasting qualities of surface (open, closed,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — planar, broken etc.) while less aention was paid to story-telling and convincing details of anatomy or costume. Greater aention was given to psychological eﬀect than
Sculpture - Wikipedia — to physical realism, and inﬂuences from earlier styles worldwide were used.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Early masters of modern classicism included: Aristide Maillol, Alexander Matveyev, Joseph Bernard, Antoine Bourdelle, Georg Kolbe, Libero Andreoi, Gustav Vigeland,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Jan Stursa, Constantin Brâncuși. As the century progressed, modern classicism was adopted as the national style of the two great European totalitarian empires: Nazi
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Germany and Soviet Russia, who co-opted the work of earlier artists such as Kolbe and Wilhelm Lehmbruck in Germany[136] and Matveyev in Russia. Over the 70 years
Sculpture - Wikipedia — of the USSR, new generations of sculptors were trained and chosen within their system, and a distinct style, socialist realism, developed, that returned to the 19th
Sculpture - Wikipedia — century's emphasis on melodrama and naturalism.
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Classical training was rooted out of art education in Western Europe (and the Americas) by 1970 and the classical variants of the 20th century were marginalized in the
Sculpture - Wikipedia — history of modernism. But classicism continued as the foundation of art education in the Soviet academies until 1990, providing a foundation for expressive ﬁgurative
Sculpture - Wikipedia — art throughout eastern Europe and parts of the Middle East. By 2000, the European classical tradition retains a wide appeal to the public but awaits an educational
Sculpture - Wikipedia — tradition to revive its contemporary development.

Sculpture - Wikipedia — Gothic) (Anton Hanak, Wilhelm Lehmbruck, Ernst Barlach, Arturo Martini)—or turned more to the Renaissance (Giacomo Manzù, Venanzo Crocei) or stayed the same

Sculpture - Wikipedia — constructions fashioned by combining disparate objects and materials into one constructed piece of sculpture; the sculptural
Sculpture - Wikipedia — equivalent of the collage in two-dimensional art. e advent of Surrealism led to things occasionally being described as
Sculpture - Wikipedia — "sculpture" that would not have been so previously, such as "involuntary sculpture" in several senses, including coulage. In
Sculpture - Wikipedia — later years Picasso became a proliﬁc poer, leading, with interest in historic poery from around the world, to a revival of
Sculpture - Wikipedia — ceramic art, with ﬁgures such as George E. Ohr and subsequently Peter Voulkos, Kenneth Price, and Robert Arneson. Marcel
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Duchamp originated the use of the "found object" (French: objet trouvé) or readymade with pieces such as Fountain (1917).
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Similarly, the work of Constantin Brâncuși at the beginning of the century paved the way for later abstract sculpture. In
Sculpture - Wikipedia — revolt against the naturalism of Rodin and his late-19th-century contemporaries, Brâncuși distilled subjects down to their
Sculpture - Wikipedia — essences as illustrated by the elegantly reﬁned forms of his Bird in Space series (1924).[137]
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Brâncuși's impact, with his vocabulary of reduction and abstraction, is seen throughout the 1930s and 1940s, and exempliﬁed
Sculpture - Wikipedia — by artists such as Gaston Lachaise, Sir Jacob Epstein, Henry Moore, Alberto Giacomei, Joan Miró, Julio González, Pablo
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Serrano, Jacques Lipchitz[138] and by the 1940s abstract sculpture was impacted and expanded by Alexander Calder, Len Lye,
Sculpture - Wikipedia — Jean Tinguely, and Frederick Kiesler who were pioneers of Kinetic art.

Painting - Wikipedia — Painting is a visual art, which is characterized by the practice of applying paint, pigment, color or other medium to a solid
Painting - Wikipedia — surface (called "matrix"[1] or "support").[2] e medium is commonly applied to the base with a brush, but other implements,
Painting - Wikipedia — such as knives, sponges, and airbrushes, may be used. One who produces paintings is called a painter.
Painting - Wikipedia — In art, the term "painting" describes both the act and the result of the action (the ﬁnal work is called "a painting"). e
Painting - Wikipedia — support for paintings includes such surfaces as walls, paper, canvas, wood, glass, lacquer, poery, leaf, copper and concrete,
Painting - Wikipedia — and the painting may incorporate multiple other materials, including sand, clay, paper, plaster, gold leaf, and even whole
Painting - Wikipedia — objects.
Painting - Wikipedia — Painting is an important form of visual art, bringing in elements such as drawing, composition, gesture, narration, and
Painting - Wikipedia — abstraction.[3] Paintings can be naturalistic and representational (as in still life and landscape painting), photographic,
Painting - Wikipedia — abstract, narrative, symbolistic (as in Symbolist art), emotive (as in Expressionism) or political in nature (as in Artivism).
Painting - Wikipedia — A portion of the history of painting in both Eastern and Western art is dominated by religious art. Examples of this kind of
Painting - Wikipedia — painting range from artwork depicting mythological ﬁgures on poery, to Biblical scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, to
Painting - Wikipedia — scenes from the life of Buddha (or other images of Eastern religious origin).
Painting - Wikipedia — e oldest known are more than 40,000-60,000 years old (art of the Upper Paleolithic) and found in the caves in the district of
Painting - Wikipedia — Maros (Sulawesi, Indonesia). e oldest are oen constructed from hand stencils and simple geometric shapes.[4][a]
Painting - Wikipedia — In November 2018, scientists reported the discovery of the then-oldest known ﬁgurative art painting, over 40,000 (perhaps as
Painting - Wikipedia — old as 52,000) years old, of an unknown animal, in the cave of Lubang Jeriji Saléh on the Indonesian island of Borneo.[6][7] In December 2019, cave paintings portraying
Painting - Wikipedia — pig hunting within the Maros-Pangkep karst region in Sulawesi were discovered to be even older, with an estimated age of at least 43,900 years. is ﬁnding was
Painting - Wikipedia — recognized as "the oldest known depiction of storytelling and the earliest instance of ﬁgurative art in human history."[8][9] In 2021, cave art of a pig found in Sulawesi,
Painting - Wikipedia — Indonesia, and dated to over 45,500 years ago, has been reported.[10][11] On July 3, 2024, the journal Nature published research ﬁndings indicating that the cave paintings
Painting - Wikipedia — which depict anthropomorphic ﬁgures interacting with a pig and measure 36 by 15 inches (91 by 38 cm) in Leang Karampuang are approximately 51,200 years old,
Painting - Wikipedia — establishing them as the oldest known paintings in the world.[12][13]

Painting - Wikipedia — e invention of photography had a major impact on painting. In the decades aer the ﬁrst photograph
Painting - Wikipedia — was produced in 1829, photographic processes improved and became more widely practiced, depriving
Painting - Wikipedia — painting of much of its historic purpose to provide an accurate record of the observable world. A series
Painting - Wikipedia — of art movements in the late 19th and early 20th centuries—notably Impressionism, Post-Impressionism,
Painting - Wikipedia — Fauvism, Expressionism, Cubism, and Dadaism—challenged the Renaissance view of the world. Eastern
Painting - Wikipedia — and African painting, however, continued a long history of stylization and did not undergo an
Painting - Wikipedia — equivalent transformation at the same time.
Painting - Wikipedia — Modern and Contemporary art has moved away from the historic value of cra and documentation in
Painting - Wikipedia — favour of concept. is has not deterred the majority of living painters from continuing to practice
Painting - Wikipedia — painting either as a whole or part of their work. e vitality and versatility of painting in the 21st
Painting - Wikipedia — century defy the previous "declarations" of its demise. In an epoch characterized by the idea of
Painting - Wikipedia — pluralism, there is no consensus as to a representative style of the age. Artists continue to make
Painting - Wikipedia — important works of art in a wide variety of styles and aesthetic temperaments—their merits are le to the public and the
Painting - Wikipedia — marketplace to judge.

Painting - Wikipedia — rights and equal opportunities for female artists internationally.
Painting - Wikipedia — Color, made up of hue, saturation, and value, dispersed over a surface is the essence of painting, just as pitch and rhythm are
Painting - Wikipedia — the essence of music. Color is highly subjective, but has observable psychological eﬀects, although these can diﬀer from one
Painting - Wikipedia — culture to the next. Black is associated with mourning in the West, but in the East, white is. Some painters, theoreticians,
Painting - Wikipedia — writers, and scientists, including Goethe,[16] Kandinsky,[17] and Newton,[18] have wrien their own color theory.
Painting - Wikipedia — Moreover, the use of language is only an abstraction of color equivalent. e word "red", for example, can cover a wide range of variations from the pure red of the
Painting - Wikipedia — visible spectrum of light. ere is not a formalized register of diﬀerent colors in the way that there is agreement on diﬀerent notes in music, such as F or C♯. For a
Painting - Wikipedia — painter, color is not simply divided into basic (primary) and derived (complementary or mixed) colors (like red, blue, green, brown, etc.).

Painting - Wikipedia — Painters deal practically with pigments, so "blue" for a painter can be any of the blues: phthalocyanine blue, Prussian blue,
Painting - Wikipedia — indigo, Cobalt blue, ultramarine, and so on. Psychological and symbolical meanings of color are not, strictly speaking, means
Painting - Wikipedia — of painting. Colors only add to the potential, derived context of meanings, and because of this, the perception of a painting is
Painting - Wikipedia — highly subjective. e analogy with music is quite clear—sound in music (like a C note) is analogous to "light" in painting,
Painting - Wikipedia — "shades" to dynamics, and "coloration" is to painting as the speciﬁc timbre of musical instruments is to music. ese elements
Painting - Wikipedia — do not necessarily form a melody (in music) of themselves; rather, they can add diﬀerent contexts to it.
Painting - Wikipedia — Modern artists have extended the practice of painting considerably to include, as one example, collage, which began with
Painting - Wikipedia — Cubism and is not painting in the strict sense. Some modern painters incorporate diﬀerent materials such as metal, plastic,
Painting - Wikipedia — sand, cement, straw, leaves or wood for the texture. Examples of this are the works of Jean Dubuﬀet and Anselm Kiefer. ere
Painting - Wikipedia — is a growing community of artists who use computers to "paint" color onto a digital "canvas" using programs such as Adobe
Painting - Wikipedia — Photoshop, Corel Painter, and many others. ese images can be printed onto traditional canvas if required.
Painting - Wikipedia — Jean Metzinger's mosaic-like Divisionist technique had its parallel in literature; a characteristic of the alliance between
Painting - Wikipedia — Symbolist writers and Neo-Impressionist artists:
Painting - Wikipedia — I ask of divided brushwork not the objective rendering of light, but iridescences and certain aspects of color still
Painting - Wikipedia — foreign to painting. I make a kind of chromatic versiﬁcation and for syllables, I use strokes which, variable in
Painting - Wikipedia — quantity, cannot diﬀer in dimension without modifying the rhythm of a pictorial phraseology destined to
Painting - Wikipedia — translate the diverse emotions aroused by nature. (Jean Metzinger, c. 1907)[20]
Painting - Wikipedia — Rhythm, for artists such as Piet Mondrian,[21][22] is important in painting as it is in music. If one deﬁnes rhythm as "a pause
Painting - Wikipedia — incorporated into a sequence", then there can be rhythm in paintings. ese pauses allow creative force to intervene and add
Painting - Wikipedia — new creations—form, melody, coloration. e distribution of form or any kind of information is of crucial importance in the
Painting - Wikipedia — given work of art, and it directly aﬀects the aesthetic value of that work. is is because the aesthetic value is functionality
Painting - Wikipedia — dependent, i.e. the freedom (of movement) of perception is perceived as beauty. Free ﬂow of energy, in art as well as in other
Painting - Wikipedia — forms of "techne", directly contributes to the aesthetic value.[21]
Painting - Wikipedia — Music was important to the birth of abstract art since music is abstract by nature—it does not try to represent the exterior
Painting - Wikipedia — world, but expresses in an immediate way the inner feelings of the soul. Wassily Kandinsky oen used musical terms to
Painting - Wikipedia — identify his works; he called his most spontaneous paintings "improvisations" and described more elaborate works as
Painting - Wikipedia — "compositions". Kandinsky theorized that "music is the ultimate teacher",[23] and subsequently embarked upon the ﬁrst seven of his ten Compositions. Hearing tones and
Painting - Wikipedia — chords as he painted, Kandinsky theorized that (for example), yellow is the color of middle C on a brassy trumpet; black is the color of closure, and the end of things;

Painting - Wikipedia — Aesthetics is the study of art and beauty; it was an important issue for 18th- and 19th-century philosophers such as Kant and
Painting - Wikipedia — Hegel. Classical philosophers like Plato and Aristotle also theorized about art and painting in particular. Plato disregarded
Painting - Wikipedia — painters (as well as sculptors) in his philosophical system; he maintained that painting cannot depict the truth—it is a copy of
Painting - Wikipedia — reality (a shadow of the world of ideas) and is nothing but a cra, similar to shoemaking or iron casting.[28] By the time of
Painting - Wikipedia — Leonardo, painting had become a closer representation of the truth than painting was in Ancient Greece. Leonardo da Vinci,
Painting - Wikipedia — on the contrary, said that "Italian: La Piura è cosa mentale" ("English: painting is a thing of the mind").[29] Kant distinguished
Painting - Wikipedia — between Beauty and the Sublime, in terms that clearly gave priority to the former. Although he did not refer to painting in
Painting - Wikipedia — particular, this concept was taken up by painters such as J.M.W. Turner and Caspar David Friedrich.
Painting - Wikipedia — Hegel recognized the failure of aaining a universal concept of beauty and, in his aesthetic essay, wrote that painting is one

Painting - Wikipedia — minerals called color oxides provide coloration. Aer ﬁring at a temperature of 750–850 degrees Celsius (1380–1560 degrees
Painting - Wikipedia — Fahrenheit), the result is a fused lamination of glass and metal. Unlike most painted techniques, the surface can be handled
Painting - Wikipedia — and weed. Enamels have traditionally been used for decoration of precious objects,[42] but have also been used for other

Painting - Wikipedia — scenes in decorated surrounds, on plaques or objects such as salts or caskets. In the 18th century, enamel painting enjoyed a

Painting - Wikipedia — enamel on metal has been used as a durable medium for outdoor murals.[44]

Painting - Wikipedia — ceilings. e word fresco comes from the Italian word aﬀresco [afˈfresːko], which

Painting - Wikipedia — other early time periods. Buon fresco technique consists of painting in pigment mixed with

Painting - Wikipedia — drying oil, such as linseed oil, poppyseed oil which was widely used in early modern
Painting - Wikipedia — Europe. Oen the oil was boiled with a resin such as pine resin or even frankincense; these

Painting - Wikipedia — the height of the Renaissance oil painting techniques had almost completely replaced
Painting - Wikipedia — tempera paints in the majority of Europe.
Painting - Wikipedia — Pastel is a painting medium in the form of a stick, consisting of pure powdered pigment and a binder.[45] e pigments used
Painting - Wikipedia — in pastels are the same as those used to produce all colored art media, including oil paints; the binder is of a neutral hue and
Painting - Wikipedia — low saturation. e color eﬀect of pastels is closer to the natural dry pigments than that of any other process.[46] Because the
Painting - Wikipedia — surface of a pastel painting is fragile and easily smudged, its preservation requires protective measures such as framing under glass; it may also be sprayed with a
Painting - Wikipedia — ﬁxative. Nonetheless, when made with permanent pigments and properly cared for, a pastel painting may endure unchanged for centuries. Pastels are not susceptible, as
Painting - Wikipedia — are paintings made with a ﬂuid medium, to the cracking and discoloration that result from changes in the color, opacity, or dimensions of the medium as it dries.

Painting - Wikipedia — Acrylic paint is fast drying paint containing pigment suspension in acrylic polymer
Painting - Wikipedia — emulsion. Acrylic paints can be diluted with water but become water-resistant when dry.
Painting - Wikipedia — Depending on how much the paint is diluted (with water) or modiﬁed with acrylic gels,
Painting - Wikipedia — media, or pastes, the ﬁnished acrylic painting can resemble a watercolor or an oil painting,
Painting - Wikipedia — or have its own unique characteristics not aainable with other media. e main practical
Painting - Wikipedia — diﬀerence between most acrylics and oil paints is the inherent drying time.[47] Oils allow
Painting - Wikipedia — for more time to blend colors and apply even glazes over under-paintings. is slow drying
Painting - Wikipedia — aspect of oil can be seen as an advantage for certain techniques but may also impede the
Painting - Wikipedia — artist's ability to work quickly. Another diﬀerence is that watercolors must be painted onto
Painting - Wikipedia — a porous surface, primarily watercolor paper. Acrylic paints can be used on many diﬀerent
Painting - Wikipedia — surfaces.[47][48] Both acrylic and watercolor are easy to clean up with water. Acrylic paint
Painting - Wikipedia — should be cleaned with soap and water immediately following use. Watercolor paint can be
Painting - Wikipedia — cleaned with just water.[49][50][51]

Painting - Wikipedia — can be applied directly to bare metal and many plastics.

Painting - Wikipedia — miniatures either as book illustrations or as single works to be kept in albums (muraqqa). It emerged[73] from Persian miniature painting (itself partly of Chinese origin)

Painting - Wikipedia — was typical of Persian miniatures. Animals and plants were the main subject of many miniatures for albums, and were more realistically depicted.[74][75][76]
