Aesthetics - Wikipedia — e philosopher Denis Duon identiﬁed six universal signatures in human aesthetics:[32]
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — 1. Expertise or virtuosity. Humans cultivate, recognize, and admire technical artistic skills.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — 2. Nonutilitarian pleasure. People enjoy art for art's sake, and do not demand that it keep them warm or put food on the table.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — 3. Style. Artistic objects and performances satisfy rules of composition that place them in a recognizable style.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — 4. Criticism. People make a point of judging, appreciating, and interpreting works of art.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — 5. Imitation. With a few important exceptions like abstract painting, works of art simulate experiences of the world.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — 6. Special focus. Art is set aside from ordinary life and made a dramatic focus of experience.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — Artists such as omas Hirschhorn have indicated that there are too many exceptions to Duon's categories. For example, Hirschhorn's installations deliberately
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — eschew technical virtuosity. People can appreciate a Renaissance Madonna for aesthetic reasons, but such objects oen had (and sometimes still have) speciﬁc
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — devotional functions. "Rules of composition" that might be read into Duchamp's Fountain or John Cage's 4′33″ do not locate the works in a recognizable style (or
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — Aesthetic universals
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — certainly not a style recognizable at the time of the works' realization). Moreover, some of Duon's categories seem too broad: a physicist might entertain hypothetical
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — worlds in his/her imagination in the course of formulating a theory. Another problem is that Duon's categories seek to universalize traditional European notions of
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — aesthetics and art forgeing that, as André Malraux and others have pointed out, there have been large numbers of cultures in which such ideas (including the idea "art"
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — itsel) were non-existent.[33]
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — Aesthetic ethics refers to the idea that human conduct and behaviour ought to be governed by that which is beautiful and aractive. John Dewey[34] has pointed out
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — that the unity of aesthetics and ethics is in fact reﬂected in our understanding of behaviour being "fair"—the word having a double meaning of aractive and morally
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — acceptable. More recently, James Page[35] has suggested that aesthetic ethics might be taken to form a philosophical rationale for peace education.
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — Beauty is one of the main subjects of aesthetics, together with art and taste.[36][37] Many of its deﬁnitions include the idea that an object is beautiful if perceiving it is
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — accompanied by aesthetic pleasure. Among the examples of beautiful objects are landscapes, sunsets, humans and works of art. Beauty is a positive aesthetic value that
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — contrasts with ugliness as its negative counterpart.[38]
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — Diﬀerent intuitions commonly associated with beauty and its nature are in conﬂict with each other, which poses certain diﬃculties for understanding it.[39][40][41] On
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — the one hand, beauty is ascribed to things as an objective, public feature. On the other hand, it seems to depend on the subjective, emotional response of the observer. It
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — is said, for example, that "beauty is in the eye of the beholder".[42][36] It may be possible to reconcile these intuitions by aﬃrming that it depends both on the objective
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — features of the beautiful thing and the subjective response of the observer. One way to achieve this is to hold that an object is beautiful if it has the power to bring about
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — certain aesthetic experiences in the perceiving subject. is is oen combined with the view that the subject needs to have the ability to correctly perceive and judge
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — beauty, sometimes referred to as "sense of taste".[36][40][41] Various conceptions of how to deﬁne and understand beauty have been suggested. Classical conceptions
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — emphasize the objective side of beauty by deﬁning it in terms of the relation between the beautiful object as a whole and its parts: the parts should stand in the right
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — proportion to each other and thus compose an integrated harmonious whole.[36][38][41] Hedonist conceptions, on the other hand, focus more on the subjective side by
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — drawing a necessary connection between pleasure and beauty, e.g. that for an object to be beautiful is for it to cause disinterested pleasure.[43] Other conceptions include
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — deﬁning beautiful objects in terms of their value, of a loving aitude towards them or of their function.[44][38][36]
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — During the ﬁrst half of the twentieth century, a signiﬁcant shi to general aesthetic theory took place which aempted to apply aesthetic theory between various forms
Aesthetics - Wikipedia — of art, including the literary arts and the visual arts, to each other. is resulted in the rise of the New Criticism school and debate concerning the intentional fallacy. At

Aesthetics - Wikipedia — evaluation of the ﬁnal product of the work of art, or, if the work of art should be evaluated on its own merits independent of the intentions of the artist.

Idea - Wikipedia — Idea
Idea - Wikipedia — In philosophy and in common usage, an idea (from the Greek word: ἰδέα (idea), meaning 'a form, or a paern') is the results
Idea - Wikipedia — of thought.[1] Also in philosophy, ideas can also be mental representational images of some object. Many philosophers have
Idea - Wikipedia — considered ideas to be a fundamental ontological category of being. e capacity to create and understand the meaning of
Idea - Wikipedia — ideas is considered to be an essential and deﬁning feature of human beings.
Idea - Wikipedia — An idea arises in a reﬂexive, spontaneous manner, even without thinking or serious reﬂection, for example, when we talk
Idea - Wikipedia — about the idea of a person or a place. A new or an original idea can oen lead to innovation. Our actions are based upon
Idea - Wikipedia — beliefs, beliefs are paerns or organized sets of ideas.[2]
Idea - Wikipedia — e word idea comes from Greek ἰδέα, romanized: idea, 'form, paern', from the root of ἰδεῖν idein, 'to see'.[3]
Idea - Wikipedia — e argument over the underlying nature of ideas was opened by Plato, whose exposition of his theory of forms—which
Idea - Wikipedia — recurs and accumulates over the course of his many dialogs—appropriates and adds a new sense to the Greek word for things
Idea - Wikipedia — that are "seen" (re. εἶδος) that highlights those elements of perception which are encountered without material or objective reference available to the eyes (re. ἰδέα). As
Idea - Wikipedia — this argument was disseminated the word "idea" began to take on connotations that would be more familiarly associated with the term today. In the ﬁh book of his
Idea - Wikipedia — Republic, Plato deﬁnes philosophy as the love of this formal (as opposed to visual) way of seeing.
Idea - Wikipedia — Plato advanced the theory that perceived but immaterial objects of awareness constitute a realm of deathless forms or ideas from which the material world emanates.
Idea - Wikipedia — Aristotle challenged Plato in this area, positing that the phenomenal world of ideas arises as mental composites of remembered observations. ough it is anachronistic
Idea - Wikipedia — to apply these terms to thinkers from antiquity, it clariﬁes the argument between Plato and Aristotle if we call Plato an idealist thinker and Aristotle an empiricist
Idea - Wikipedia — thinker.
Idea - Wikipedia — is antagonism between empiricism and idealism generally characterizes the dynamism of the argument over the theory of ideas up to the present. is schism in
Idea - Wikipedia — theory has never been resolved to the satisfaction of thinkers from both sides of the disagreement and is represented today in the split between analytic and continental
Idea - Wikipedia — schools of philosophy. Persistent contradictions between classical physics and quantum mechanics may be pointed to as a rough analogy for the gap between the two
Idea - Wikipedia — schools of thought.
Idea - Wikipedia — Etymology
Idea - Wikipedia — History
Idea - Wikipedia — Plato in Ancient Greece was one of the earliest philosophers to provide a detailed discussion of ideas and of the thinking process (in Plato's Greek the word idea carries
Idea - Wikipedia — a rather diﬀerent sense of our modern English term). Plato argued in dialogues such as the Phaedo, Symposium, Republic, and Timaeus that there is a realm of ideas or
Idea - Wikipedia — forms (eidei), which exist independently of anyone who may have thoughts on these ideas, and it is the ideas which distinguish mere opinion from knowledge, for
Idea - Wikipedia — unlike material things which are transient and liable to contrary properties, ideas are unchanging and nothing but just what they are. Consequently, Plato seems to
Idea - Wikipedia — assert forcefully that material things can only be the objects of opinion; real knowledge can only be had of unchanging ideas. Furthermore, ideas for Plato appear to
Idea - Wikipedia — serve as universals; consider the following passage from the Republic:
Idea - Wikipedia — "We both assert that there are," I said, "and distinguish in speech, many fair things, many good things, and so on for each kind of thing."
Idea - Wikipedia — "Yes, so we do."
Idea - Wikipedia — "And we also assert that there is a fair itself, a good itself, and so on for all things that we set down as many. Now, again, we refer to them as one idea of each
Idea - Wikipedia — as though the idea were one; and we address it as that which really is."
Idea - Wikipedia — "at's so."
Idea - Wikipedia — "And, moreover, we say that the former are seen, but not intellected, while the ideas are intellected but not seen."
Idea - Wikipedia — — Plato, Bk. VI 507b-c
Idea - Wikipedia — Descartes oen wrote of the meaning of the idea as an image or representation, oen but not necessarily "in the mind", which was well known in the vernacular.
Idea - Wikipedia — Despite Descartes' invention of the non-Platonic use of the term, he at ﬁrst followed this vernacular use.b In his Meditations on First Philosophy he says, "Some of my
Idea - Wikipedia — thoughts are like images of things, and it is to these alone that the name 'idea' properly belongs." He sometimes maintained that ideas were innate[4] and uses of the
Idea - Wikipedia — term idea diverge from the original primary scholastic use. He provides multiple non-equivalent deﬁnitions of the term, uses it to refer to as many as six distinct kinds
Idea - Wikipedia — of entities, and divides ideas inconsistently into various genetic categories.[5] For him knowledge took the form of ideas and philosophical investigation is devoted to the
Idea - Wikipedia — consideration of these entities.
Idea - Wikipedia — John Locke's use of idea stands in striking contrast to Plato's.[6] In his Introduction to An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Locke deﬁnes idea as "that term
Idea - Wikipedia — Philosophy
Idea - Wikipedia — Plato
Idea - Wikipedia — René Descartes
Idea - Wikipedia — John Locke
Idea - Wikipedia — which, I think, serves best to stand for whatsoever is the object of the understanding when a man thinks, I have used it to express whatever is meant by phantasm,
Idea - Wikipedia — notion, species, or whatever it is which the mind can be employed about in thinking; And I could not avoid frequently using it."[7] He said he regarded the contribution
Idea - Wikipedia — oﬀered in his essay as necessary to examine our own abilities and discern what objects our understandings were, or were not, ﬁed to deal with. In this style of ideal
Idea - Wikipedia — conception other outstanding ﬁgures followed in his footsteps — Hume and Kant in the 18th century, Arthur Schopenhauer in the 19th century, and Bertrand Russell,
Idea - Wikipedia — Ludwig Wigenstein, and Karl Popper in the 20th century. Locke always believed in the good sense — not pushing things to extremes and while taking fully into account
Idea - Wikipedia — the plain facts of the maer. He prioritized common-sense ideas that struck him as "good-tempered, moderate, and down-to-earth."
Idea - Wikipedia — As John Locke studied humans in his work "An Essay Concerning Human Understanding" he continually referenced Descartes for ideas as he asked this fundamental
Idea - Wikipedia — question: "When we are concerned with something about which we have no certain knowledge, what rules or standards should guide how conﬁdent we allow ourselves
Idea - Wikipedia — to be that our opinions are right?"[8] Put in another way, he inquired into how humans might verify their ideas, and considered the distinctions between diﬀerent types
Idea - Wikipedia — of ideas. Locke found that an idea "can simply mean some sort of brute experience."[9] He shows that there are "No innate principles in the mind."[10] us, he concludes
Idea - Wikipedia — that "our ideas are all experienced in nature."[11] An experience can either be a sensation or a reﬂection: "consider whether there are any innate ideas in the mind before
Idea - Wikipedia — any are brought in by the impression from sensation or reﬂection."[8] erefore, an idea was an experience in which the human mind apprehended something.
Idea - Wikipedia — In a Lockean view, there are really two types of ideas: complex and simple. Simple ideas are the building blocks for more complex ideas, and "While the mind is wholly
Idea - Wikipedia — passive in the reception of simple ideas, it is very active in the building of complex ideas…"[12] Complex ideas, therefore, can either be modes, substances, or relations.
Idea - Wikipedia — Modes combine simpler ideas in order to convey new information. For instance, David Banach [13] gives the example of beauty as a mode. He points to combinations of
Idea - Wikipedia — color and form as qualities constitutive of this mode. Substances, however, are distinct from modes. Substances convey the underlying formal unity of certain objects,
Idea - Wikipedia — such as dogs, cats, or tables. Relations represent the relationship between two or more ideas that contain analogous elements to one another without the implication of
Idea - Wikipedia — underlying formal unity. A painting or a piece of music, for example, can both be called 'art' without belonging to the same substance. ey are related as forms of art
Idea - Wikipedia — (the term 'art' in this illustration would be a 'mode of relations'). In this way, Locke concluded that the formal ambiguity around ideas he initially sought to clarify had
Idea - Wikipedia — been resolved.

Idea - Wikipedia — Whereas Kant declares limits to knowledge ("we can never know the thing in itself"), in his epistemological work, Rudolf Steiner sees ideas as
Idea - Wikipedia — "objects of experience" which the mind apprehends, much as the eye apprehends light. In Goethean Science (1883), he declares, "inking … is

Idea - Wikipedia — Wundt widens the term from Kant's usage to include conscious representation of some object or process of the external world. In so doing, he
Idea - Wikipedia — includes not only ideas of memory and imagination, but also perceptual processes, whereas other psychologists conﬁne the term to the ﬁrst two groups.[15] One of
Idea - Wikipedia — Wundt's main concerns was to investigate conscious processes in their own context by experiment and introspection. He regarded both of these as exact methods,
Idea - Wikipedia — interrelated in that experimentation created optimal conditions for introspection. Where the experimental method failed, he turned to other objectively valuable aids,
Idea - Wikipedia — speciﬁcally to those products of cultural communal life which lead one to infer particular mental motives. Outstanding among these are speech, myth, and social custom.
Idea - Wikipedia — Wundt designed the basic mental activity apperception — a unifying function which should be understood as an activity of the will. Many aspects of his empirical
Idea - Wikipedia — physiological psychology are used today. One is his principles of mutually enhanced contrasts and of assimilation and dissimilation (i.e. in color and form perception
Idea - Wikipedia — and his advocacy of objective methods of expression and of recording results, especially in language. Another is the principle of heterogony of ends — that multiply
Idea - Wikipedia — motivated acts lead to unintended side eﬀects which in turn become motives for new actions.[20]
Idea - Wikipedia — C. S. Peirce published the ﬁrst full statement of pragmatism in his important works "How to Make Our Ideas Clear" (1878) and "e Fixation of Belief" (1877).[21] In
Idea - Wikipedia — "How to Make Our Ideas Clear" he proposed that a clear idea (in his study he uses concept and idea as synonymic) is deﬁned as one, when it is apprehended such as it
Idea - Wikipedia — will be recognized wherever it is met, and no other will be mistaken for it. If it fails of this clearness, it is said to be obscure. He argued that to understand an idea clearly
Idea - Wikipedia — we should ask ourselves what diﬀerence its application would make to our evaluation of a proposed solution to the problem at hand. Pragmatism (a term he
Idea - Wikipedia — appropriated for use in this context), he defended, was a method for ascertaining the meaning of terms (as a theory of meaning). e originality of his ideas is in their
Idea - Wikipedia — rejection of what was accepted as a view and understanding of knowledge as impersonal facts which had been accepted by scientists for some 250 years. Peirce
Idea - Wikipedia — contended that we acquire knowledge as participants, not as spectators. He felt "the real", sooner or later, is composed of information that has been acquired through
Idea - Wikipedia — ideas and knowledge and ordered by the application of logical reasoning. e rational distinction of the empirical object is not prior to its perception by a
Idea - Wikipedia — knowledgeable subject, in other words. He also published many papers on logic in relation to ideas.

Idea - Wikipedia — G. F. Stout and J. M. Baldwin, in the Dictionary of Philosophy and Psychology, deﬁne the idea as "the reproduction with a more or less adequate image, of an object not
Idea - Wikipedia — actually present to the senses." [22] ey point out that an idea and a perception are by various authorities contrasted in various ways. "Diﬀerence in degree of intensity",
Idea - Wikipedia — "comparative absence of bodily movement on the part of the subject", "comparative dependence on mental activity", are suggested by psychologists as characteristic of
Idea - Wikipedia — an idea as compared with a perception.[15]
Idea - Wikipedia — An idea, in the narrower and generally accepted sense of a mental reproduction, is frequently composite. at is, as in the example given above of the idea of a chair, a
Idea - Wikipedia — great many objects, diﬀering materially in detail, all call a single idea. When a man, for example, has obtained an idea of chairs in general by comparison with which he
Idea - Wikipedia — can say "is is a chair, that is a stool", he has what is known as an "abstract idea" distinct from the reproduction in his mind of any particular chair (see abstraction).
Idea - Wikipedia — Furthermore, a complex idea may not have any corresponding physical object, though its particular constituent elements may severally be the reproductions of actual
Idea - Wikipedia — perceptions. us the idea of a centaur is a complex mental picture composed of the ideas of man and horse, that of a mermaid of a woman and a ﬁsh.[15]
Idea - Wikipedia — "Ideas are to objects [of perception] as constellations are to stars,"[23] writes Walter Benjamin in the introduction to his e Origin of German Tragic Drama. "e set of
Idea - Wikipedia — concepts which assist in the representation of an idea lend it actuality as such a conﬁguration. For phenomena are not incorporated into ideas. ey are not contained in
Idea - Wikipedia — them. Ideas are, rather, their objective virtual arrangement, their objective interpretation."
Idea - Wikipedia — Benjamin advances, "at an idea is that moment in the substance and being of a word in which this word has become, and performs, as a symbol." as George Steiner
Idea - Wikipedia — summarizes.[23] In this way techne--art and technology—may be represented, ideally, as "discrete, fully autonomous objects…[thus entering] into fusion without losing
Idea - Wikipedia — their identity."[23]
Idea - Wikipedia — Diﬀusion studies explore the spread of ideas from culture to culture. Some anthropological theories hold that all cultures imitate ideas from one or a few original
Idea - Wikipedia — cultures, the Adam of the Bible, or several cultural circles that overlap. Evolutionary diﬀusion theory holds that cultures are inﬂuenced by one another but that similar
Idea - Wikipedia — ideas can be developed in isolation.
Idea - Wikipedia — In the mid-20th century, social scientists began to study how and why ideas spread from one person or culture to another. Evere Rogers pioneered diﬀusion of
Idea - Wikipedia — innovations studies, using research to prove factors in adoption and proﬁles of adopters of ideas. In 1976, in his book e Selﬁsh Gene, Richard Dawkins suggested
Idea - Wikipedia — applying biological evolutionary theories to the spread of ideas. He coined the term meme to describe an abstract unit of selection, equivalent to the gene in
Idea - Wikipedia — evolutionary biology.

Idea - Wikipedia — Ideas and intellectual property
Idea - Wikipedia — It has been pretended by some, (and in England especially,) that inventors have a natural and exclusive right to their inventions, and not merely for their own
Idea - Wikipedia — lives, but inheritable to their heirs. But while it is a moot question whether the origin of any kind of property is derived from nature at all, it would be singular
Idea - Wikipedia — to admit a natural and even an hereditary right to inventors. It is agreed by those who have seriously considered the subject, that no individual has, of natural
Idea - Wikipedia — right, a separate property in an acre of land, for instance.
Idea - Wikipedia — By a universal law, indeed, whatever, whether ﬁxed or movable, belongs to all men equally and in common, is the property for the moment of him who
Idea - Wikipedia — occupies it, but when he relinquishes the occupation, the property goes with it. Stable ownership is the gi of social law, and is given late in the progress of
Idea - Wikipedia — society. It would be curious then, if an idea, the fugitive fermentation of an individual brain, could, of natural right, be claimed in exclusive and stable
Idea - Wikipedia — property.
Idea - Wikipedia — If nature has made any one thing less susceptible than all others of exclusive property, it is the action of the thinking power called an idea, which an individual
Idea - Wikipedia — may exclusively possess as long as he keeps it to himself; but the moment it is divulged, it forces itself into the possession of every one, and the receiver
Idea - Wikipedia — cannot dispossess himself of it. Its peculiar character, too, is that no one possesses the less, because every other possesses the whole of it. He who receives an
Idea - Wikipedia — idea from me, receives instruction himself without lessening mine; as he who lights his taper at mine, receives light without darkening me.
Idea - Wikipedia — at ideas should freely spread from one to another over the globe, for the moral and mutual instruction of man, and improvement of his condition, seems to
Idea - Wikipedia — have been peculiarly and benevolently designed by nature, when she made them, like ﬁre, expansible over all space, without lessening their density in any
Idea - Wikipedia — point, and like the air in which we breathe, move, and have our physical being, incapable of conﬁnement or exclusive appropriation. Inventions then cannot,
Idea - Wikipedia — in nature, be a subject of property.
Idea - Wikipedia — Society may give an exclusive right to the proﬁts arising from them, as an encouragement to men to pursue ideas which may produce utility, but this may or
Idea - Wikipedia — may not be done, according to the will and convenience of the society, without claim or complaint from anybody. Accordingly, it is a fact, as far as I am
Idea - Wikipedia — informed, that England was, until we copied her, the only country on earth which ever, by a general law, gave a legal right to the exclusive use of an idea. In
Idea - Wikipedia — some other countries it is sometimes done, in a great case, and by a special and personal act but, generally speaking, other nations have thought that these
Idea - Wikipedia — monopolies produce more embarrassment than advantage to society.[24]
Idea - Wikipedia — — omas Jeﬀerson, leer to Isaac McPherson, 13 August 1813

Idea - Wikipedia — the term intellectual property is used mistakenly in place of copyright. Copyright law regulating the aforementioned monopolies generally
Idea - Wikipedia — does not cover the actual ideas. e law does not bestow the legal status of property upon ideas per se. Instead, laws purport to regulate
Idea - Wikipedia — events related to the usage, copying, production, sale and other forms of exploitation of the fundamental expression of a work, that may or
Idea - Wikipedia — may not carry ideas. Copyright law is fundamentally diﬀerent from patent law in this respect: patents do grant monopolies on ideas (more
Idea - Wikipedia — on this below).
Idea - Wikipedia — A copyright is meant to regulate some aspects of the usage of expressions of a work, not an idea. us, copyrights have a negative
Idea - Wikipedia — relationship to ideas.
Idea - Wikipedia — Work means a tangible medium of expression. It may be an original or derivative work of art, be it literary, dramatic, musical recitation,
Idea - Wikipedia — artistic, related to sound recording, etc. In (at least) countries adhering to the Berne Convention, copyright automatically starts covering the
Idea - Wikipedia — work upon the original creation and ﬁxation thereof, without any extra steps. While creation usually involves an idea, the idea in itself does
Idea - Wikipedia — not suﬃce for the purposes of claiming copyright.[25][26][27][28][29]
Idea - Wikipedia — Conﬁdentiality and nondisclosure agreements are legal instruments that assist corporations and individuals in keeping ideas from escaping to the general public.
Idea - Wikipedia — Generally, these instruments are covered by contract law.

Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Arbitrariness
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Arbitrariness is the quality of being "determined by chance, whim, or impulse, and not by necessity, reason, or principle". It is also used to refer to a choice made
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — without any speciﬁc criterion or restraint.[1]
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Arbitrary decisions are not necessarily the same as random decisions. For example, during the 1973 oil crisis, Americans were allowed to purchase gasoline only on odd-
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — numbered days if their license plate was odd, and on even-numbered days if their license plate was even. e system was well-deﬁned and not random in its
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — restrictions; however, since license plate numbers are completely unrelated to a person's ﬁtness to purchase gasoline, it was still an arbitrary division of people.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Similarly, schoolchildren are oen organized by their surname in alphabetical order, a non-random yet an arbitrary method—at least in cases where surnames are
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — irrelevant.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Arbitrary actions are closely related to teleology, the study of purpose. Actions lacking a telos, a goal, are necessarily
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — arbitrary. With no end to measure against, there can be no standard applied to choices, so all decisions are alike. Note that
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — arbitrary or random methods in the standard sense of arbitrary may not qualify as arbitrary choices philosophically if they
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — were done in furtherance of a larger purpose (such as the examples above for the purposes of establishing discipline in school
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — and avoiding overcrowding at gas stations).
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Nihilism is the philosophy that believes that there is no purpose in the universe, and that every choice is arbitrary.[2]
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — According to nihilism, the universe contains no value and is essentially meaningless. Because the universe and all of its
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — constituents contain no higher goal for us to make subgoals from, all aspects of human life and experiences are completely
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — arbitrary. ere is no right or wrong decision, thought or practice and whatever choice a human being makes is just as
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — meaningless and empty as any other choice he or she could have made.[3]
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Many brands of theism, the belief in a deity or deities, believe that everything has a purpose and that nothing is arbitrary. In
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — these philosophies, God created the universe for a reason, and every event ﬂows from that. Even seemingly random events cannot escape God's hand and purpose. is
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — is somewhat related to the argument from design—the argument for God's existence because a purpose can be found in the universe.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Arbitrariness is also related to ethics, the philosophy of decision-making. Even if a person has a goal, they may choose to aempt to achieve it in ways that may be
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — considered arbitrary. Rationalism holds that knowledge comes about through intellectual calculation and deduction; many rationalists (though not all) apply this to
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — ethics as well. All decisions should be made through reason and logic, not via whim or how one "feels" what is right. Randomness may occasionally be acceptable as
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — part of a subtask in furtherance of a larger goal, but not in general.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Philosophy
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — The symbol of a universal quantiﬁer
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — In semiotics, the general theory of signs, sign systems, and sign processes, Saussure introduced the notion of arbitrariness according to which there is no necessary
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — connection between the material sign (or signiﬁer), and the entity it refers to or denotes as its meaning (or signiﬁed) as a mental concept or real object.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — e principle of semiotic arbitrariness (introduced by Ferdinand de Saussure in his Course in General Linguistics) is the idea that social convention is what imbues
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — meaning to a given semiosis (any activity, conduct, or process that involves signs, including the production of meaning) or sign.[4]
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — A logical symbol is a fundamental concept in logic, tokens of which may be marks or a conﬁguration of marks which form a
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — particular paern.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — In mathematics, arbitrary corresponds to the term "every" and the universal quantiﬁer
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — , as in an arbitrary division of a set or
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — an arbitrary permutation of a sequence. Its use implies generality and that a statement does not only apply to special cases,
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — but to every available choice. For example, one might say that:
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — "Given an arbitrary integer, multiplying it by two will result in an even number."
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Even further, the implication of the use of "arbitrary" is that generality will hold—even if an opponent were to choose the
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — item in question. In which case, arbitrary can be regarded as synonymous to worst-case.[5]
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Arbitrary comes from the Latin arbitrarius, the source of arbiter; someone who is tasked to judge some maer.[6] An arbitrary
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — legal judgment is a decision made at the discretion of the judge, not one that is ﬁxed by law.[7][1] In some countries, a
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — prohibition of arbitrariness is enshrined into the constitution. Article 9 of the Swiss Federal Constitution theoretically overrides even democratic decisions in prohibiting
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — arbitrary government action.[8] e US Supreme Court has overturned laws for having "no rational basis." A recent study of the U.S. asylum system suggests that
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — arbitrariness in decision-making might be the cause of large disparities in outcomes between diﬀerent adjudicators, a phenomenon described as refugee roulee.
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — Article 330 of the Russian penal code deﬁnes arbitrariness as a speciﬁc crime, but with a very broad deﬁnition encompassing any "actions contrary to the order
Arbitrariness - Wikipedia — presented by a law".[9]

Derivative work - Wikipedia — In copyright law, a derivative work is an expressive creation that includes major copyrightable elements of a ﬁrst,
Derivative work - Wikipedia — previously created original work (the underlying work). e derivative work becomes a second, separate work
Derivative work - Wikipedia — independent from the ﬁrst. e transformation, modiﬁcation or adaptation of the work must be substantial and bear
Derivative work - Wikipedia — its author's personality suﬃciently to be original and thus protected by copyright. Translations, cinematic adaptations
Derivative work - Wikipedia — and musical arrangements are common types of derivative works.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Most countries' legal systems seek to protect both original and derivative works.[1] ey grant authors the right to
Derivative work - Wikipedia — impede or otherwise control their integrity and the author's commercial interests. Derivative works and their authors
Derivative work - Wikipedia — beneﬁt in turn from the full protection of copyright without prejudicing the rights of the original work's author.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, an international copyright treaty, stipulates that derivative works shall be protected although it
Derivative work - Wikipedia — does not use the term, namely that "Translations, adaptations, arrangements of music and other alterations of a literary or artistic work shall be protected as original
Derivative work - Wikipedia — works without prejudice to the copyright in the original work".[2]

Derivative work - Wikipedia — A "derivative work" is a work based upon one or more preexisting works, such as a translation, musical arrangement, dramatization, ﬁctionalization, motion
Derivative work - Wikipedia — picture version, sound recording, art reproduction, abridgment, condensation, or any other form in which a work may be recast, transformed, or adapted. A
Derivative work - Wikipedia — work consisting of editorial revisions, annotations, elaborations, or other modiﬁcations which, as a whole, represent an original work of authorship, is a
Derivative work - Wikipedia — "derivative work".

Derivative work - Wikipedia — decision in Feist v. Rural, some pre-Feist lower court decisions addressed this requirement in relation to derivative works. In Durham Industries, Inc. v. Tomy Corp.[13] and
Derivative work - Wikipedia — earlier in L. Batlin & Son, Inc. v. Snyder.[14] the Second Circuit held that a derivative work must be original relative to the underlying work on which it is based.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Otherwise, it cannot enjoy copyright protection and copying it will not infringe any copyright of the derivative work itself (although copying it may infringe the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — copyright, if any, of the underlying work on which the derivative work was based).
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e Batlin case rested on the copyrightability of an "Uncle Sam" toy bank, ﬁrst copyrighted in 1886. ese toys have Uncle Sam's extended arm and outstretched hand

Derivative work - Wikipedia — making a very similar toy bank which was based on Snyder's version (and not, incidentally, on the 19th century original). When the laer aempted to import the toy
Derivative work - Wikipedia — banks, the US Customs service notiﬁed them that they appeared to be infringing on Snyder's copyright, and would not allow the toy banks to be imported. Batlin then
Derivative work - Wikipedia — got an injunction against Snyder to deny the recording of his copyright and allowing them to import their banks. On appeal to the Second Circuit Court, Snyder took
Derivative work - Wikipedia — great pains to demonstrate how his banks varied in size and shape from the 19th century original, arguing that his banks, though similar to the older work, diﬀered in a
Derivative work - Wikipedia — number of signiﬁcant ways and warranted protection under a new copyright. However, his appeal was denied and the injunction against Snyder's copyright upheld (six
Derivative work - Wikipedia — members of the court voted to deny, the other three ﬁling a dissenting opinion). Much of this decision focused on the fact that nearly all of the alterations in Snyder's
Derivative work - Wikipedia — version were made solely to allow the object to be more easily manufactured in plastic rather than metal, and therefore were functional, not artistic or creative.[15][16]

Derivative work - Wikipedia — In the subsequent Durham case, the court applied the same principle in a suit between two diﬀerent Disney toy licensees in which one licensee claimed that the other
Derivative work - Wikipedia — had pirated his Mickey Mouse, Donald Duck and Pluto. Durham conceded that in making these toys it used Tomy's Disney ﬁgures as models. at was not
Derivative work - Wikipedia — determinative. e court said that "the only aspects of Tomy's Disney ﬁgures entitled to copyright protection are the non-trivial, original features, if any, contributed by
Derivative work - Wikipedia — the author or creator of these derivative works." But Tomy's toys reﬂected "no independent creation, no distinguishable variation from preexisting works, nothing
Derivative work - Wikipedia — recognizably the author's own contribution that sets Tomy's ﬁgures apart from the prototypical Mickey, Donald, and Pluto, authored by Disney and subsequently
Derivative work - Wikipedia — represented by Disney or its licensees in a seemingly limitless variety of forms and media." Because the court considered that "it is clear that the originality requirement
Derivative work - Wikipedia — imposed by the Constitution and the Copyright Act has particular signiﬁcance in the case of derivative works based on copyrighted preexisting works," it denied relief
Derivative work - Wikipedia — and dismissed the claim. us the law is clear that a derivative work is protectable only to the extent that it embodies original expression. Its non-original aspects are
Derivative work - Wikipedia — not copyright-protectable (what is loosely called "uncopyrightable").
Derivative work - Wikipedia — In both of these cases, the defendants were held not to be liable for copyright infringement, even though they presumably copied a considerable amount from the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — plaintiﬀ's work. ey were not liable because the plaintiﬀ did not enjoy copyright protection. e plaintiﬀs' works lacked enough originality to acquire copyright
Derivative work - Wikipedia — protection of their own. ey were too close to the original works on which they were based.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Copyright ownership in a derivative work aaches only if the derivative work is lawful, because of a license or other "authorization." e U.S. Copyright Oﬃce says in
Derivative work - Wikipedia — its circular on derivative works:
Derivative work - Wikipedia — In any case where a copyrighted work is used without the permission of the copyright owner, copyright protection will not extend to any part of the work
Derivative work - Wikipedia — in which such material has been used unlawfully.[17][18]
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e courts have so far addressed lile aention to the issue of lawful (i.e., not unlawful) use without authorization, as in fair-use cases such as the Prey Woman case.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Recently, however, in Keeling v. Hars,[19] the Second Circuit held that, if the creator of an unauthorized work stays within the bounds of fair use and adds suﬃcient
Derivative work - Wikipedia — original content, the original contributions in such an unauthorized derivative work are protectable under the Copyright Act. In that case, the plaintiﬀ created a parody
Derivative work - Wikipedia — stage adaptation of a motion picture, without authorization.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — is issue sometimes arises in the context of the defendant purchasing a copy of a picture or some other work from the copyright owner or a licensee and then reselling
Derivative work - Wikipedia — it in diﬀerent context. For example, pictures from greeting cards might be aﬃxed to tiles or one kind of textile product might be turned into another that can be sold at a
Derivative work - Wikipedia — higher price. In Lee v. A.R.T. Co., (the Annie Lee case), the defendant aﬃxed the copyright owner's copyright-protected note cards and small lithographs to tiles and then
Derivative work - Wikipedia — resold them.[20] e original art was not changed or reproduced, only bonded to ceramic and sold. e court held that this act was not original and creative enough to

Derivative work - Wikipedia — Liability of derivative-work
Derivative work - Wikipedia — rise to the level of creating a derivative work, but eﬀectively similar to any other form of display or art frame.[21]
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Distribution rights diﬀer from reproduction rights. While the ﬁrst-sale doctrine entitles the copyright holder to begin the distribution chain of a copyrighted work - by
Derivative work - Wikipedia — selling note cards, for instance, or giving them away - it does not permit the copyright holder to control what is done with the item aer it is distributed. Unless there is
Derivative work - Wikipedia — a separate contract between the parties, the person who owns the object has the right to give it away or resell it themself. In the case of Lee v. A.R.T., since bonding the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — cards to ceramic did not create a derivative work, A.R.T. Co. was legally within their rights to resell the cards in such a fashion.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — When the defendant's modiﬁcation of the plaintiﬀ's work is de minimis, too insubstantial to "count", there is no infringing preparation of a derivative work. So long as
Derivative work - Wikipedia — there is no derivative work, there is no infringement—since no conduct that the Copyright Act forbids has occurred.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — In a House Report,[22] Congress said:
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e exclusive right to prepare derivative works, speciﬁed separately in clause (2) of section 106, overlaps the exclusive right of reproduction to some extent.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — It is broader than that right, however, in the sense that reproduction requires ﬁxation in copies or phonorecords, whereas the preparation of a derivative
Derivative work - Wikipedia — work, such as a ballet, pantomime, or improvised performance, may be an infringement even though nothing is ever ﬁxed in tangible form.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e 9th Circuit, however, has resisted this expansive view of liability for derivative works by imposing its own quasi-ﬁxation requirement. In Micro Star v. FormGen Inc.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — [23] Judge Kozinski wrote:
Derivative work - Wikipedia — To narrow the statute to a manageable level, we have developed certain criteria a work must satisfy in order to qualify as a derivative work. One of these is
Derivative work - Wikipedia — that a derivative work must exist in a "concrete or permanent form,"….e requirement that a derivative work must assume a concrete or permanent form
Derivative work - Wikipedia — was recognized without much discussion in Galoob.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Even if a work is found to be an unauthorized derivative work, an alleged infringer can escape liability via the defense of fair use. For example, in Campbell v. Acuﬀ-Rose
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Music, Inc., the Supreme Court found that although a parody of the song "Oh, Prey Woman" by 2 Live Crew was an unauthorized derivative work, fair use was still
Derivative work - Wikipedia — available as a complete defense. is case marked the Supreme Court's pointing to transformativeness as a major clue to application of the fair use defense to derivative
Derivative work - Wikipedia — works.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e defense of fair use has become very important in computer- and Internet-related works. Two 1992 Ninth Circuit decisions are illustrative.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — In Lewis Galoob Toys, Inc. v. Nintendo of America, Inc.,[24] the appellate court held that it was a fair use for owners of copies of video games, such as Super Mario Bros., to
Derivative work - Wikipedia — use Galoob's product the Game Genie to customize the diﬃculty or other characteristics of the game by granting a character more strength, speed, or endurance.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Fixation requirement
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e fair use defense in derivative work cases
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Nintendo strongly opposed Galoob's product, allegedly because it interfered with the maintenance of the "Nintendo Culture," which Nintendo claimed was important to
Derivative work - Wikipedia — its marketing program.[25] e court held, among other things, that the fair use defense shielded Galoob's conduct. e court said that "a party who distributes a
Derivative work - Wikipedia — copyrighted work cannot dictate how that work is to be enjoyed. Consumers may use … a Game Genie to enhance a Nintendo Game cartridge's audiovisual display in
Derivative work - Wikipedia — such a way as to make the experience more enjoyable."
Derivative work - Wikipedia — In Sega Enterprises, Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc.,[26] the court excused Accolade from copyright infringement liability on fair use grounds. Nintendo and Sega produced video
Derivative work - Wikipedia — game consoles. Each stored the games in plastic cartridges that provided game data to the consoles. By way of analogy, the Sega hardware console's "platform" diﬀered
Derivative work - Wikipedia — from Nintendo's, as a Macintosh platform diﬀers from that of a PC. Hence, a video game cartridge that works on one system does not work on the other. Sega and
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Nintendo sought to "license" access to their hardware platforms, and each company developed soware "locks" to keep out cartridges that did not have the proper "key."
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Accolade sought a license from Sega for its key, but negotiations broke down over price. Accolade then decided to reverse engineer Sega's lock and key system. To do so,
Derivative work - Wikipedia — it had to download (copy) all of the computer code from Sega's product and disassemble it (translate it from machine code into human-readable assembly). Accolade
Derivative work - Wikipedia — succeeded and began to market new video games that it independently wrote, which were capable of being operated in Sega consoles. is led to copyright
Derivative work - Wikipedia — infringement litigation, in which Sega alleged that the downloading was improper copying (reproduction) of Sega's code. e court held that Sega was trying to use the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — copyright in its computer code to maintain a monopoly over the sale of video games, to which it was not legally entitled. Accolade downloaded the computer code only
Derivative work - Wikipedia — to ascertain how the lock worked, so that it could make a key that would permit its games to work in Sega consoles. e court held that such a use was fair use: "We
Derivative work - Wikipedia — conclude that where disassembly is the only way to gain access to the ideas and functional elements embodied in a copyrighted computer program and where there is a
Derivative work - Wikipedia — legitimate reason for seeking such access, disassembly is a fair use of the copyrighted work, as a maer of law."[27] However, since the passage of the anti-circumvention
Derivative work - Wikipedia — statutes contained in the DMCA, further court cases involving the fair-use defense of such activities have yet to be actually litigated.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — A crucial factor in current legal analysis of derivative works is transformativeness, largely as a result of the Supreme Court's 1994 decision in Campbell v. Acuﬀ-Rose
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Music, Inc. e Court's opinion emphasized the importance of transformativeness in its fair use analysis of the parody of "Oh, Prey Woman" involved in the Campbell
Derivative work - Wikipedia — case. In parody, as the Court explained, the transformativeness is the new insight that readers, listeners, or viewers gain from the parodic treatment of the original work.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — As the Court pointed out, the words of the parody "derisively demonstrat[e] how bland and banal the Orbison [Prey Woman] song" is.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e modern emphasis of transformativeness in fair use analysis stems from a 1990 article by Judge Pierre N. Leval in the Harvard Law Review, "Toward a Fair Use
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Standard",[28] which the Court quoted and cited extensively in its Campbell opinion. In his article, Leval explained the social importance of transformative use of
Derivative work - Wikipedia — another's work and what justiﬁes such a taking:
Derivative work - Wikipedia — I believe the answer to the question of justiﬁcation turns primarily on whether, and to what extent, the challenged use is transformative. e use must be
Derivative work - Wikipedia — productive and must employ the quoted maer in a diﬀerent manner or for a diﬀerent purpose from the original. …[I] the secondary use adds value to the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — original--if the quoted maer is used as raw material, transformed in the creation of new information, new aesthetics, new insights and understandings--
Derivative work - Wikipedia — this is the very type of activity that the fair use doctrine intends to protect for the enrichment of society.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Transformative uses may include criticizing the quoted work, exposing the character of the original author, proving a fact, or summarizing an idea argued
Derivative work - Wikipedia — in the original in order to defend or rebut it. ey also may include parody, symbolism, aesthetic declarations, and innumerable other uses.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Transformativeness
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e concept, as Leval and the Campbell Court described it, developed in relation to fair use of traditional works: literary works, musical works, and pictorial works. But
Derivative work - Wikipedia — recently courts have extended this rationale to Internet and computer-related works. In such cases, as illustrated by Kelly v. Arriba So Corporation[29] and Perfect 10, Inc.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — v. Amazon.com, Inc.,[30] the courts ﬁnd a use (such as that of thumbnails in an image search engine, for indexing purposes) transformative because it provides an added
Derivative work - Wikipedia — beneﬁt to the public, which was not previously available and might remain unavailable without the derivative or secondary use. e Ninth Circuit Court explained this
Derivative work - Wikipedia — in the Perfect 10 case:
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Google's use of thumbnails is highly transformative. In Kelly we concluded that Arriba's use of thumbnails was transformative because "Arriba's use of the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — images served a diﬀerent function than Kelly's use — improving access to information on the Internet versus artistic expression." Although an image may
Derivative work - Wikipedia — have been created originally to serve an entertainment, aesthetic, or informative function, a search engine transforms the image into a pointer directing a
Derivative work - Wikipedia — user to a source of information. Just as a "parody has an obvious claim to transformative value" because "it can provide social beneﬁt, by shedding light on
Derivative work - Wikipedia — an earlier work, and, in the process, creating a new one," a search engine provides social beneﬁt by incorporating an original work into a new work, namely,
Derivative work - Wikipedia — an electronic reference tool. Indeed, a search engine may be more transformative than a parody because a search engine provides an entirely new use for
Derivative work - Wikipedia — the original work, while a parody typically has the same entertainment purpose as the original work.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — …In conducting our case-speciﬁc analysis of fair use in light of the purposes of copyright, we must weigh Google's superseding and commercial uses of
Derivative work - Wikipedia — thumbnail images against Google's signiﬁcant transformative use, as well as the extent to which Google's search engine promotes the purposes of copyright
Derivative work - Wikipedia — and serves the interests of the public. Although the district court acknowledged the "truism that search engines such as Google Image Search provide great
Derivative work - Wikipedia — value to the public," the district court did not expressly consider whether this value outweighed the signiﬁcance of Google's superseding use or the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — commercial nature of Google's use. e Supreme Court, however, has directed us to be mindful of the extent to which a use promotes the purposes of
Derivative work - Wikipedia — copyright and serves the interests of the public.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — …We conclude that the signiﬁcantly transformative nature of Google's search engine, particularly in light of its public beneﬁt, outweighs Google's
Derivative work - Wikipedia — superseding and commercial uses of the thumbnails in this case. … We are also mindful of the Supreme Court's direction that "the more transformative the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — new work, the less will be the signiﬁcance of other factors, like commercialism, that may weigh against a ﬁnding of fair use."
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e Ninth Circuit's treatment of transformativeness and fair use in the Arriba So and Perfect 10 cases illustrates diﬀerent data points on the copyright infringement
Derivative work - Wikipedia — spectrum, at least with respect to transformativeness and fair use. Arriba So was a relatively polar case. e harm to Kelly, the copyright owner, was negligible; it was
Derivative work - Wikipedia — hardly more than hurt feelings, because as the Ninth Circuit said in its opinion – "Arriba's creation and use of the thumbnails [the derivative work] does not harm the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — market for or value of Kelly' s images." On the other hand, the court found that Arriba's use beneﬁted the public: "Arriba's use of the images serves a diﬀerent function
Derivative work - Wikipedia — than Kelly's use — improving access to information on the internet versus artistic expression." e balance thus tilted strongly in Arriba's favor. e foregoing analysis
Derivative work - Wikipedia — in this case thus made the Ninth Circuit to be the ﬁrst court to make the equation highly beneﬁcial to public = transformative, and as the Supreme Court explained in
Derivative work - Wikipedia — Campbell, the more transformative a derivative use the more likely the use is to be a fair use.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e Campbell Court recognized that the balance may not always be one-sided, as it was in Campbell itself and in Arriba So. In the Perfect 10 case the interests were
Derivative work - Wikipedia — more evenly balanced, for the ﬁrst time in a derivative work case involving new information technology. Both Google and Perfect 10 had legitimate interests at stake
Derivative work - Wikipedia — and support for their respective positions. us, there was a ﬁnding that "Google's wide-ranging use of thumbnails is highly transformative: their creation and display is

Derivative work - Wikipedia — Trivia books based on TV shows, such as Seinfeld, are considered derivative works, for purposes of infringement liability, at
Derivative work - Wikipedia — least if they incorporate a substantial amount of copyright-protected content from the TV episodes.[39] In Castle Rock the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — court found that any transformative purpose possessed in the derivative work was "slight to non-existent." Accordingly, the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — court held that defendants had prepared an infringing derivative work.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — A 2007 lawsuit, CBS Operations v. Reel Funds International, ruled that television series that have some episodes lapse into the
Derivative work - Wikipedia — public domain can be classiﬁed as derivative works and subject to indirect copyright accordingly. e lawsuit centered
Derivative work - Wikipedia — around 16 episodes of e Andy Griﬃth Show from the show's third season that had lapsed into the public domain in 1989;
Derivative work - Wikipedia — CBS successfully argued that because all of the episodes from the show's ﬁrst two seasons were still under valid copyright,
Derivative work - Wikipedia — that CBS still held copyright on the characters used in those episodes and could block a public domain distributor from
Derivative work - Wikipedia — selling DVDs with those episodes.[40][41]
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e musical West Side Story, is a derivative work based on Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, because it uses numerous
Derivative work - Wikipedia — expressive elements from the earlier work.[42] However, Shakespeare's drama Romeo and Juliet is also a derivative work that
Derivative work - Wikipedia — draws heavily from Pyramus and isbe and other sources. Nevertheless, no legal rule prevents a derivative work from being
Derivative work - Wikipedia — based on a work that is itself a derivative work based on a still earlier work — at least, so long as the last work borrows
Derivative work - Wikipedia — expressive elements from the second work that are original with the second work rather than taken from the earliest work.
Derivative work - Wikipedia — e key is whether the copied elements are original and expressive (not merely conventional or mise en scène); if that is so, the second or derivative work is
Derivative work - Wikipedia — independently subject to copyright protection, and if that is not, the second work (if unauthorized) may infringe the ﬁrst, but it is not independently copyrightable.[43]

Career - Wikipedia — Career
Career - Wikipedia — A career is an individual's metaphorical "journey" through learning, work and other aspects of life. ere
Career - Wikipedia — are a number of ways to deﬁne career and the term is used in a variety of ways.
Career - Wikipedia — e Oxford English Dictionary deﬁnes "career" as a person's "course or progress through life (or a distinct
Career - Wikipedia — portion of life)". is deﬁnition relates "career" to a range of aspects of an individual's life, learning, and
Career - Wikipedia — work. "Career" is also frequently understood to relate to the working aspects of an individual's life - as in
Career - Wikipedia — "career woman", for example. A third way in which the term "career" is used describes an occupation or a
Career - Wikipedia — profession that usually involves speciﬁc training and/or formal education,[1] considered to be a person's
Career - Wikipedia — lifework.[2] In this case "a career" is seen as a sequence of related jobs, usually pursued within a single
Career - Wikipedia — industry or sector: one can speak for example of "a career in education", of "a criminal career" or of "a
Career - Wikipedia — career in the building trade". A career has been deﬁned by organizational behavior researchers as "an

Career - Wikipedia — the phrase likely was in regular use by the year 1800.[7]

Career - Wikipedia — Historic changes in careers
Career - Wikipedia — 20th/early 21st centuries to have dual or multiple careers, either sequentially or concurrently. us, professional identities have become hyphenated or hybridized to
Career - Wikipedia — reﬂect this shi in work ethic. Economist Richard Florida notes this trend generally and more speciﬁcally among the "creative class".
Career - Wikipedia — Career management or career development describes the active and purposeful management of a career by an individual. Ideas of what comprise "career management
Career - Wikipedia — skills" are described by the Blueprint model (in the United States, Canada, Australia, Scotland, and England[8])[9] and the Seven C's of Digital Career Literacy
Career - Wikipedia — (speciﬁcally relating to the Internet skills).[10]
Career - Wikipedia — Key skills include the ability to reﬂect on one's current career, research the labour market, determine whether education is necessary, ﬁnd openings, and make career
Career - Wikipedia — changes.
Career - Wikipedia — According to Behling and others, an individual's decision to join a ﬁrm may depend on any of the three factors viz. objective factor, subjective factor and critical contact.
Career - Wikipedia — [11]
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Objective factor theory assumes that the applicants are rational. The choice, therefore, is exercised after an objective assessment of the
Career - Wikipedia — tangible beneﬁts of the job. Factors may include the salary, other beneﬁts, location, opportunities for career advancement, etc.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Subjective factor theory suggests that decision making is dominated by social and psychological factors. The status of the job, reputation of
Career - Wikipedia — the organization, and other similar factors plays an important role.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Critical contact theory advances the idea that a candidate's observations while interacting with the organization plays a vital role in decision
Career - Wikipedia — making. For example, how the recruiter keeps in touch with the candidate, the promptness of response and similar factors are important. This
Career - Wikipedia — theory is more valid with experienced professionals.
Career - Wikipedia — ese theories assume that candidates have a free choice of employers and careers. In reality, the scarcity of jobs and strong competition for desirable jobs severely
Career - Wikipedia — skews the decision-making process. In many markets, employees work particular careers simply because they were forced to accept whatever work was available to
Career - Wikipedia — them. Additionally, O-Holland and colleagues found that culture can have a major inﬂuence on career choice, depending on the type of culture.[12]
Career - Wikipedia — When choosing a career that's best for you, according to US News, there are multiple things to consider. Some of those include: natural talents, work style, social
Career - Wikipedia — interaction, work–life balance, whether or not you are looking to give back, whether you are comfortable in the public eye, dealing with stress or not, and ﬁnally, how
Career - Wikipedia — much money you want to make. If choosing a career feels like too much pressure, here's another option: pick a path that feels right today by making the best decision
Career - Wikipedia — you can, and know that you can change your mind in the future. In today's workplace, choosing a career doesn't necessarily mean you have to stick with that line of
Career - Wikipedia — work for your entire life. Make a smart decision, and plan to re-evaluate down the line based on your long-term objectives.[13]

Career - Wikipedia — Career (occupation) changing
Career - Wikipedia — Changing occupation is an important aspect of career and career management. Over a lifetime, both the individual and the labour market will change; it is to be
Career - Wikipedia — expected that many people will change occupations during their lives. Data collected by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics through the National Longitudinal Survey of
Career - Wikipedia — Youth in 1979 showed that individuals between the ages of 18 and 38 will hold more than 10 jobs.[14]
Career - Wikipedia — ere are various reasons why people might want to change their careers. Sometimes career change can come as the result of a long-anticipated layoﬀ, while other
Career - Wikipedia — times it can occur unexpectedly and without warning.[15]
Career - Wikipedia — A survey conducted by Right Management[16] suggests the following reasons for career changing.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ The downsizing or the restructuring of an organization (54%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ New challenges or opportunities that arise (30%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Poor or ineﬀective leadership (25%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Having a poor relationship with a manager(s) (22%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ For the improvement of work/life balance (21%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Contributions are not being recognized (21%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ For better compensation and beneﬁts (18%),
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ For better alignment with personal and organizational values (17%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Personal strengths and capabilities are not a good ﬁt with an organization (16%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ The ﬁnancial instability of an organization (13%).
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ An organization relocated (12%).
Career - Wikipedia — According to an article on Time.com, one out of three people currently employed (as of 2008) spends about an hour per day searching for another position.[16]
Career - Wikipedia — Career success is a term used frequently in academic and popular writing about career. It refers to the extent and ways in which an individual can be described as
Career - Wikipedia — successful in his or her working life so far.[17]
Career - Wikipedia — During the 1950s and 1960s, individuals typically worked for one or two ﬁrms during their career and success was deﬁned by the organization and measured by
Career - Wikipedia — promotions, increases in salary, and/or status.[18] Such traditional careers were exempliﬁed by Donald Super's career stage model.[19] Super's linear career stage model
Career - Wikipedia — suggested that careers take place within the context of stable, organizational structures. Individuals moved up the organization's hierarchy seeking greater extrinsic
Career - Wikipedia — rewards.[20]
Career - Wikipedia — Early career success may breed disappointment later, especially when a person's self-worth is tied up in their career or achievements.[21] Professional success tends to
Career - Wikipedia — come early in some ﬁelds, such as scientiﬁc research, and later in other ﬁelds, such as teaching.[21]
Career - Wikipedia — Career success
Career - Wikipedia — Earnings can be expressed either in absolute terms (e.g. the amount a person earns) or in relative terms (e.g. the amount a person earns compared with their starting
Career - Wikipedia — salary). Earnings and status are examples of objective criteria of success, where "objective" means that they can be factually veriﬁed, and are not purely a maer of
Career - Wikipedia — opinion.
Career - Wikipedia — Many observers argue that careers are less predictable than they once were, due to the fast pace of economic and technological change.[22] is means that career
Career - Wikipedia — management is more obviously the responsibility of the individual rather than his or her employing organisation, because a "job for life" is a thing of the past. is has
Career - Wikipedia — put more emphasis on subjective criteria of career success.[23] ese include job satisfaction, career satisfaction, work-life balance, a sense of personal achievement, and
Career - Wikipedia — aaining work that is consistent with one's personal values. A person's assessment of his or her career success is likely to be inﬂuenced by social comparisons, such as
Career - Wikipedia — how well family members, friends, or contemporaries at school or college have done.[24]
Career - Wikipedia — e amount and type of career success a person achieves is aﬀected by several forms of career capital.[25] ese include social capital (the extent and depth of personal
Career - Wikipedia — contacts a person can draw upon), human capital (demonstrable abilities, experiences and qualiﬁcations), economic capital (money and other material resources which
Career - Wikipedia — permit access to career-related resources), and cultural capital (having skills, aitudes or general know-how to operate eﬀectively in a particular social context).[26]
Career - Wikipedia — ere are a range of diﬀerent educational, counseling, and human resource management interventions that can support individuals to develop and manage their careers.
Career - Wikipedia — Career support is commonly oﬀered while people are in education, when they are transitioning to the labour market, when they are changing career, during periods of
Career - Wikipedia — unemployment, and during transition to retirement. Support may be oﬀered by career professionals, other professionals or by non-professionals such as family and
Career - Wikipedia — friends. Professional career support is sometimes known as "career guidance" as in the OECD deﬁnition of career guidance:
Career - Wikipedia — e activities may take place on an individual or group basis, and may be face-to-face or at a distance (including helplines and web-based services). ey
Career - Wikipedia — include career information provision (in print, ICT-based and other forms), assessment and self-assessment tools, counselling interviews, career education
Career - Wikipedia — programmes (to help individuals develop their self-awareness, opportunity awareness, and career management skills), taster programmes (to sample options
Career - Wikipedia — before choosing them), work search programmes, and transition services."[27]
Career - Wikipedia — However this use of the term "career guidance" can be confusing as the term is also commonly used to describe the activities of career counselors.
Career - Wikipedia — Career support is oﬀered by a range of diﬀerent mechanisms. Much career support is informal and provided through personal networks or existing relationships such as
Career - Wikipedia — management. ere is a market for private career support however the bulk of career support that exists as a professionalised activity is provided by the public sector.

Career - Wikipedia — Types of career support
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career information describes information that supports career and learning choices. An important sub-set of career information is labour
Career - Wikipedia — market information (LMI), such as salaries of various professions, employment rate in various professions, available training programs, and
Career - Wikipedia — current job openings.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career assessments are tests that come in a variety of forms and rely on both quantitative and qualitative methodologies. Career assessments
Career - Wikipedia — can help individuals identify and better articulate their unique interests, personality, values, and skills to determine how well they may match
Career - Wikipedia — with a certain career. Some skills that career assessments could help determine are job-speciﬁc skills, transferable skills, and self-management
Career - Wikipedia — skills.[28] Career assessments can also provide a window of potential opportunities by helping individuals discover the tasks, experience,
Career - Wikipedia — education and training that is needed for a career they would want to pursue.[29] Career counselors, executive coaches, educational
Career - Wikipedia — institutions, career development centers, and outplacement companies often administer career assessments to help individuals focus their
Career - Wikipedia — search on careers that closely match their unique personal proﬁle.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career counseling assesses people's interests, personality, values and skills, and helps them to explore career options and research graduate
Career - Wikipedia — and professional schools. Career counseling provides one-on-one or group professional assistance in exploration and decision making tasks
Career - Wikipedia — related to choosing a major/occupation, transitioning into the world of work or further professional training.
Career - Wikipedia — ▪ Career education describes a process by which individuals come to learn about themselves, their careers and the world of work. There is a
Career - Wikipedia — strong tradition of career education in schools,[30] however career education can also occur in a wider range of other contexts including further
Career - Wikipedia — and higher education and the workplace. A commonly used framework for careers education is DOTS which stands for decision learning (D),
Career - Wikipedia — opportunity awareness (O), transition learning (T), and self-awareness (S).[31] Oftentimes, higher education is thought of as being too narrow or
Career - Wikipedia — too researched based and lacking of a deeper understanding of the material to develop the skills necessary for a certain career.[32]
Career - Wikipedia — Some research shows adding one year of schooling beyond high school creates an increase of wages 17.8% per worker. However, additional years of schooling, beyond 9
Career - Wikipedia — or 10 years, have lile eﬀect on worker's wages. In summary, beer educated, bigger beneﬁts. In 2010, 90% of the U.S. Workforce had a high school diploma, 64% had
Career - Wikipedia — some college, and 34% had at least a bachelor's degree.[33]
Career - Wikipedia — e common problem that people may encounter when trying to achieve an education for a career is the cost. e career that comes with the education must pay well
Career - Wikipedia — enough to be able to pay oﬀ the schooling. e beneﬁts of schooling can diﬀer greatly depending on the degree (or certiﬁcation) obtained, the programs the school may
Career - Wikipedia — oﬀer, and the ranking of the school. Sometimes, colleges provide students more with just education to prepare for careers. It is not uncommon for colleges to provide
Career - Wikipedia — pathways and support straight into the workforce the students may desire.[34]
Career - Wikipedia — Much career support is delivered face-to-face, but an increasing amount of career support is delivered online.[10]

Employment - Wikipedia — Employment
Employment - Wikipedia — Employment is a relationship between two parties regulating the provision of paid labour services. Usually based on a contract, one party, the employer, which might
Employment - Wikipedia — be a corporation, a not-for-proﬁt organization, a co-operative, or any other entity, pays the other, the employee, in return for carrying out assigned work.[1] Employees
Employment - Wikipedia — work in return for wages, which can be paid on the basis of an hourly rate, by piecework or an annual salary, depending on the type of work an employee does, the
Employment - Wikipedia — prevailing conditions of the sector and the bargaining power between the parties. Employees in some sectors may receive gratuities, bonus payments or stock options.
Employment - Wikipedia — In some types of employment, employees may receive beneﬁts in addition to payment. Beneﬁts may include health insurance, housing, and disability insurance.
Employment - Wikipedia — Employment is typically governed by employment laws, organization or legal contracts.
Employment - Wikipedia — An employee contributes labour and expertise to an endeavor of an employer or of a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCB)[2] and is usually hired to
Employment - Wikipedia — perform speciﬁc duties which are packaged into a job. In a corporate context, an employee is a person who is hired to provide services to a company on a regular basis
Employment - Wikipedia — in exchange for compensation and who does not provide these services as part of an independent business.[3]
Employment - Wikipedia — An issue that arises in most companies, especially the ones that are in the gig economy, is the classiﬁcation of workers. A lot of workers that fulﬁll gigs are oen hired
Employment - Wikipedia — as independent contractors.
Employment - Wikipedia — To categorize a worker as an independent contractor rather than an employee, an independent contractor must agree with the client on what the ﬁnished work product
Employment - Wikipedia — will be and then the contractor controls the means and manner of achieving the desired outcome. Secondly, an independent contractor oﬀers services to the public at
Employment - Wikipedia — large, not just to one business, and is responsible for disbursing payments from the client, paying unreimbursed expenses, and providing his or her own tools to
Employment - Wikipedia — complete the job. ird, the relationship of the parties is oen evidenced by a wrien agreement that speciﬁes that the worker is an independent contractor and is not
Employment - Wikipedia — entitled to employee beneﬁts; the services provided by the worker are not key to the business; and the relationship is not permanent.[4]

Employment - Wikipedia — an employee unless speciﬁc guidelines are met, which can be determined by the ABC test.[5][6] us, clarifying whether someone who performs work is an independent
Employment - Wikipedia — contractor or an employee from the beginning, and treating them accordingly, can save a company from trouble later on.

Employment - Wikipedia — Wage labor is the socioeconomic relationship between a worker and an employer, where the worker sells their labor under a formal or informal employment contract.
Employment - Wikipedia — ese transactions usually occur in a labor market where wages are market-determined.[10][16] In exchange for the wages paid, the work product generally becomes the
Employment - Wikipedia — undiﬀerentiated property of the employer, except for special cases such as the vesting of intellectual property patents in the United States where patent rights are
Employment - Wikipedia — usually vested in the original personal inventor. A wage laborer is a person whose primary means of income is from the selling of his or her labor in this way.[17]
Employment - Wikipedia — In modern mixed economies such as that of the OECD countries, it is currently the dominant form of work arrangement. Although most work occurs following this
Employment - Wikipedia — structure, the wage work arrangements of CEOs, professional employees, and professional contract workers are sometimes conﬂated with class assignments, so that
Employment - Wikipedia — "wage labor" is considered to apply only to unskilled, semi-skilled or manual labor.[18]
