Employment - Wikipedia — According to Swedish law,[43] there are three types of employment.
Employment - Wikipedia — ▪ Test employment (Swedish: Provanställning), where the employer hires a person for a test period of 6 months maximum. The employment can
Employment - Wikipedia — be ended at any time without giving any reason. This type of employment can be oﬀered only once per employer and in employee
Employment - Wikipedia — combination. Usually, a time limited or normal employment is oﬀered after a test employment.[44]
Employment - Wikipedia — ▪ Time limited employment (Swedish: Tidsbegränsad anställning). The employer hires a person for a speciﬁed time. Usually, they are extended for
Employment - Wikipedia — a new period. Total maximum two years per employer and employee combination, then it automatically counts as a normal employment.
Employment - Wikipedia — ▪ Normal employment (Swedish: Tillsvidareanställning / Fast anställning), which has no time limit (except for retirement etc.). It can still be ended
Employment - Wikipedia — for two reasons: personal reason, immediate end of employment only for strong reasons such as crime, or lack of work tasks (Swedish:
Employment - Wikipedia — Arbetsbrist), cancellation of employment, usually because of bad income for the company. There is a cancellation period of 1–6 months, and
Employment - Wikipedia — rules for how to select employees, basically those with shortest employment time shall be cancelled ﬁrst.[44]

Employment - Wikipedia — Scholars conceptualize the employment relationship in various ways.[60] A key assumption is the extent to which the employment relationship necessarily includes
Employment - Wikipedia — conﬂicts of interests between employers and employees, and the form of such conﬂicts.[61] In economic theorizing, the labor market mediates all such conﬂicts such that
Employment - Wikipedia — employers and employees who enter into an employment relationship are assumed to ﬁnd this arrangement in their own self-interest. In human resource management
Employment - Wikipedia — theorizing, employers and employees are assumed to have shared interests (or a unity of interests, hence the label "unitarism"). Any conﬂicts that exist are seen as a
Employment - Wikipedia — manifestation of poor human resource management policies or interpersonal clashes such as personality conﬂicts, both of which can and should be managed away.
Employment - Wikipedia — From the perspective of pluralist industrial relations, the employment relationship is characterized by a plurality of stakeholders with legitimate interests (hence the
Employment - Wikipedia — label “pluralism), and some conﬂicts of interests are seen as inherent in the employment relationship (e.g., wages v. proﬁts). Lastly, the critical paradigm emphasizes
Employment - Wikipedia — Models of the employment relationship
Employment - Wikipedia — antagonistic conﬂicts of interests between various groups (e.g., the competing capitalist and working classes in a Marxist framework) that are part of a deeper social
Employment - Wikipedia — conﬂict of unequal power relations. As a result, there are four common models of employment:[62]
Employment - Wikipedia — 1. Mainstream economics: employment is seen as a mutually advantageous transaction in a free market between self-interested legal and
Employment - Wikipedia — economic equals
Employment - Wikipedia — 2. Human resource management (unitarism): employment is a long-term partnership of employees and employers with common interests
Employment - Wikipedia — 3. Pluralist industrial relations: employment is a bargained exchange between stakeholders with some common and some competing economic
Employment - Wikipedia — interests and unequal bargaining power due to imperfect labor markets[44]
Employment - Wikipedia — 4. Critical industrial relations: employment is an unequal power relation between competing groups that is embedded in and inseparable from
Employment - Wikipedia — systemic inequalities throughout the socio-politico-economic system.
Employment - Wikipedia — ese models are important because they help reveal why individuals hold diﬀering perspectives on human resource management policies, labor unions, and
Employment - Wikipedia — employment regulation.[63] For example, human resource management policies are seen as dictated by the market in the ﬁrst view, as essential mechanisms for aligning
Employment - Wikipedia — the interests of employees and employers and thereby creating proﬁtable companies in the second view, as insuﬃcient for looking out for workers’ interests in the third
Employment - Wikipedia — view, and as manipulative managerial tools for shaping the ideology and structure of the workplace in the fourth view.[64]
Employment - Wikipedia — Literature on the employment impact of economic growth and on how growth is associated with employment at a macro, sector and industry level was aggregated in
Employment - Wikipedia — 2013.[65]
Employment - Wikipedia — Researchers found evidence to suggest growth in manufacturing and services have good impact on employment. ey found GDP growth on employment in agriculture
Employment - Wikipedia — to be limited, but that value-added growth had a relatively larger impact.[44] e impact on job creation by industries/economic activities as well as the extent of the
Employment - Wikipedia — body of evidence and the key studies. For extractives, they again found extensive evidence suggesting growth in the sector has limited impact on employment. In
Employment - Wikipedia — textiles, however, although evidence was low, studies suggest growth there positively contributed to job creation. In agri-business and food processing, they found
Employment - Wikipedia — impact growth to be positive.[65]
Employment - Wikipedia — ey found that most available literature focuses on OECD and middle-income countries somewhat, where economic growth impact has been shown to be positive on
Employment - Wikipedia — employment. e researchers didn't ﬁnd suﬃcient evidence to conclude any impact of growth on employment in LDCs despite some pointing to the positive impact,
Employment - Wikipedia — others point to limitations. ey recommended that complementary policies are necessary to ensure economic growth's positive impact on LDC employment. With
Employment - Wikipedia — trade, industry and investment, they only found limited evidence of positive impact on employment from industrial and investment policies and for others, while large
Employment - Wikipedia — bodies of evidence does exist, the exact impact remains contested.[65]
Employment - Wikipedia — Researchers have also explored the relationship between employment and illicit activities. Using evidence from Africa, a research team found that a program for
Employment - Wikipedia — Liberian ex-ﬁghters reduced work hours on illicit activities. e employment program also reduced interest in mercenary work in nearby wars. e study concludes that
Employment - Wikipedia — while the use of capital inputs or cash payments for peaceful work created a reduction in illicit activities, the impact of training alone is rather low.[66]
Employment - Wikipedia — Academic literature
Employment - Wikipedia — e balance of economic eﬃciency and social equity is the ultimate debate in the ﬁeld of employment relations.[67] By meeting the needs of the employer; generating
Employment - Wikipedia — proﬁts to establish and maintain economic eﬃciency; whilst maintaining a balance with the employee and creating social equity that beneﬁts the worker so that he/she
Employment - Wikipedia — can fund and enjoy healthy living; proves to be a continuous revolving issue in westernized societies.[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — Globalization has aﬀected these issues by creating certain economic factors that disallow or allow various employment issues. Economist Edward Lee (1996) studies the
Employment - Wikipedia — eﬀects of globalization and summarizes the four major points of concern that aﬀect employment relations:
Employment - Wikipedia — 1. International competition, from the newly industrialized countries, will cause unemployment growth and increased wage disparity for unskilled
Employment - Wikipedia — workers in industrialized countries. Imports from low-wage countries exert pressure on the manufacturing sector in industrialized countries
Employment - Wikipedia — and foreign direct investment (FDI) is attracted away from the industrialized nations, towards low-waged countries.[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — 2. Economic liberalization will result in unemployment and wage inequality in developing countries. This happens as job losses in uncompetitive
Employment - Wikipedia — industries outstrip job opportunities in new industries.
Employment - Wikipedia — 3. Workers will be forced to accept worsening wages and conditions, as a global labor market results in a “race to the bottom”. Increased
Employment - Wikipedia — international competition creates a pressure to reduce the wages and conditions of workers.[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — 4. Globalization reduces the autonomy of the nation state. Capital is increasingly mobile and the ability of the state to regulate economic activity
Employment - Wikipedia — is reduced.
Employment - Wikipedia — What also results from Lee's (1996) ﬁndings is that in industrialized countries an average of almost 70 per cent of workers are employed in the service sector, most of
Employment - Wikipedia — which consists of non-tradable activities. As a result, workers are forced to become more skilled and develop sought aer trades, or ﬁnd other means of survival.
Employment - Wikipedia — Ultimately this is a result of changes and trends of employment, an evolving workforce, and globalization that is represented by a more skilled and increasing highly
Employment - Wikipedia — diverse labor force, that are growing in non standard forms of employment (Markey, R. et al. 2006).[67]
Employment - Wikipedia — Various youth subcultures have been associated with not working, such as the hippie subculture in the 1960s and 1970s (which endorsed the idea of "dropping out" of
Employment - Wikipedia — society) and the punk subculture.

Employment - Wikipedia — Post-secondary education
Employment - Wikipedia — secondary education is the opportunity cost of forgone wages due to not working. At times when jobs are hard to ﬁnd, such as during recessions, unemployed
Employment - Wikipedia — individuals may decide to get post-secondary education, because there is less of an opportunity cost.
Employment - Wikipedia — In some countries, individuals who are not working can receive social assistance support (e.g., welfare or food stamps) to enable them to rent housing, buy food, repair
Employment - Wikipedia — or replace household goods, maintenance of children and observe social customs that require ﬁnancial expenditure.
Employment - Wikipedia — Workers who are not paid wages, such as volunteers who perform tasks for charities, hospitals or not-for-proﬁt organizations, are generally not considered employed.
Employment - Wikipedia — One exception to this is an internship, an employment situation in which the worker receives training or experience (and possibly college credit) as the chief form of
Employment - Wikipedia — compensation.[68]
Employment - Wikipedia — ose who work under obligation for the purpose of fulﬁlling a debt, such as indentured servants, or as property of the person or entity they work for, such as slaves, do
Employment - Wikipedia — not receive pay for their services and are not considered employed. Some historians suggest that slavery is older than employment, but both arrangements have existed
Employment - Wikipedia — for all recorded history. Indentured servitude and slavery are not considered compatible with human rights or with democracy.[68]
Employment - Wikipedia — Self-employment is the state of working for oneself rather than an employer. Tax authorities will generally view a person as self-employed if the person chooses to be
Employment - Wikipedia — recognised as such or if the person is generating income for which a tax return needs to be ﬁled. In the real world, the critical issue for tax authorities is not whether a
Employment - Wikipedia — person is engaged in business activity (called trading even when referring to the provision of a service) but whether the activity is proﬁtable and therefore potentially
Employment - Wikipedia — taxable. In other words, the trading is likely to be ignored if there is no proﬁt, so occasional and hobby- or enthusiast-based economic activity is generally ignored by
Employment - Wikipedia — tax authorities. Self-employed people are usually classiﬁed as a sole proprietor (or sole trader), independent contractor, or as a member of a partnership.
Employment - Wikipedia — Self-employed people generally ﬁnd their own work rather than being provided with work by an employer and instead earn income from a profession, a trade, or a
Employment - Wikipedia — business that they operate. In some countries, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, the authorities are placing more emphasis on clarifying whether an
Employment - Wikipedia — individual is self-employed or engaged in disguised employment, in other words pretending to be in a contractual intra-business relationship to hide what is in fact an
Employment - Wikipedia — employer-employee relationship.

Work (physics) - Wikipedia — In science, work is the energy transferred to or from an object via the application of force along a displacement. In its
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — simplest form, for a constant force aligned with the direction of motion, the work equals the product of the force
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — strength and the distance traveled. A force is said to do positive work if it has a component in the direction of the
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — displacement of the point of application. A force does negative work if it has a component opposite to the direction of
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — the displacement at the point of application of the force.[1]
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — For example, when a ball is held above the ground and then dropped, the work done by the gravitational force on the
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — ball as it falls is positive, and is equal to the weight of the ball (a force) multiplied by the distance to the ground (a
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — displacement). If the ball is thrown upwards, the work done by the gravitational force is negative, and is equal to the
Work (physics) - Wikipedia — weight multiplied by the displacement in the upwards direction.

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — all their members have died. Period LEB is the mean length of life of a hypothetical cohort[3][4] assumed to be
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — exposed, from birth through death, to the mortality rates observed at a given year.[5] National LEB ﬁgures reported by
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — national agencies and international organizations for human populations are estimates of period LEB.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Human remains from the early Bronze Age indicate an LEB of 24.[6] In 2019, world LEB was 73.3.[7] A combination of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — high infant mortality and deaths in young adulthood from accidents, epidemics, plagues, wars, and childbirth, before
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — modern medicine was widely available, signiﬁcantly lowers LEB. For example, a society with a LEB of 40 would have
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — relatively few people dying at exactly 40: most will die before 30 or aer 55. In populations with high infant mortality
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — rates, LEB is highly sensitive to the rate of death in the ﬁrst few years of life. Because of this sensitivity, LEB can be
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — grossly misinterpreted, leading to the belief that a population with a low LEB would have a small proportion of older
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — people.[8] A diﬀerent measure, such as life expectancy at age 5 (e5), can be used to exclude the eﬀect of infant
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — mortality to provide a simple measure of overall mortality rates other than in early childhood. For instance, in a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — society with a life expectancy of 30, it may nevertheless be common to have a 40-year remaining timespan at age 5
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — (but not a 60-year one).
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Aggregate population measures—such as the proportion of the population in various age groups—are also used
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — alongside individual-based measures—such as formal life expectancy—when analyzing population structure and
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — dynamics. Pre-modern societies had universally higher mortality rates and lower life expectancies at every age for
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — both males and females.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Life expectancy, longevity, and maximum lifespan are not synonymous. Longevity refers to the relatively long
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — lifespan of some members of a population. Maximum lifespan is the age at death for the longest-lived individual of a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — species. Mathematically, life expectancy is denoted
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — [a] and is the mean number of years of life remaining at a given age , with a particular mortality.[9] Because life
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — expectancy is an average, a particular person may die many years before or aer the expected survival.

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — context of manufactured objects,[11] though the related term shelf life is commonly used for consumer products, and the terms "mean time to breakdown" and "mean

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — and longevity also highlighted haem metabolism as an important pathway, and found genetic variants which lower
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — blood protein levels of LPA and VCAM1 were associated with increased healthy lifespan.[104]

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e greater mortality of people with mental disorders may be due to death from injury,

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Education
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — According to a paper from 2015, the mortality rate for the Caucasian population in the United States from 1993 to 2001 is four times higher for those who did not
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — complete high school compared to those who have at least 16 years of education.[135] In fact, within the U.S. adult population, people with less than a high school
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — education have the shortest life expectancies.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Preschool education also plays a large role in life expectancy. It was found that high-quality early-stage childhood education had positive eﬀects on health. Researchers
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — discovered this by analyzing the results of the Carolina Abecedarian Project, ﬁnding that the disadvantaged children who were randomly assigned to treatment had
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — lower instances of risk factors for cardiovascular and metabolic diseases in their mid-30s.[137]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — In June 2024, Italian researchers showed that the Covid-19 mRNA vaccination raised all-cause mortality risks and caused a statistically signiﬁcant loss of life expectancy.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e retrospective cohort study found that the adjusted hazard ratio (HR) in terms of all-cause deaths between those who got two doses of the mRNA vaccine and the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — unvaccinated group was 1.98, and the restricted mean survival time (RMST) diﬀerence was -2.71. e study showed that the restricted mean time lost (RMTL) ratio
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — between the two-dose group and the unvaccinated was 1.37, suggesting that those who received two doses of the shots could lose 37 percent of their life expectancy.[138]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Various species of plants and animals, including humans, have diﬀerent lifespans. Evolutionary theory states that organisms which—by virtue of their defenses or
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — lifestyle—live for long periods and avoid accidents, disease, predation, etc. are likely to have genes that code for slow aging, which oen translates to good cellular
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — repair. One theory is that if predation or accidental deaths prevent most individuals from living to an old age, there will be less natural selection to increase the intrinsic
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — life span.[139] at ﬁnding was supported in a classic study of opossums by Austad;[140] however, the opposite relationship was found in an equally prominent study of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — guppies by Reznick.[141][142]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — One prominent and very popular theory states that lifespan can be lengthened by a tight budget for food energy called caloric restriction.[143] Caloric restriction
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — observed in many animals (most notably mice and rats) shows a near doubling of life span from a very limited caloriﬁc intake. Support for the theory has been bolstered
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — by several new studies linking lower basal metabolic rate to increased life expectancy.[144][145][146] at is the key to why animals like giant tortoises can live so long.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — [147] Studies of humans with life spans of at least 100 have shown a link to decreased thyroid activity, resulting in their lowered metabolic rate.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e ability of skin ﬁbroblasts to perform DNA repair aer UV irradiation was measured in shrew, mouse, rat, hamster, cow, elephant and human.[148] It was found that
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — DNA repair capability increased systematically with species life span. Since this original study in 1974, at least 14 additional studies were performed on mammals to test
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — this correlation.[149] In all, but two of these studies, lifespan correlated with DNA repair levels, suggesting that DNA repair capability contributes to life expectancy.[149]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — See DNA damage theory of aging.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — In a broad survey of zoo animals, no relationship was found between investment of the animal in reproduction and its life span.[150]

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — If the assumption is made that, on average, people live a half year on the year of their death, the complete life expectancy at
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — age would be
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — , which is denoted by e̊x, and is the intuitive deﬁnition of life expectancy.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — By deﬁnition, life expectancy is an arithmetic mean. It can also be calculated by integrating the survival curve from 0 to
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — positive inﬁnity (or equivalently to the maximum lifespan, sometimes called 'omega'). For an extinct or completed cohort (all
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — people born in the year 1850, for example), it can of course simply be calculated by averaging the ages at death. For cohorts with some survivors, it is estimated by using
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — mortality experience in recent years. e estimates are called period cohort life expectancies.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e starting point for calculating life expectancy is the age-speciﬁc death rates of the population members. If a large amount of data is available, a statistical population
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — can be created that allow the age-speciﬁc death rates to be simply taken as the mortality rates actually experienced at each age (the number of deaths divided by the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — number of years "exposed to risk" in each data cell). However, it is customary to apply smoothing to remove (as much as possible) the random statistical ﬂuctuations
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — from one year of age to the next. In the past, a very simple model used for this purpose was the Gompertz function, but more sophisticated methods are now used.[153]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e most common modern methods include:
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — ▪ ﬁtting a mathematical formula (such as the Gompertz function, or an extension of it) to the data.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — ▪ looking at an established mortality table derived from a larger population and making a simple adjustment to it (such as multiplying by a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — constant factor) to ﬁt the data. (In cases of relatively small amounts of data.)
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Calculation
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — A 2024 study estimated that each
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — cigarette reduces life expectancy by 20
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — minutes.[154][155]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — ▪ looking at the mortality rates actually experienced at each age and applying a piecewise model (such as by cubic splines) to ﬁt the data. (In
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — cases of relatively large amounts of data.)
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e age-speciﬁc death rates are calculated separately for separate groups of data that are believed to have diﬀerent mortality
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — rates (such as males and females, or smokers and non-smokers) and are then used to calculate a life table from which one can
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — calculate the probability of surviving to each age. While the data required are easily identiﬁed in the case of humans, the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — computation of life expectancy of industrial products and wild animals involves more indirect techniques. e life expectancy
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — and demography of wild animals are oen estimated by capturing, marking, and recapturing them.[156] e life of a product,
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — more oen termed shelf life, is also computed using similar methods. In the case of long-lived components, such as those
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — used in critical applications (e.g. aircra), methods like accelerated aging are used to model the life expectancy of a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — component.[11]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e life expectancy statistic is usually based on past mortality experience and assumes that the same age-speciﬁc mortality
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — rates will continue. us, such life expectancy ﬁgures need to be adjusted for temporal trends before calculating how long a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — currently living individual of a particular age is expected to live. Period life expectancy remains a commonly used statistic to
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — summarize the current health status of a population. However, for some purposes, such as pensions calculations, it is usual to
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — adjust the life table used by assuming that age-speciﬁc death rates will continue to decrease over the years, as they have
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — usually done in the past. at is oen done by simply extrapolating past trends, but some models exist to account for the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — evolution of mortality, like the Lee–Carter model.[157]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — As discussed above, on an individual basis, some factors correlate with longer life. Factors that are associated with variations in life expectancy include family history,
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — marital status, economic status, physique, exercise, diet, drug use (including smoking and alcohol consumption), disposition, education, environment, sleep, climate, and
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — health care.[14]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — To assess the quality of these additional years of life, 'healthy life expectancy' has been calculated for the last 30 years. Since 2001, the World Health Organization has
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — published statistics called Healthy life expectancy (HALE), deﬁned as the average number of years that a person can expect to live in "full health" excluding the years
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — lived in less than full health due to disease and/or injury.[158][159] Since 2004, Eurostat publishes annual statistics called Healthy Life Years (HLY) based on reported
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — activity limitations. e United States uses similar indicators in the framework of the national health promotion and disease prevention plan "Healthy People 2010".
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — More and more countries are using health expectancy indicators to monitor the health of their population.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Healthy life expectancy
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — e long-standing quest for longer life led in the 2010s to a more promising focus on increasing HALE, also known as a person's "healthspan". Besides the beneﬁts of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — keeping people healthier longer, a goal is to reduce health-care expenses on the many diseases associated with cellular senescence. Approaches being explored include
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — fasting, exercise, and senolytic drugs.[160]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Forecasting life expectancy and mortality form an important subdivision of demography. Future trends in life expectancy have huge implications for old-age support
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — programs (like U.S. Social Security and pension) since the cash ﬂow in these systems depends on the number of recipients who are still living (along with the rate of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — return on the investments or the tax rate in pay-as-you-go systems). With longer life expectancies, the systems see increased cash outﬂow; if the systems underestimate
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — increases in life-expectancies, they will be unprepared for the large payments that will occur, as humans live longer and longer.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Life expectancy forecasting is usually based on one of two diﬀerent approaches:
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — 1. Forecasting the life expectancy directly, generally using ARIMA or other time-series extrapolation procedures. This has the advantage of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — simplicity, but it cannot account for changes in mortality at speciﬁc ages, and the forecast number cannot be used to derive other life table
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — results. Analyses and forecasts using this approach can be done with any common statistical/mathematical software package, like EViews, R,
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — SAS, Stata, Matlab, or SPSS.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — 2. Forecasting age-speciﬁc death rates and computing the life expectancy from the results with life table methods. This is usually more complex
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — than simply forecasting life expectancy because the analyst must deal with correlated age-speciﬁc mortality rates, but it seems to be more
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — robust than simple one-dimensional time series approaches. It also yields a set of age-speciﬁc rates that may be used to derive other
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — measures, such as survival curves or life expectancies at diﬀerent ages. The most important approach in this group is the Lee-Carter model,[161]

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — "Remaining" life expectancy—expected
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — number of remaining years of life as a
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — function of current age—is used in
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — retirement income planning.[165]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — which uses the singular value decomposition on a set of transformed age-speciﬁc mortality rates to reduce their dimensionality to a single time
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — series, forecasts that time series, and then recovers a full set of age-speciﬁc mortality rates from that forecasted value. The software includes
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Professor Rob J. Hyndman's R package called 'demography' (https://web.archive.org/web/20100822170736/http://robjhyndman.com/software/
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — demography/) and UC Berkeley's LCFIT system (http://lcﬁt.demog.berkeley.edu/).

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — of the lifespans of all individuals, including those who die before adulthood. One may compare the life expectancy of the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — period aer childhood to estimate also the life expectancy of an adult.[166]

Life expectancy - Wikipedia — A further concept is that of modal age at death, the single age when deaths among a population are more numerous than at
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — any other age. In all pre-modern societies the most common age at death is the ﬁrst year of life: it is only as infant mortality
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — falls below around 33–34 per thousand (roughly a tenth of estimated ancient and medieval levels) that deaths in a later year
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — of life (usually around age 80) become more numerous. While the most common age of death in adulthood among modern
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — hunter-gatherers (oen taken as a guide to the likely most favourable Paleolithic demographic experience) is estimated to
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — average 72 years,[169] the number dying at that age is dwarfed by those (over a ﬁh of all infants) dying in the ﬁrst year of
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — life, and only around a quarter usually survive to the higher age.
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — Maximum life span is an individual-speciﬁc concept, and therefore is an upper bound rather than an average.[166] Science author Christopher Wanjek writes, "[H]as the
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — human race increased its life span? Not at all. is is one of the biggest misconceptions about old age: we are not living any longer." e maximum life span, or oldest
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — age a human can live, may be constant.[166] Further, there are many examples of people living signiﬁcantly longer than the average life expectancy of their time period,
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — such as Socrates (71), Saint Anthony the Great (105), Michelangelo (88), and John Adams (90).[166]
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — However, anthropologist John D. Hawks criticizes the popular conﬂation of life span (life expectancy) and maximum life span when popular science writers falsely
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — imply that the average adult human does not live longer than their ancestors. He writes, "[a]ge-speciﬁc mortality rates have declined across the adult lifespan. A smaller
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — fraction of adults die at 20, at 30, at 40, at 50, and so on across the lifespan. As a result, we live longer on average… In every way we can measure, human lifespans are
Life expectancy - Wikipedia — longer today than in the immediate past, and longer today than they were 2000 years ago… age-speciﬁc mortality rates in adults really have reduced substantially."[170]

Everyday life - Wikipedia — example, nomadic life diﬀers from sedentism, and among the sedentary, urban people live diﬀerently

Everyday life - Wikipedia — Everyday life is a key concept in cultural studies and is a specialized subject in the ﬁeld of sociology. Some argue that, motivated by capitalism and industrialism's
Everyday life - Wikipedia — degrading eﬀects on human existence and perception, writers and artists of the 19th century turned more towards self-reﬂection and the portrayal of everyday life
Everyday life - Wikipedia — represented in their writings and art to a noticeably greater degree than in past works, for example Renaissance literature's interest in hagiography and politics.[1] Other
Everyday life - Wikipedia — theorists dispute this argument based on a long history of writings about daily life which can be seen in works from Ancient Greece, medieval Christianity and the Age
Everyday life - Wikipedia — of Enlightenment.[2][3]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — In the study of everyday life, gender has been an important factor in its conceptions. Some theorists regard women as the quintessential representatives and victims of
Everyday life - Wikipedia — everyday life.[2]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — e connotation of everyday life is oen negative, and is distinctively separated from exceptional moments by its lack of distinction and diﬀerentiation. Ultimately this
Everyday life - Wikipedia — is deﬁned as the essential, taken-for-granted continuum of mundane activity that outlines forays into more esoteric experiences. It is the non-negotiable reality that
Everyday life - Wikipedia — exists amongst all social groupings without discrimination and is an unavoidable basis for which all human endeavor exists.[1]
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Much of everyday life is automatic in that it is driven by current environmental features as mediated by automatic cognitive processing of those features, and without
Everyday life - Wikipedia — any mediation by conscious choice, according to social psychologist John A. Bargh.[4] Daily life is also studied by sociologists to investigate how it is organised and
Everyday life - Wikipedia — given meaning. A sociological journal called the Journal of Mundane Behavior,[5] published from 2000 to 2004, studied these everyday actions.

Everyday life - Wikipedia — Activities of daily living (ADL) is a term used in healthcare to refer to daily self care activities within an individual's place of residence, in outdoor environments, or both.
Everyday life - Wikipedia — Health professionals routinely refer to the ability or inability to perform ADLs as a measurement of the functional status of a person, particularly in regard to people
Everyday life - Wikipedia — with disabilities and the elderly.[10] ADLs are deﬁned as "the things we normally do…such as feeding ourselves, bathing, dressing, grooming, work, homemaking, and
Everyday life - Wikipedia — leisure".[11] e ability and the extent to which the elderly can perform these activities is at the focus of gerontology and understandings of later life.[12]

Personal life - Wikipedia — Personal life
Personal life - Wikipedia — Personal life is the course or state of an individual's life, especially when viewed as the sum of personal choices
Personal life - Wikipedia — contributing to one's personal identity.[1]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Apart from hunter-gatherers, most pre-modern peoples' time was limited by the need to meet necessities such as food and
Personal life - Wikipedia — shelter through subsistence farming; leisure time was scarce.[2] People identiﬁed with their social role in their community
Personal life - Wikipedia — and engaged in activities based on necessity rather than on personal choice. Privacy in such communities was rare.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e modern conception of "personal life" is an oﬀshoot of modern Western society. Modern people tend to distinguish their
Personal life - Wikipedia — work activities from their personal life and may seek work–life balance.[3] It is a person's choices and preferences outside of
Personal life - Wikipedia — work that deﬁne personal life, including one's choice of hobbies, cultural interests, manner of dress, mate, friends, and so on.
Personal life - Wikipedia — In particular, what activities one engages in during leisure-time deﬁnes a person's personal life. Religious authorities,
Personal life - Wikipedia — moralists, managers and personal-development gurus have seized on the concept of an individual life as a fulcrum for
Personal life - Wikipedia — potential control and manipulation.[4][5][6]
Personal life - Wikipedia — People in Western countries, such as the United States and Canada, tend to value privacy. Privacy includes both information
Personal life - Wikipedia — privacy and decisional privacy; people expect to be le alone with respect to intimate details of their life and they expect to
Personal life - Wikipedia — be free from undue control by others.[7]
Personal life - Wikipedia — In the past, before modern technology largely alleviated issues of economic scarcity in industrialised countries, most people spent a large portion of their time
Personal life - Wikipedia — aempting to provide their basic survival needs, including water, food, and protection from the weather.[8] Humans needed survival skills for the sake of both
Personal life - Wikipedia — themselves and their community; food needed to be harvested and shelters needed to be maintained.[9] ere was lile privacy in a community, and people identiﬁed
Personal life - Wikipedia — one another according to their social role.[10] Jobs were assigned out of necessity rather than personal choice.[11]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Furthermore, individuals in many ancient cultures primarily viewed their self-existence under the aspect of a larger social whole, oen one with mythological
Personal life - Wikipedia — underpinnings which placed the individual in relation to the cosmos.[12] People in such cultures found their identity not through their individual choices—indeed, they
Personal life - Wikipedia — may not have been able to conceive a choice which was purely individual. Such individuals, if asked to describe themselves, would speak of the collective of which they
Personal life - Wikipedia — were part: the tribe, the Church, the nation.[13] Even in the 21st century, survival issues dominate in many countries and societies. For example, the continents of Africa
Personal life - Wikipedia — and Asia are still largely mired in poverty and third-world conditions, without technology, secure shelter, or reliable food sources. In such places, the concepts of a
Personal life - Wikipedia — "personal life", "self-actualization", "personal fulﬁllment", or "privacy" are oen unaﬀordable luxuries.[14]

Personal life - Wikipedia — e English philosopher John Locke (1632–1704) gures among the pioneers in discussing the concept of individual rights. In
Personal life - Wikipedia — the 17th century he promoted the natural rights of the individual to life, liberty, and property, and included the pursuit of
Personal life - Wikipedia — happiness as one of the individual's goals.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e notion of a personal life, as currently understood in the west is in part an artefact of modern Western society. People in
Personal life - Wikipedia — the United States of America, especially, place a high value on privacy. Since the colonial period, commentators have noted
Personal life - Wikipedia — Americans' individualism and their pursuit of self-deﬁnition.[15][16] Indeed, the United States Declaration of Independence
Personal life - Wikipedia — and the Constitution explicitly raise the pursuit of happiness and the expectation of privacy to the level of rights.
Personal life - Wikipedia — George Lakoﬀ sees the metaphor of life as "a journey" as a noteworthy structuring idea in "our culture".[17] Compare the
Personal life - Wikipedia — traditional Chinese concept of tao.
Personal life - Wikipedia — In modern times, many people have come to think of their personal lives as separate from their work.[18] is 9 to 5 paradigm
Personal life - Wikipedia — regards work and recreation as distinct; one is either on the job or not, and the transition is abrupt. Employees have certain
Personal life - Wikipedia — hours they are bound to work, and work during recreational time is rare. is may reﬂect the continuing specialisation of
Personal life - Wikipedia — jobs and the demand for increased eﬃciency, both at work and at home. e common phrase "Work hard, play hard"
Personal life - Wikipedia — illustrates this mindset. ere is a growing trend, however, towards living more holistically and minimising such rigid
Personal life - Wikipedia — distinctions between work and play, in order to achieve an "appropriate" work–life balance.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e concept of personal life also tends to be associated with the way individuals dress, the food they eat, their schooling and
Personal life - Wikipedia — further education as well as their hobbies, leisure activities, and cultural interests. Increasingly, in the developed world, a
Personal life - Wikipedia — person's daily life is also inﬂuenced by leisure-time use of consumer electronics such as televisions, computers and the
Personal life - Wikipedia — Internet, mobile phones and digital cameras.[19]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Other factors aﬀecting personal life include individuals' health, personal relationships, pets as well as home and personal possessions.
Personal life - Wikipedia — e way in which individuals make use of their spare time also plays an important role in deﬁning their personal lives. In general, leisure activities can be categorised as
Personal life - Wikipedia — either passive, in cases when no real eﬀort is required, or active, when substantial physical or mental energy is needed.[20]
Personal life - Wikipedia — Passive activities include watching television, listening to music, watching sports activities or going to the cinema. e individual simply relaxes without any special
Personal life - Wikipedia — eﬀort.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Meaning of life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e meaning of life is the concept of an individual's life, or existence in general, having an inherent signiﬁcance or a philosophical point. ere is no consensus on the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — speciﬁcs of such a concept or whether the concept itself even exists in any objective sense. inking and discourse on the topic is sought in the English language
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — through questions such as—but not limited to—"What is the meaning of life?", "What is the purpose of existence?", and "Why are we here?". ere have been many
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — proposed answers to these questions from many diﬀerent cultural and ideological backgrounds. e search for life's meaning has produced much philosophical,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — scientiﬁc, theological, and metaphysical speculation throughout history. Diﬀerent people and cultures believe diﬀerent things for the answer to this question. Opinions
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — vary on the usefulness of using time and resources in the pursuit of an answer. Excessive pondering can be indicative of, or lead to, an existential crisis.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e meaning of life can be derived from philosophical and religious contemplation of, and scientiﬁc inquiries about, existence, social ties, consciousness, and happiness.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Many other issues are also involved, such as symbolic meaning, ontology, value, purpose, ethics, good and evil, free will, the existence of one or multiple gods,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — conceptions of God, the soul, and the aerlife. Scientiﬁc contributions focus primarily on describing related empirical facts about the universe, exploring the context and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — parameters concerning the "how" of life. Science also studies and can provide recommendations for the pursuit of well-being and a related conception of morality. An
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — alternative, humanistic approach poses the question, "What is the meaning of my life?"
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst English use of the expression "meaning of life" appears in omas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus (1833–1834), book II chapter IX, "e Everlasting Yea".[1]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Our Life is compassed round with Necessity; yet is the meaning of Life itself no other than Freedom, than Voluntary Force: thus have we a warfare; in the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — beginning, especially, a hard-fought bale.[2]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Carlyle may have been inspired by earlier usage of the equivalent German expression der Sinn des Lebens by German Romantic writers Novalis and Friedrich Schlegel.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Schlegel was the ﬁrst to use it in print by way of his novel Lucinde (1799), though Novalis had done so in a 1797–1798 manuscript, in which he wrote: "Only an artist can
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — divine the meaning of life." Additionally, the word lebenssinn, translated as life's meaning, had been used by Goethe in a 1796 leer to Schiller.[3] ese authors grappled
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — with the rationalism and materialism of modernity. Carlyle called this the "Torch of Science", which burned "more ﬁercely than ever" and made religion "all parched
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — away, under the Droughts of practical and spiritual Unbelief", resulting in the "Wilderness" of "the wide World in an Atheistic Century".[4]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Arthur Schopenhauer was the ﬁrst to explicitly ask the question,[1] in an essay entitled "Character".

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Socrates
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Since a man does not alter, and his moral character remains absolutely the same all through his life; since he must play out
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the part which he has received, without the least deviation from the character; since neither experience, nor philosophy,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — nor religion can eﬀect any improvement in him, the question arises, What is the meaning of life at all? To what
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — purpose is it played, this farce in which everything that is essential is irrevocably ﬁxed and determined?[5]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — estions about the meaning of life, and similar, have been expressed in a broad variety of other ways, including:
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the meaning of life? What's it all about? Who are we?[6][7][8]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ Why are we here? What are we here for?[9][10][11]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the origin of life?[12]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the nature of life? What is the nature of reality?[12][13][14]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the signiﬁcance of life?[16] (See also #Psychological signiﬁcance and value in life)
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is meaningful and valuable in life?[17]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the value of life?[18]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ What is the reason to live? What are we living for?[11][19]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ese questions have resulted in a wide range of competing answers and explications, from scientiﬁc theories, to philosophical, theological, and spiritual explanations.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Many members of the scientiﬁc community and philosophy of science communities think that science can provide the relevant context, and set of parameters necessary
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — for dealing with topics related to the meaning of life. In their view, science can oﬀer a wide range of insights on topics ranging from the science of happiness to death
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — anxiety. Scientiﬁc inquiry facilitates this through nomological investigation into various aspects of life and reality, such as the Big Bang, the origin of life, and evolution,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — and by studying the objective factors which correlate with the subjective experience of meaning and happiness.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Researchers in positive psychology study empirical factors that lead to life satisfaction,[20] full engagement in activities,[21] making a fuller contribution by using one's
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — personal strengths,[22] and meaning based on investing in something larger than the self.[23] Large-data studies of ﬂow experiences have consistently suggested that
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — humans experience meaning and fulﬁllment when mastering challenging tasks and that the experience comes from the way tasks are approached and performed rather
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — than the particular choice of task. For example, ﬂow experiences can be obtained by prisoners in concentration camps with minimal facilities, and occur only slightly
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — more oen in billionaires. A classic example[21] is of two workers on an apparently boring production line in a factory. One treats the work as a tedious chore while the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — other turns it into a game to see how fast they can make each unit and achieves ﬂow in the process.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Scientiﬁc inquiry and perspectives
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Psychological signiﬁcance and value in life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Neuroscience describes reward, pleasure, and motivation in terms of neurotransmier activity, especially in the limbic system and the ventral tegmental area in
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — particular. If one believes that the meaning of life is to maximize pleasure and to ease general life, then this allows normative predictions about how to act to achieve
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — this. Likewise, some ethical naturalists advocate a science of morality—the empirical pursuit of ﬂourishing for all conscious creatures.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Experimental philosophy and neuroethics research collects data about human ethical decisions in controlled scenarios such as trolley problems. It has shown that many
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — types of ethical judgment are universal across cultures, suggesting that they may be innate, whilst others are culture-speciﬁc. e ﬁndings show actual human ethical
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reasoning to be at odds with most philosophical theories, for example consistently showing distinctions between action by cause and action by omission which would
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — be absent from utility-based theories. Cognitive science has theorized about diﬀerences between conservative and liberal ethics and how they may be based on diﬀerent
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — metaphors from family life such as strong fathers vs nurturing mother models.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Neurotheology is a controversial ﬁeld which tries to ﬁnd neural correlates and mechanisms of religious experience. Some researchers have suggested that the human
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — brain has innate mechanisms for such experiences and that living without using them for their evolved purposes may be a cause of imbalance. Studies have reported
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — conﬂicting results on correlating happiness with religious belief and it is diﬃcult to ﬁnd unbiased meta-analyses.[24][25]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Sociology examines value at a social level using theoretical constructs such as value theory, norms, anomie, etc. One value system suggested by social psychologists,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — broadly called Terror Management eory, states that human meaning is derived from a fundamental fear of death, and values are selected when they allow us to escape
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the mental reminder of death.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Alongside this, there are a number of theories about the way in which humans evaluate the positive and negative aspects of their existence and thus the value and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — meaning they place on their lives. For example, depressive realism posits an exaggerated positivity in all except those experiencing depressive disorders who see life as
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — it truly is, and David Benatar theorises that more weight is generally given to positive experiences, providing bias towards an over-optimistic view of life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Emerging research shows that meaning in life predicts beer physical health outcomes. Greater meaning has been associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — [26][27] reduced risk of heart aack among individuals with coronary heart disease,[28] reduced risk of stroke,[29] and increased longevity in both American and Japanese
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — samples.[30] ere is also growing evidence for a small decline in purpose in life in the early stages of cognitive impairment.[31]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In 2014, the British National Health Service began recommending a ﬁve-step plan for mental well-being based on meaningful lives, whose steps are:[32]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 1. Connect with community and family
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 2. Physical exercise
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 3. Lifelong learning
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 4. Giving to others
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 5. Mindfulness of the world around you
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e exact mechanisms of abiogenesis are unknown: notable hypotheses include the RNA world hypothesis (RNA-based replicators) and the iron-sulfur world hypothesis
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Origin and nature of biological life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — DNA contains the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — genetic instructions
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — for the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — development and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — functioning of all
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — known organisms.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — (metabolism without genetics). e process by which diﬀerent lifeforms have developed throughout history via genetic mutation and natural
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — selection is explained by evolution.[33] At the end of the 20th century, based upon insight gleaned from the gene-centered view of evolution,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — biologists George C. Williams, Richard Dawkins, and David Haig, among others, concluded that if there is a primary function to life, it is the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — replication of DNA and the survival of one's genes.[34][35] Responding to an interview question from Richard Dawkins about "what it is all for",
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — James Watson stated "I don't think we're for anything. We're just the products of evolution."[36]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ough scientists have intensively studied life on Earth, deﬁning life in unequivocal terms is still a challenge.[37][38] Physically, one may say
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — that life "feeds on negative entropy"[39][40][41] which refers to the process by which living entities decrease their internal entropy at the expense
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — of some form of energy taken in from the environment.[42][43][44] Biologists generally agree that lifeforms are self-organizing systems which
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — regulate their internal environments as to maintain this organized state, metabolism serves to provide energy, and reproduction causes life to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — continue over a span of multiple generations. Typically, organisms are responsive to stimuli and genetic information changes from generation
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — to generation, resulting in adaptation through evolution; this optimizes the chances of survival for the individual organism and its descendants
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — respectively.[45]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Non-cellular replicating agents, notably viruses, are generally not considered to be organisms because they are incapable of independent
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reproduction or metabolism. is classiﬁcation is problematic, though, since some parasites and endosymbionts are also incapable of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — independent life. Astrobiology studies the possibility of diﬀerent forms of life on other worlds, including replicating structures made from
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — materials other than DNA.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — All forms of life that are in existence today possess a self-replicating informational molecule (genome), and such an informational molecule is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — presumably intrinsic to life. us the earliest forms of life also likely possessed a self-replicating informational molecule, possibly RNA[46][47] or
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — perhaps an informational molecule more primitive than RNA. e speciﬁc genomic sequences in all currently extant organisms contain order
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — generating information that promotes survival, reproduction, and the ability to acquire resources necessary for reproduction. Sequences with
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — such basic functions probably emerged early in the evolution of life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — It has been proposed[48] that both the evolution of macroscopic order in life (including its basic functions) and the evolution of order in particular physical systems obey
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — a common fundamental principle that was termed the Darwinian dynamic. is principal was formulated by considering, ﬁrst, how macroscopic order is generated in a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — simple physical, non-biological system far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and then extending consideration to short RNA replicating molecules and then further to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — more complex forms of life. It was concluded that the fundamental order-generating process was basically similar for both types of process.[48][49] us the idea that life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — likely emerged as a natural extension of simpler non- or pre-biological physical processes should logically be included in the concept "meaning of life".
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ough the Big Bang theory was met with much skepticism when ﬁrst introduced, it has become well-supported by several independent observations.[50] However,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — current physics can only describe the early universe from around 10−43 seconds aer the Big Bang (where zero time corresponds to inﬁnite temperature); a theory of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — quantum gravity would be required to understand events before that time. Nevertheless, many physicists have speculated about what would have preceded this limit,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — and how the universe came into being.[51] For example, one interpretation is that the Big Bang occurred coincidentally, and when considering the anthropic principle, it
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — is sometimes interpreted as implying the existence of a multiverse.[52]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Crunch.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — eoretical cosmology studies many alternative speculative models for the origin and fate of the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — universe beyond the Big Bang theory. A recent trend has been models of the creation of 'baby
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — universes' inside black holes, with our own Big Bang being a white hole on the inside of a black hole
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — in another parent universe.[53] Many-worlds theories claim that every possibility of quantum
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — mechanics is played out in parallel universes.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e nature and origin of consciousness and the mind are also widely debated in science. e
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — explanatory gap is generally equated with the hard problem of consciousness, and the question of free
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — will is also considered to be of fundamental importance. ese subjects are mostly addressed in the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ﬁelds of cognitive science, neuroscience (e.g. the neuroscience of free will) and philosophy of mind,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — though some evolutionary biologists and theoretical physicists have also made several allusions to the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — subject.[54][55]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Reductionistic and eliminative materialistic approaches, for example the Multiple Dras Model, hold that consciousness can be wholly explained by neuroscience
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — through the workings of the brain and its neurons, thus adhering to biological naturalism.[55][56][57]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — On the other hand, some scientists, like Andrei Linde, have considered that consciousness, like spacetime, might have its own intrinsic degrees of freedom, and that
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — one's perceptions may be as real as (or even more real than) material objects.[58] Hypotheses of consciousness and spacetime explain consciousness in describing a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — "space of conscious elements",[58] oen encompassing a number of extra dimensions.[59] Electromagnetic theories of consciousness solve the binding problem of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — consciousness in saying that the electromagnetic ﬁeld generated by the brain is the actual carrier of conscious experience; there is however disagreement about the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — implementations of such a theory relating to other workings of the mind.[60][61] antum mind theories use quantum theory in explaining certain properties of the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — mind. Explaining the process of free will through quantum phenomena is an alternative to determinism.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Based on the premises of non-materialistic explanations of the mind, some have suggested the existence of a cosmic consciousness, asserting that consciousness is
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — actually the "ground of all being".[14][62][63] Proponents of this view cite accounts of paranormal phenomena, primarily extrasensory perceptions and psychic powers, as
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — evidence for an incorporeal higher consciousness. In hopes of proving the existence of these phenomena, parapsychologists have orchestrated various experiments, but
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — successful results might be due to poor experimental controls and might have alternative explanations.[64][65][66][67]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Nature of meaning in life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Reker and Wong deﬁne personal meaning as the "cognizance of order, coherence and purpose in one's existence, the pursuit and aainment of worthwhile goals, and an
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — accompanying sense of fulﬁllment" (p. 221).[68] In 2016, Martela and Steger deﬁned meaning as coherence, purpose, and signiﬁcance.[69] In contrast, Wong has proposed
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — a four-component solution to the question of meaning in life,[70][71] with the four components purpose, understanding, responsibility, and enjoyment (PURE):
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 1. You need to choose a worthy purpose or a signiﬁcant life goal.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 2. You need to have suﬃcient understanding of who you are, what life demands of you, and how you can play a signiﬁcant role in life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 3. You and you alone are responsible for deciding what kind of life you want to live, and what constitutes a signiﬁcant and worthwhile life goal.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — 4. You will enjoy a deep sense of signiﬁcance and satisfaction only when you have exercised your responsibility for self-determination and actively
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — pursue a worthy life-goal.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — us, a sense of signiﬁcance permeates every dimension of meaning, rather than standing as a separate factor.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Although most psychology researchers consider meaning in life as a subjective feeling or judgment, most philosophers (e.g., addeus Metz, Daniel Haybron) propose
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — that there are also objective, concrete criteria for what constitutes meaning in life.[72][73] Wong has proposed that whether life is meaningful depends not only on
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — subjective feelings but, more importantly, on whether a person's goal-striving and life as a whole is meaningful according to some objective normative standard.[71]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e philosophical perspectives on the meaning of life are those ideologies that explain life in terms of ideals or abstractions deﬁned by humans.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Plato, a pupil of Socrates, was one of the earliest, most inﬂuential philosophers. His reputation comes from his idealism of believing in the existence of universals. His
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — theory of forms proposes that universals do not physically exist, like objects, but as heavenly forms. In the dialogue of the Republic, the character of Socrates describes
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the Form of the Good. His theory on justice in the soul relates to the idea of happiness relevant to the question of the meaning of life.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — In Platonism, the meaning of life is in aaining the highest form of knowledge, which is the Idea (Form) of the Good, from which all good and just things derive utility
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — and value.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Aristotle, an apprentice of Plato, was another early and inﬂuential philosopher, who argued that ethical knowledge is not certain knowledge (such as metaphysics and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — epistemology), but is general knowledge. Because it is not a theoretical discipline, a person had to study and practice in order to become "good"; thus if the person were
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — to become virtuous, he could not simply study what virtue is, he had to be virtuous, via virtuous activities. To do this, Aristotle established what is virtuous:

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — — Nicomachean Ethics 1.1
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Yet, if action A is done towards achieving goal B, then goal B also would have a goal, goal C, and goal C also would have a goal, and so
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — would continue this paern, until something stopped its inﬁnite regression. Aristotle's solution is the Highest Good, which is desirable
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — for its own sake. It is its own goal. e Highest Good is not desirable for the sake of achieving some other good, and all other "goods"
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — desirable for its sake. is involves achieving eudaemonia, usually translated as "happiness", "well-being", "ﬂourishing", and "excellence".
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — What is the highest good in all maers of action? To the name, there is an almost complete agreement; for uneducated and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — educated alike call it happiness, and make happiness identical with the good life and successful living. ey disagree, however,
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — about the meaning of happiness.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — — Nicomachean Ethics 1.4
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Antisthenes, a pupil of Socrates, ﬁrst outlined the themes of Cynicism, stating that the purpose of life is living a life of Virtue which agrees with Nature. Happiness
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — depends upon being self-suﬃcient and master of one's mental aitude; suﬀering is the consequence of false judgments of value, which cause negative emotions and a
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — concomitant vicious character.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e Cynical life rejects conventional desires for wealth, power, health, and fame, by being free of the possessions acquired in pursuing the conventional.[74][75] As
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reasoning creatures, people could achieve happiness via rigorous training, by living in a way natural to human beings. e world equally belongs to everyone, so
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — suﬀering is caused by false judgments of what is valuable and what is worthless per the customs and conventions of society.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Aristippus of Cyrene, a pupil of Socrates, founded an early Socratic school that emphasized only one side of Socrates's teachings—that happiness is one of the ends of
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — moral action and that pleasure is the supreme good; thus a hedonistic world view, wherein bodily gratiﬁcation is more intense than mental pleasure. Cyrenaics prefer
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — immediate gratiﬁcation to the long-term gain of delayed gratiﬁcation; denial is unpleasant unhappiness.[76][77]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Epicurus, a pupil of the Platonist Pamphilus of Samos, taught that the greatest good is in seeking modest pleasures, to aain tranquility and freedom from fear (ataraxia)
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — via knowledge, friendship, and virtuous, temperate living; bodily pain (aponia) is absent through one's knowledge of the workings of the world and of the limits of one's
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — desires. Combined, freedom from pain and freedom from fear are happiness in its highest form. Epicurus' lauded enjoyment of simple pleasures is quasi-ascetic

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Kantianism is a philosophy based on the ethical, epistemological, and metaphysical works of Immanuel Kant. Kant is known for his
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — deontological theory where there is a single moral obligation, the "Categorical Imperative", derived from the concept of duty. Kantians
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — believe all actions are performed in accordance with some underlying maxim or principle, and for actions to be ethical, they must
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — adhere to the categorical imperative.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Simply put, the test is that one must universalize the maxim (imagine that all people acted in this way) and then see if it would still be
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — possible to perform the maxim in the world without contradiction. In Groundwork, Kant gives the example of a person who seeks to
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — borrow money without intending to pay it back. is is a contradiction because if it were a universal action, no person would lend
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — money anymore as he knows that he will never be paid back. e maxim of this action, says Kant, results in a contradiction in
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — conceivability (and thus contradicts perfect duty).
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Kant also denied that the consequences of an act in any way contribute to the moral worth of that act, his reasoning being that the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — physical world is outside one's full control and thus one cannot be held accountable for the events that occur in it.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e ﬁrst English use of the expression "meaning of life" appeared in omas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus (1833–August 1834): "Our Life is compassed round with Necessity;
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — yet is the meaning of Life itself no other than Freedom, than Voluntary Force: thus have we a warfare; in the beginning, especially, a hard-fought bale."[80]
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — e origins of utilitarianism can be traced back as far as Epicurus, but, as a school of thought, it is credited to Jeremy Bentham,[81] who
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — found that "nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure"; then, from that moral
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — insight, he derived the Rule of Utility: "that the good is whatever brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number of people". He
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — deﬁned the meaning of life as the "greatest happiness principle".
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Jeremy Bentham's foremost proponent was James Mill, a signiﬁcant philosopher in his day, and father of John Stuart Mill. e younger
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Mill was educated per Bentham's principles, including transcribing and summarizing much of his father's work.[82]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — nihilist as a natural result of the idea that God is dead, and insisting it was something to overcome, his questioning of the nihilist's life-
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — negating values returned meaning to the Earth.[84]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Pragmatism originated in the late-19th-century US, concerning itself (mostly) with truth, and positing that "only in struggling
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — with the environment" do data, and derived theories, have meaning, and that consequences, like utility and practicality, are
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — also components of truth. Moreover, pragmatism posits that anything useful and practical is not always true, arguing that
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — what most contributes to the most human good in the long course is true. In practice, theoretical claims must be practically
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — veriﬁable, i.e. one should be able to predict and test claims, and, that, ultimately, the needs of humankind should guide human intellectual inquiry.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Pragmatic philosophers suggest that the practical, useful understanding of life is more important than searching for an impractical abstract truth about life. William
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — James argued that truth could be made, but not sought.[89][90] To a pragmatist, the meaning of life is discoverable only via experience.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — free will, and the concomitant awareness of death. According to Jean-Paul Sartre, existence precedes essence; the (essence) of one's life
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — arises only aer one comes to existence.

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ Suicide (or, "escaping existence"): a solution in which a person simply ends one's own life. Both
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Kierkegaard and Camus dismiss the viability of this option.
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — ▪ Religious belief in a transcendent realm or being: a solution in which one believes in the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — existence of a reality that is beyond the Absurd, and, as such, has meaning. Kierkegaard stated
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — that a belief in anything beyond the Absurd requires a non-rational but perhaps necessary
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — religious acceptance in such an intangible and empirically unprovable thing (now commonly
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — referred to as a "leap of faith"). However, Camus regarded this solution as "philosophical
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — suicide".

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — continues to live in spite of it. Camus endorsed this solution (notably in his 1947 allegorical novel The Plague or La Peste), while Kierkegaard

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — Per secular humanism, the human species came to be by reproducing successive generations in a progression of unguided evolution as

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — lives of personal fulﬁllment that aspire to the greater good of humanity".[99] Humanism aims to promote enlightened self-interest and
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — the common good for all people. It is based on the premises that the happiness of the individual person is inextricably linked to the
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — well-being of all humanity, in part because humans are social animals who ﬁnd meaning in personal relations and because cultural
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — progress beneﬁts everybody living in the culture.[98][99]

Meaning of life - Wikipedia — reconstruction of meaning by individuals (as in deconstructionism) to theories in which individuals are primarily extensions of language and society, without real
Meaning of life - Wikipedia — autonomy (as in poststructuralism).
